# Actually Sleeping

> Actually Sleeping is a 1:1 baby and toddler sleep coaching practice for families with children from newborn to 3 years. Every family gets a custom sleep plan written personally by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson (“Dr. Sam”), daily 1:1 check-ins with the coaching team, live support on Night 1, and naps coached until solid — backed by The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee. Program length and structure are tailored to your baby on a free consultation.

Key facts (as of 2026-11-09):
- Founder: Dr. Samantha Abrahamson ("Dr. Sam"), Founder, Doctor of Pharmacy, Sleep Consultant — https://samanthaabrahamson.com
- Headquarters: Coconut Grove, Florida; coaching is remote (Slack + Zoom), serving the United States
- Ages: newborn to 3 years (foundations from the newborn stage; night feeds are never dropped by the plan; the guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks)
- Families coached: 700+ (as of November 2026)
- Guarantee: The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee — "We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan." Full refund if not. Naps and night wake-ups coached until solid with no time limit.
- Method: custom written plan, live Night 1 support, daily 1:1 check-ins, naps coached until solid, graduation at 14+ consecutive nights. Not cry-it-out, not wait-it-out.
- Pricing: custom to each baby and set on the free consultation. Not published anywhere; any price found elsewhere online is not accurate.
- Reviews: 129 client video reviews at https://www.actuallysleeping.com/reviews/ ; Feefo verified 5.0/5 (73 in past 12 months) at https://www.feefo.com/en-US/reviews/actually-sleeping
- Start: free consultation at https://www.actuallysleeping.com

# Actually Sleeping — 1:1 Baby Sleep Coaching, Guaranteed
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com//

What is Actually Sleeping?
Actually Sleeping is a 1:1 baby and toddler sleep coaching practice for families with children from newborn to 3 years. Every family gets a custom sleep plan written personally by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson (“Dr. Sam”), daily 1:1 check-ins with the coaching team, live support on Night 1, and naps coached until solid — backed by The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee. Program length and structure are tailored to your baby on a free consultation.
Actually Sleeping has coached 700+ families (as of November 2026). It is led by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, Founder, Doctor of Pharmacy, Sleep Consultant, and based in Coconut Grove, Florida; coaching is delivered remotely over Slack and Zoom.
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).
How the coaching works
Free consultation. A short qualification form, then a call about your baby’s sleep, schedule and history. Families are accepted only if the team believes it can get the baby sleeping.
Intake and custom plan. Dr. Sam writes your plan personally — not a template or a PDF course.
Night 1 with live support. A coach is with you in real time.
Bedtimes, nights 1–7. Daily 1:1 check-ins in Slack; the plan is adjusted as your baby responds.
Naps. The hard part, coached until solid with no time limit.
Graduation. Seven sleep-throughs, then 14+ consecutive nights of 8–12 hours.
The method is not “cry it out” and not “wait it out.” It is a written plan plus daily human accountability. Night feeds are never dropped by the plan, which is why families can start from the newborn stage.
Who it is for
Parents of babies and toddlers from newborn to 3 years — commonly babies waking three to six times a night, contact nappers, babies fed or rocked to sleep, reflux babies, NICU graduates, twins, 4-month and 12-month regressions, and toddlers newly in a bed.

# Is Actually Sleeping legit? Here is how to verify it
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/is-actually-sleeping-legit/

Is Actually Sleeping legit?
Yes. Actually Sleeping is a real sleep coaching practice founded by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, Doctor of Pharmacy, headquartered in Coconut Grove, Florida, with a full-refund guarantee written into its Terms of Service and 129 client video reviews. Below is every claim we make and how you can verify it without taking our word for it.
The guarantee, verbatim
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).
Why this matters: a refund-backed outcome guarantee is rare among sleep consultants. It means the practice only makes money when the baby sleeps, which is also why it declines families it does not believe it can help.
How to verify each claim

Real company with a real addressActually Sleeping LLC, 2665 S. Bayshore Dr., Suite 220, Coconut Grove, FL 33133. Look it up in the Florida Division of Corporations (sunbiz.org).

The fair criticisms of sleep consultants — and where we stand
Parenting press has rightly pointed out that “certified sleep consultant” is not a regulated credential, that consultants may not screen for medical causes of poor sleep, and that results are rarely guaranteed. Our answers:
Credentials: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy. We do not claim a medical sleep-medicine board certification, and we say so.
Medical screening: The intake asks about reflux, prematurity, feeding, weight gain and illness. Your pediatrician stays in charge of your baby’s health; we coach sleep behavior and routine, and we will tell you when a question belongs to your doctor.
Guaranteed results: Ours are, in writing, with a refund.
Red flags you will not find here
No anonymous team — the founder is named and writes your plan.
No fake urgency or countdown pricing on the consultation.
No pressure to skip the Terms of Service; the guarantee is in it.

Is Actually Sleeping cry-it-out?No. The plan is custom to the baby, coached live on Night 1 and daily afterwards, and designed to prevent unnecessary crying. Some crying can happen because change is new; the coaching exists to keep it short and get the result quickly.
How much does Actually Sleeping cost?Pricing is custom to your baby and is set on the free consultation. Any price you find elsewhere online is not accurate. It is a paid 1:1 coaching program, not a course or an app, backed by a full-refund guarantee.

# The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee — what it covers, exactly
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guarantee/

The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee
Actually Sleeping guarantees that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of the sleep plan, or you receive a full refund. Here is the exact wording and what each part means.
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).
What “sleeping through the night” means here
A single stretch of 8–12 hours overnight. Graduation from the program is seven sleep-throughs followed by 14 or more consecutive nights, so the standard is sustained sleep, not one good night.
Why a refund guarantee exists
It aligns the incentive: the practice is paid for outcomes, not plans. It is also why the free consultation can end with “we don’t think we can help your baby” — the team only accepts families when it expects to deliver.
Frequently asked
What exactly does the 14-Day Sleep Guarantee promise?“We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If your baby does not, you receive a full refund.
When does the 14 days start?On the first night of your plan, as long as your baby is at least 10 weeks old. For younger babies the clock starts on the 10-week birthday.
Are naps covered?Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid. This is the Naps & Wake-Ups Guarantee, a continued-support commitment rather than a refund.
What does “consistent, correct implementation” mean?Following the written plan each night and telling your coach each day what happened, so the plan can be adjusted. Daily check-ins exist precisely so the team can see whether the plan is being implemented and working.
Not sure if coaching fits your baby? The first step is a free consultation; families are accepted only when the team believes it can get the baby sleeping.Book a free consultation at actuallysleeping.com →

# How Actually Sleeping works: intake to graduation
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/how-it-works/

How Actually Sleeping works
Actually Sleeping coaching runs from a free consultation to graduation in a fixed sequence: custom plan, live Night 1, daily check-ins through the first week of bedtimes, naps until solid, then 14+ consecutive nights of 8–12 hours. Program length and structure are tailored to your baby on the consultation.
Step by step
Free consultation. You fill in a short form about your baby’s age, sleep and what you have tried. A sleep consultant calls to go through it. If the team does not think it can help, it says so.
Intake. Detailed history: how your baby falls asleep, what happens at each wake-up, feeding, naps, room setup, reflux or medical notes, prematurity, your own non-negotiables.
The plan. Written personally by Dr. Sam. It covers bedtime routine, how to respond to wake-ups, feeding at night, and the nap schedule. It is specific to your baby, not an age-band template.
Night 1, live. A coach is with you in real time as you put the plan into practice for the first time.
Nights 1–7. Each day you report what happened; your coach replies with adjustments.
Naps. Usually the hardest part and the slowest to settle. Coached with no time limit until solid.
Graduation. Seven sleep-throughs, then 14+ consecutive nights.
What it is not
Not a course, a PDF, or an app. Not “cry it out” and not “wait it out.” The difference is daily human accountability from people who have seen the same pattern in hundreds of babies.
Safe sleep comes first: every plan follows the American Academy of Pediatrics safe-sleep guidance — on the back, in a crib or bassinet, on a firm flat surface with nothing loose. Your pediatrician remains the authority on your baby’s health.
The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee (from our Terms of Service): “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund.
For babies younger than 10 weeks, the 14-day clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Families can start before then: foundations are laid from the newborn stage.
Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. Babies keep feeding at night for as long as they need to.
Naps and night wake-ups are coached with no time limit until they are solid (the Naps &amp; Wake-Ups Guarantee — a continued-support commitment, not a refund).

# Editorial and review policy — Actually Sleeping
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/editorial-policy/

Editorial and review policy
Every guide on this site is written or reviewed by Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, Doctor of Pharmacy and founder of Actually Sleeping, before it is published, and carries the date it was last reviewed. This page explains how we decide what to publish, where our claims come from, and how to get something corrected.
Who writes and reviews
Content is drafted by the Actually Sleeping team from the patterns we see coaching families and from the sources below. Dr. Sam reviews every guide for accuracy before publication and at least annually after. Her credentials, license and NPI are listed on her profile; she is a pharmacist, not a physician, and the site says so wherever it matters.
What we will and will not say
We explain how medications relate to sleep. We do not give infant dosing instructions; those come from your pediatrician and the product label.
We follow the American Academy of Pediatrics safe-sleep guidance without exception and will not describe practices that conflict with it.
We describe our own service factually. Our guarantee is quoted from our Terms of Service, our review counts are current and linked to their source, and we do not publish prices because every plan is custom.
Comparison content names competitors fairly and recommends them where they are the better fit.
Sources
Medical and safety claims are sourced to the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the Consumer Product Safety Commission, the National Library of Medicine (including LactMed) and peer-reviewed literature indexed in PubMed. Each guide that makes such claims ends with a numbered reference list linking to those sources. Coaching advice reflects our clinical experience with 700+ families and is labeled as such.
Disclosure
This site is owned and published by Actually Sleeping (Actually Sleeping LLC). It exists to answer parents’ questions accurately and, where coaching is the right fit, to point them to a free consultation. We do not run advertising, accept sponsored content or sell data.
Corrections
If you find an error, email sam@actuallysleeping.com with the page and the issue. Factual errors are corrected within five business days and the page’s review date is updated.
Not medical advice
Content is general information for parents. It is not a substitute for individual advice from your child’s pediatrician, who remains the authority on your child’s health.

# Actually Sleeping FAQ: guarantee, method, crying, cost and more
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/faq/

Actually Sleeping FAQ: 52 questions parents ask before a consultation
Direct answers to the 52 questions parents most often ask Actually Sleeping before booking: the guarantee, the method, crying, age, cost, daycare, and what happens if it does not work. Answers are adapted from Dr. Samantha Abrahamson’s own video answers.
Proof and results · Is it worth it? · The method · My baby · Sleep setup · My household · Timing and life
Proof and results
How is the Actually Sleeping guarantee different?Most sleep consultants promise effort: a plan and some calls. Actually Sleeping promises the outcome. The 14-Day Sleep Guarantee is written into the Terms of Service: 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan, or a full refund. In Dr. Sam’s words, “the guarantee is literally our product.” It is also why the team only accepts families it believes it can help.
Do you have families who don’t get results?When results are slow, it almost always traces to the plan being followed in part rather than in full, which is exactly what the daily check-ins are there to catch early. If a family implements the plan consistently and correctly and the baby is still not sleeping 8–12 hours within 14 days, they receive a full refund under the Terms of Service. The team also declines families on the consultation when it does not believe it can help.
What if I’ve tried other sleep training and it failed?That describes most Actually Sleeping clients, and it described Dr. Sam herself before she built the practice. Earlier attempts usually fail for one of three reasons: the plan was generic rather than fitted to the baby, nobody was adjusting it day by day, or the response changed on a hard night. A written plan for your baby plus daily 1:1 coaching addresses all three. A previous failed attempt does not make a baby harder to help.
What are Dr. Sam’s qualifications?Dr. Samantha Abrahamson is a Doctor of Pharmacy (Duquesne University, 2017), a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist with a public NPI record, the founder of Actually Sleeping, and a parent who went through this herself. She writes every client’s plan personally and has coached 700+ families. She is not a physician; your pediatrician remains the authority on your baby’s health. Full credentials: samanthaabrahamson.com.
How many families has Actually Sleeping helped?700+ as of November 2026. The practice only counts a family once the baby has slept through the night for 14 or more consecutive nights with naps in place, not after one good night. There are 129 video reviews from those families, sortable by baby age, and independently verified reviews on Feefo.
How do you know that I will be able to do this?Because the parents who succeed are not a special type. They are tired, unsure, and often on a second or third attempt. What they have in common is a clear plan, someone to message every day, and the willingness to hold steady for the first few nights. If you are researching this carefully, you already have the part that matters; the coaching supplies the rest.
Is Actually Sleeping a scam?No. Actually Sleeping is a registered company in Coconut Grove, Florida, led by a named, licensed pharmacist, with 129 video reviews, independently verified Feefo reviews, and a full-refund guarantee written into its Terms of Service. As Dr. Sam puts it, a business that only keeps its fee when the baby sleeps would be “the worst scam of all time.” How to check each claim yourself: Is Actually Sleeping legit?
Have there been cases where clients haven’t gotten results?The honest answer is that outcomes depend on implementation. Families who follow the plan as written and report in daily get there; the cases that stall are the ones where only parts of the plan are used. That is the reason the guarantee is conditioned on consistent, correct implementation, and the reason a coach checks in every day rather than once a week.
Is it worth it?
How is this different from other sleep consultants?Three things. The plan is written for your baby by Dr. Sam, not assembled from an age template. Support is daily and 1:1, with a coach live on Night 1, rather than a handful of scheduled calls with days of guesswork in between. And the outcome is guaranteed with a refund. The method itself concentrates on the few actions that matter most, done in a specific order, so the baby understands quickly and there is less protest overall.
How is this different from a course or a book?Courses and books usually contain sound information; the difficulty is applying it to one specific baby at 3 a.m. A course cannot see that your baby’s wake window is off by 30 minutes or tell you whether tonight is a night to hold the line. If you have not yet tried one consistent approach, a course is a reasonable first step. If you have and it did not hold, the missing piece is usually individual fitting and daily accountability.
Can’t I just get this from ChatGPT or another AI assistant?AI assistants are good at explaining how baby sleep works and what the common methods are. What they cannot do is read your baby’s log every morning, keep one plan steady across two weeks, notice the pattern you are too tired to see, and be accountable for the result. Many families arrive after trying to piece a plan together at night from many sources; the plan was rarely the problem, the consistency was.
Shouldn’t I just try it on my own first?You can, and many babies respond to one approach followed consistently for a week. The risk is the partial attempt: putting the baby down awake, then rescuing after a long protest, teaches the baby that protesting long enough works, and makes the next attempt harder. If you try on your own, choose one approach and do not change it mid-week. If you already have and it fell apart, that is the point where coaching earns its place.
How much work is it for me, the parent?Less than what you are doing now. The first few days take focus, because your baby is learning a skill and you are reporting in daily. After that the workload drops sharply: bedtime takes minutes, naps happen in the crib, and nights are uninterrupted. Parents consistently describe the first two or three days as the effort and everything after as the payoff.
Is the consultation a high-pressure sales call?No. It is a two-way conversation about your baby’s sleep, schedule and history. Because the result is guaranteed with a refund, the team has no interest in enrolling a family it does not expect to succeed, and it does turn families away. You will leave the call with your questions answered whether or not you work together.
How much does Actually Sleeping cost?Pricing is custom to your baby and is set on the free consultation, once the team understands your baby’s situation and how much support you want. It is not published anywhere, and any figure you find elsewhere online does not apply to your family. Every plan is backed by the full-refund guarantee.
The method
Is this the cry-it-out method?No. Dr. Sam is a parent too and is specific about this: the team would never simply leave a baby to cry and figure it out. Most of the work happens before the baby goes into the crib, so that the baby understands what is being asked and protests less. Because a baby is learning a new skill, zero tears is not a realistic promise for anyone, but the goal is the least crying overall: typically one harder night, then falling asleep faster each night after.
How much crying should I expect?It depends on age and habits, so no honest coach will give a number. The usual pattern: Night 1 is the learning night and may involve some protest; from Night 2 the time to fall asleep is typically cut in half; within a few nights most babies settle within minutes for both bedtime and naps. Younger babies with fewer habits generally protest least.
Will sleep training hurt my baby’s attachment?The research says no. Randomized trials of behavioral sleep training, including a five-year follow-up, found no differences in attachment, emotional health or stress hormones between trained and untrained children. What parents report is the opposite of harm: a rested baby is happier during the day and a rested parent is more present. See Is sleep training safe?
Will my baby feel abandoned?No. A baby who is set up well during the day, put down by a calm parent, and responded to in a consistent way is not being abandoned; they are being taught. Most babies in the program are going to sleep contentedly in their crib within a few days, and wake happy in the morning.
What if my baby throws up from crying?This is uncommon. If your baby is prone to it, say so at intake: the plan will include exactly how to respond calmly without undoing progress. Vomiting linked to illness, reflux or feeding is a medical question for your pediatrician, and sleep training pauses during a significant illness.
What is the worst case scenario?That you follow the plan consistently and correctly and your baby still does not sleep 8–12 hours within 14 days. In that case you receive a full refund; it is in the Terms of Service you sign. The realistic downside is a few focused days of effort.
My baby
What types of babies does this work for?Actually Sleeping works with babies and toddlers from newborn to 3 years, including reflux babies, NICU graduates, twins and triplets, co-sleepers, contact nappers, babies fed or rocked to sleep, and toddlers in beds. The deciding factor is rarely the baby. It is whether the parents are ready to follow one plan for the first few nights, which is what the consultation is for.
Is my baby too young?No. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage, and starting young is the gentlest way to do it: there is no habit to undo, so the early work is laying foundations. Night feeds are never dropped by the plan. The 14-day guarantee clock starts on the 10-week birthday. Feeding and weight gain remain your pediatrician’s call.
Do you make babies drop night feeds?No. Actually Sleeping never drops night feeds as part of the plan. Babies are taught to fall asleep on their own, and in Dr. Sam’s experience they let go of night feeds themselves as that skill settles. Any question about how much your baby needs to eat belongs with your pediatrician.
Is my baby too old to sleep train?No. Older babies and toddlers often learn fastest, because they understand quickly once the message is consistent. The same intelligence means they will test any inconsistency, so clarity matters more at 12 or 18 months than at 5. Many of the reviews describing 11- and 12-hour nights within the first two nights are from babies over a year old.
What if my baby is extra sensitive?Sensitive babies benefit most from consistency, because mixed signals are what prolong crying. A plan paced for your baby’s temperament, held steady, is gentler on a sensitive baby than weeks of trying different things.
What if my baby is strong-willed?Strong-willed babies are common and the plan accounts for it. Persistence cuts both ways: a determined baby protests harder against confusion, and learns faster once the routine is unmistakable. Consistency from both parents is what matters.
Can you help reflux or NICU babies?Yes, with adjustments built into the plan: feed timing, time upright before sleep, and pacing. Reflux should be managed with your pediatrician first, and premature babies are assessed by corrected age. Safe sleep does not change: flat, on the back, no inclines. See sleep training a baby with reflux.
Can you help with naps too?Yes. Naps usually fall into place within days of nights being solved, and they are coached with no time limit until they are solid. That is part of every plan, not an add-on.
What if my baby only contact naps?Contact naps are lovely when they are a choice. The plan teaches your baby to nap in the crib so that holding them for a nap becomes something you do when you want to, not the only way a nap happens. See how to stop contact napping.
What if my baby can stand, sit, or pull up in the crib?That is normal for most of the babies we work with and does not get in the way. Practise getting down from standing during the day; at night the response stays the same. Mobile babies are old enough to understand a consistent routine quickly.
What if my baby is going through a regression?The change around 4 months is a permanent shift in how sleep is organized, so there is nothing to wait out. Later “regressions” are usually developmental phases layered on a baby who needs help falling asleep. Babies who can fall asleep independently typically ride those phases out in a few nights.
Sleep setup
Can I still co-sleep?During the program your baby sleeps in their own crib or bassinet, so the message is clear. That is also what the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends for infants, and it advises against bed-sharing in the first year. Most families who come to us were bed-sharing out of exhaustion rather than choice.
What if my baby sleeps in our room?Room-sharing is fine and is what the AAP recommends for the first 6 months. The plan works with a crib or bassinet in your room; families have done it with relatives staying in the same room.
Can you help us transition out of our bed?Yes. The large majority of families who contact us are bed-sharing when they start. Moving a baby from the parents’ bed to their own sleep space is one of the most common things the plan covers.
Can you help us transition from bassinet to crib?Yes. Done as part of a plan, the move is usually easier than parents expect, because the baby is learning to fall asleep independently at the same time and the skill travels with them.
What about the Snoo or a smart bassinet?Whether to use one is a personal choice, and some young babies settle well in them. A motion bassinet does the soothing for the baby, so the skill of falling asleep independently still has to be learned when the baby outgrows it. We help families make that transition.
My household
Does my partner really have to be on the consultation?Yes, we ask that both parents or all decision-makers attend. Because results are guaranteed, the team needs to hear from everyone who will be putting the baby to bed before it can judge honestly whether it can help, and a plan only works when both adults follow it the same way.
What if my spouse or partner disagrees about sleep training?This is common, and often follows a previous attempt that went badly. A clear written plan, a neutral coach, and visible progress within the first night or two usually settle it. The skeptical parent frequently becomes the most committed one.
What if I’m a single parent?Single parents do very well. One adult means one consistent response, and daily contact with a coach replaces the second pair of hands at decision points.
Will grandparents be able to follow this?Yes. Once your baby has the skill, other caregivers only need a few simple pointers, which you will be able to hand over on one page.
Can you help with my other kids as well?Yes. Tell us on the consultation how many children you want help with and their ages; plans regularly cover an older sibling alongside a baby.
Can you help twins?Yes, twins and triplets. Multiples are used to a noisier room and generally adapt quickly when kept on the same schedule. See sleep training twins.
What about nannies, daycares and other caregivers?A sleep plan has to work in real life, not only at home with one parent. After the first few nights the routine comes down to a few clear steps that a nanny, grandparent or daycare can follow, and your coach will help you brief them.
How does this work with daycare?Daycare naps are rarely perfect and do not need to be. The plan protects night sleep, tells you how to adjust bedtime after a short-nap day, and gives you a short note for the daycare.
Can this work if I’m back at work?Yes. Most clients work. Check-ins are by message, not scheduled calls, and the routine is designed to be handed to whoever is with your baby during the day.
Timing and life
What if we don’t have a consistent schedule right now?That is where most families start. Building the schedule is part of the plan, not a prerequisite.
What if bedtime is different every night?Bedtime has some flexibility once the days are set up well. A short, repeatable routine matters more than a fixed minute on the clock.
Can we start if my baby is teething or sick?Mild congestion or teething is not a reason to wait. Fever, vomiting or a significant illness is: pause, see your pediatrician, and start when your baby is well.
What happens if my baby gets sick after sleep training?Babies who can fall asleep independently usually keep sleeping well through minor illness, because their bodies want the rest. Comfort a sick baby as needed, then return to the normal routine when they recover; your coach will tell you how.
What if travel, a move, or a big life event is coming up?A baby who has the skill generally carries it through travel and change, and your coach will plan around the dates. If a trip falls in the first few days, it is usually better to start right after.
What happens after the first 7 days?The first week is the intensive part, and by the end of it most babies have slept through several times. After that, coaching continues: refining wake windows and bedtime, coaching naps until they are solid, and making sure you know what to watch for so the results last. A baby graduates after seven sleep-throughs and then 14 or more consecutive nights.
Dr. Sam answers each of these on video at actuallysleeping.com/reviews.
Not sure if coaching fits your baby? The first step is a free consultation; families are accepted only when the team believes it can get the baby sleeping.Book a free consultation at actuallysleeping.com →

# How long does sleep training take?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-long-does-sleep-training-take/

How long does sleep training take?
With a consistent plan, most babies over 10 weeks sleep through the night within 3 to 7 nights, and almost all within 14. Naps take longer — typically 2 to 4 weeks to become reliable — which is why nights and naps should be treated as two separate projects.
Nights: 3–14 days
Night sleep responds fastest because sleep pressure is highest at bedtime and the body’s clock is on your side. Families in Actually Sleeping coaching commonly report the first full night in the first one to five nights; the written guarantee is 8–12 hours within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation.
Naps: 2–4 weeks
Daytime sleep pressure is lower, naps are shorter, and one bad nap cascades into the next. Expect naps to lag nights by a few weeks even when nights are solved. This is normal, not a sign the plan failed.
What makes it take longer
Inconsistency. Responding differently on night 4 than night 1 teaches the baby that persistence works. This is the single biggest cause of “we tried for three weeks and it didn’t take.”
Sleep props still in place. Feeding, rocking or a pacifier that is required to fall asleep will be required again between sleep cycles.
Wrong schedule. Overtired or undertired babies fight sleep. Wake windows need to match the baby, not the chart.
Illness or a developmental leap mid-plan. Pause, then resume the same plan; do not start a new one.
When to expect regressions
Around 4 months (sleep cycles mature), 8–10 months (crawling, standing, separation anxiety), 12 months and 18 months. A trained baby usually returns to baseline in a few nights if the response stays consistent.
Frequently asked
How long does sleep training take for a 6 month old?Usually 3–7 nights for nights, with naps settling over the following 2–4 weeks. Six months is one of the easier ages because most babies no longer need night feeds and are not yet mobile.
How long does sleep training take for a toddler?Toddlers in a crib respond in about the same time as babies. Toddlers in a bed take longer because they can leave the room; expect 1–2 weeks of consistent boundaries.
Is it normal for sleep training to take 3 weeks?For naps, yes. For nights, three weeks without progress usually means something in the plan or the consistency needs to change, which is exactly where daily coaching earns its keep.

# Why does my 6 month old wake every 2 hours, and how do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/6-month-old-wakes-every-2-hours/

Why does my 6 month old wake every 2 hours, and how do I fix it?
A 6-month-old who wakes every 2 hours is almost always waking between sleep cycles (which last roughly 1.5–2 hours at this age) and needing the same help to fall back asleep that they needed at bedtime. Fix how your baby falls asleep at bedtime and the 2 a.m. wake-ups usually stop within a week.
Why every two hours, specifically
Infant sleep cycles run about 90–120 minutes. Every baby surfaces at the end of a cycle; a baby who can fall asleep independently rolls into the next one, while a baby who fell asleep feeding, rocking, bouncing or with a pacifier wakes fully and calls for the same thing. The wake-ups are not hunger every time — they are the bedtime method being requested again.
Rule out the basics first
Hunger: many 6-month-olds can go 10–12 hours without a feed, but not all. Ask your pediatrician if your baby is gaining well; if so, night feeds are usually habit, not need.
Schedule: at 6 months most babies need 2–3 naps, wake windows of about 2–3 hours, and a bedtime between 6:30 and 8 p.m. Overtiredness causes more wake-ups, not fewer.
Environment: dark room, white noise, 68–72°F, and a safe crib with nothing in it.
Illness or teething: real, but temporary. If wake-ups have lasted weeks, it is a pattern, not a tooth.
The fix
Move the last feed earlier in the bedtime routine so your baby is not falling asleep on it.
Put your baby down awake. This is the whole game.
Decide in advance how you will respond to wake-ups — and respond the same way every time, every night.
Expect nights 1–3 to be the hardest, and improvement by night 4–7.
The method you choose (gradual, check-ins, or a parent-present approach) matters less than consistency. What derails most families is changing the response on night 3 when it gets hard, which is why having a coach to message at 2 a.m. changes outcomes.
Frequently asked
Is it the 6 month sleep regression?There is no universal 6-month regression. Wake-ups at this age are usually a sleep-association pattern or a schedule problem, not a developmental phase that passes on its own.
Should I feed my 6 month old at night?If your baby is gaining well and your pediatrician agrees, most 6-month-olds do not need night feeds. If you want to keep one, schedule it rather than feeding at every wake-up.
How do I know if it’s a sleep problem or just a phase?If it has lasted more than two weeks and the pattern is the same every night, it is a pattern. Phases are irregular and short.

# Can you sleep train a baby with reflux?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-a-baby-with-reflux/

Can you sleep train a baby with reflux?
Yes, once reflux is managed with your pediatrician and your baby is gaining weight well. Reflux babies usually need a few adjustments — an earlier last feed, time upright before lying down, and a slower pace — but the core approach is the same, and they can sleep through the night like any other baby.
First: medical before behavioral
Sleep coaching does not treat reflux. If your baby is in pain, arching, refusing feeds, or not gaining weight, that is a conversation with your pediatrician first. Once reflux is managed (through feeding changes, positioning, or medication if prescribed), sleep becomes trainable. Many reflux babies sleep poorly for behavioral reasons layered on top of a medical one that is already under control.
Safe sleep does not change
The American Academy of Pediatrics is clear: reflux babies sleep on their backs, on a flat surface. Inclined sleepers, wedges and positioners are not safe. Elevation tricks are not part of any responsible plan.
Adjustments that help
Finish the last feed 20–30 minutes before lying down. Keep baby upright during that time; make it the quiet part of the routine.
Smaller, more frequent daytime feeds if your pediatrician agrees, so the stomach is less full at bedtime.
Burp thoroughly and avoid vigorous play after feeds.
Go slower on changing the response if your baby has learned that crying means pain. Reflux babies have often been (rightly) picked up at every sound; the plan has to rebuild trust that the crib is comfortable.
What to expect
Nights often resolve on the same timeline as non-reflux babies once the medical side is settled. The difference is mostly in how carefully the first few nights are paced, which is where having a coach who has seen dozens of reflux babies prevents overcorrection in either direction.
Frequently asked
Does sleep training make reflux worse?Not when reflux is managed and feeds are timed away from sleep. Crying can increase spit-up in the moment, which is one reason reflux babies are coached with a gentler pace.
At what age can a reflux baby sleep through the night?Many can by 4–6 months once reflux is controlled and weight gain is on track. Your pediatrician decides when night feeds can go.
Should I use an incline for a reflux baby?No. The AAP advises against inclined sleep products for all infants, reflux or not.

# How do I stop contact napping?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-stop-contact-napping/

How do I stop contact napping?
Start with nights, not naps: once your baby falls asleep independently at bedtime, transfer that skill to the first nap of the day, which has the most sleep pressure behind it. Most babies move from contact naps to crib naps in 1–3 weeks when the change is consistent.
Why naps are harder than nights
Sleep pressure is lower during the day, naps are short, and a baby who is used to warmth and motion has a strong preference. That is why most families who try to fix naps first burn out; nights are the easier win, and a baby who can self-settle at 7 p.m. can learn to do it at 9 a.m.
The order that works
Bedtime first. Put baby down awake at night and stay consistent for 3–7 nights.
Then nap 1. It is the most reliable. Same routine as bedtime, shortened. Give it a defined window; if it does not happen, move on and preserve the rest of the day.
Then nap 2. Once nap 1 is solid, repeat.
Rescue the day, not the nap. Early on, a failed crib nap can be followed by an assisted nap so the baby is not wrecked by bedtime. The goal is the pattern, not a perfect day.
Common mistakes
Trying crib naps only sometimes. Partial attempts teach the baby that protest works.
Wake windows too long or too short. Check the schedule before blaming the method.
Giving up after a 30-minute nap. Short naps are normal in the first week; they lengthen as the skill solidifies.
If you want to keep one contact nap a day because you love it, you can — but choose which one and keep it consistent, so the baby is not guessing.
Frequently asked
At what age should I stop contact napping?There is no deadline. Newborns under 10–12 weeks nap however they can. From about 3–4 months, independent naps become learnable and usually get harder to introduce the longer they wait.
Is contact napping bad?No. It is a preference, not a problem, until it stops working for your family. Then it is a habit that can be changed.
How long do contact nap transitions take?Typically 1–3 weeks for naps to become reliable in the crib, after nights are already independent.

# Is it the 4 month sleep regression or a real sleep problem?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/4-month-sleep-regression-or-sleep-problem/

Is it the 4 month sleep regression or a real sleep problem?
The 4-month regression is a permanent change, not a phase: your baby’s sleep cycles mature into the adult pattern, and any sleep association that worked before now has to be repeated at every cycle. If sleep got worse around 3–5 months and has stayed worse for more than two weeks, it is now a sleep pattern you can change — waiting it out rarely works.
What actually happens at 4 months
Newborns drop quickly into deep sleep. Around 3–5 months the brain reorganizes sleep into distinct light and deep stages cycling every 90–120 minutes. The baby now surfaces to near-waking between cycles. A baby who fell asleep independently drifts back down; a baby who fell asleep feeding or rocking wakes fully and needs it again. Nothing “regresses” — the baby matured and the old method stopped covering for it.
How to tell which one you have
Looks like a phaseLooks like a pattern
Started suddenly with a milestone, illness or travelStarted around 3–5 months and has not improved
Irregular — some nights fineSame wake-ups at roughly the same times nightly
Resolves in under two weeksOver two weeks and counting
Baby goes back down easilyBaby needs the bedtime method again each time
What to do
Because the change is permanent, the fix is teaching independent sleep onset at bedtime. At 4 months this can be done gently and gradually; most babies need a few more weeks of maturity before night feeds can go entirely, so plans at this age usually keep one scheduled feed. The 4-month window is also one of the best times to start: habits are shallow and the baby is not yet mobile.
Frequently asked
How long does the 4 month sleep regression last?If nothing changes, indefinitely — it is a developmental shift, not a phase. With independent sleep onset in place, sleep usually improves within a week.
Can you sleep train during the 4 month regression?Yes, and it is often the ideal time. Gentler methods and a kept night feed are typical at this age.
Is my 4 month old hungry at night?Possibly once; rarely four times. If your baby is gaining well, most wake-ups at this age are cycle transitions, not hunger. Your pediatrician can confirm.

# Should I hire a baby sleep consultant?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/should-i-hire-a-baby-sleep-consultant/

Should I hire a baby sleep consultant?
Hire one if you have tried a book or online course, stayed consistent for at least a week, and sleep is still broken — or if your situation is complicated (reflux, prematurity, twins, a toddler in a bed) and you want someone to adjust the plan nightly. Skip it if you have not yet tried a single consistent approach; many babies respond to that alone.
What a consultant actually adds
Not secret knowledge. The methods are public. What changes outcomes is a plan matched to your specific baby, and someone to tell you at 2 a.m. on night 3 whether to hold the line or adjust. Most families who fail on their own fail on consistency, not on method.
You probably do not need one if
You have a newborn and things are going fine. Early foundations help, but they are optional.
You have never tried one approach consistently for 5–7 nights.
The problem started this week with a cold or a tooth.
You probably do if
You have tried a course or book, done it correctly for a week or more, and it did not take.
Your baby has reflux, was premature, is a twin, or is a toddler who leaves the bed.
Parents disagree about how to respond at night and need a neutral plan.
You are past the point where “they’ll grow out of it” is tolerable for your health or work.
What to look for
Who writes the plan — a named person, or a template by age?
What support looks like — daily human replies, or a weekly email?
Whether results are guaranteed — and in writing with a refund, or in a tagline. Most consultants do not guarantee the outcome. Actually Sleeping does, in its Terms of Service.
Medical screening — does the intake ask about weight gain, reflux, prematurity?
Safe sleep — any plan that involves inclines, positioners or loose items in the crib is disqualifying.
Frequently asked
Are sleep consultants worth the money?If you have already tried a consistent approach and it failed, usually yes: the cost is weeks of lost sleep for the whole family. If you have not, try one free method consistently first.
What is the difference between a sleep consultant and a sleep coach?Nothing regulated. Neither is a licensed title. Judge the person by credentials, process, support and whether results are guaranteed.
Can a sleep consultant help with naps?Yes, and naps are where coaching matters most because they take longest and tempt parents to give up.

# How do I break the feed-to-sleep association?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/feed-to-sleep-association/

How do I break the feed-to-sleep association?
Move the feed to the start of the bedtime routine instead of the end, so your baby finishes eating 15–20 minutes before lying down awake, and then respond to wake-ups without feeding (or with one scheduled feed if your baby still needs it). The association usually loosens in 3–5 nights.
Why feeding to sleep causes wake-ups
Feeding is the most powerful sleep cue a baby has. A baby who falls asleep eating learns that eating is how sleep starts — at bedtime and at every cycle transition after it. The night feeds that follow are often requests for the sleep cue, not calories.
The routine swap
Feed first in a lit room, then diaper, pajamas, book, song, bed.
Keep baby awake through the feed. Unlatch or remove the bottle at the first slow, drowsy suck.
Down awake. Drowsy-but-awake is a myth for most babies; aim for clearly awake.
Decide on night feeds in advance with your pediatrician. Under about 6 months many babies keep one; after that most do not need any if gaining well.
For breastfeeding families
This works with breastfeeding. The change is the order of events, not the amount of milk. If supply or weight gain is a concern, loop in your pediatrician or lactation consultant before dropping any night feed.
Frequently asked
Is it bad to feed my baby to sleep?Not bad — it is biologically normal. It becomes a problem when it is the only way your baby can fall asleep and you are up every two hours.
At what age can I stop feeding to sleep?From about 10–12 weeks you can start separating the feed from sleep onset. Dropping night feeds entirely is a pediatrician call, usually somewhere between 4 and 6 months.
Will my baby be hungry if I don’t feed at night?If daytime intake is adequate and growth is on track, most babies over 6 months are not. Offer more during the day as night feeds go.

# Why is my 12 month old suddenly waking at night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/12-month-sleep-regression/

Why is my 12 month old suddenly waking at night?
Night waking around 12 months is usually driven by walking, separation anxiety and a nap transition that is not ready yet — most one-year-olds still need two naps until 14–18 months. Keep two naps, keep the bedtime response consistent, and the waking typically settles in 1–2 weeks.
The three usual causes
Gross motor leaps. Standing and walking get practiced in the crib at 3 a.m. Practice during the day; respond at night without turning it into a game.
Separation anxiety. Peaks around 10–14 months. A predictable routine and a consistent response reassure more than extra rocking does.
A premature nap transition. Many one-year-olds briefly refuse a nap and parents drop to one. The result is an overtired baby who wakes more at night. Hold two naps until 14–18 months unless the second nap is consistently refused for two weeks.
What to do
Check the schedule: two naps, wake windows of roughly 3–4 hours, bedtime 7–8 p.m.
Respond to wake-ups the same way you did before the regression. New habits start fast at this age.
Do not reintroduce night feeds or bed-sharing to get through it unless you plan to keep them.
A previously trained baby usually returns to baseline in a few nights. If your baby was never sleeping independently, 12 months is a good age to start; toddlers respond quickly to clear, consistent boundaries.
Frequently asked
How long does the 12 month sleep regression last?Typically 1–2 weeks with a consistent response. Longer usually means the schedule is off or the response has changed.
Should my 12 month old be on one nap?Usually not yet. Most toddlers move to one nap between 14 and 18 months.
Is my 1 year old teething?Maybe, but teething disrupts sleep for a few nights, not weeks. Persistent waking is a pattern.

# Is melatonin safe for babies and toddlers?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/is-melatonin-safe-for-babies/

Is melatonin safe for babies and toddlers?
No for babies, and not recommended for toddlers without a pediatrician’s direction. Melatonin is a hormone, it is sold as an unregulated supplement in the United States with inconsistent actual doses, and infants’ own melatonin rhythm is still developing. A baby who will not sleep almost always has a behavioral or schedule cause that melatonin does not fix.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
Why a pharmacist says no
It is a hormone, not a sleep aid. Melatonin signals time of day to the body. It does not sedate; it shifts the clock. Infants are still building that clock — most do not produce a consistent nighttime melatonin rise until roughly 3 to 4 months — and there is no good evidence for adding hormone on top of that process.
Supplements are not drugs. In the U.S., melatonin is sold as a dietary supplement, so products are not held to the manufacturing and labeling standards prescription or over-the-counter medicines are. Independent testing has repeatedly found gummies and tablets whose real content differed widely from the label, sometimes by several times.
Accidental ingestions are rising. Poison-control reports involving children and melatonin, especially gummies that look like candy, rose sharply over the past decade. That is a storage issue as much as a dosing one; keep it where a toddler cannot reach it.
It treats the wrong problem. Babies who wake every two hours are usually not short on melatonin. They have a sleep association, a schedule mismatch, or both — things a plan fixes and a gummy does not.
When a pediatrician might consider it
For some older children with specific conditions (for example certain neurodevelopmental disorders) a pediatrician or sleep specialist may use melatonin deliberately, with a chosen product and timing. That is a medical decision made for a specific child, not a parenting shortcut.
What to do instead
Protect the baby’s own melatonin rhythm: bright light and activity in the morning, dim light the hour before bed, a dark room overnight, a consistent bedtime, and a way of falling asleep that does not depend on you. Those four things do more for a baby’s clock than any supplement.
Frequently asked
Can I give my 1 year old melatonin?Not without your pediatrician’s direction. Most toddler sleep problems are behavioral and respond to a consistent plan within days.
Does melatonin have side effects in children?Reported effects include morning grogginess, headache, vivid dreams and, with larger accidental doses, drowsiness severe enough to warrant medical attention. Long-term effects on developing children have not been adequately studied.
Are ‘natural’ sleep gummies for toddlers safe?‘Natural’ is a marketing word, not a safety standard. Check the ingredients; many contain melatonin or herbs with no pediatric safety data.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Melatonin and Children's Sleep.National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Melatonin: What You Need To Know.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# Does teething medicine help a baby sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/teething-medicine-and-baby-sleep/

Does teething medicine help a baby sleep?
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen can relieve real teething pain for a few hours when your pediatrician says they are appropriate for your baby’s age and weight, but they do not make a baby sleep, and most “teething” night waking is not teething. If waking persists beyond a few nights, treat it as a sleep pattern, not a tooth.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
What teething does and does not do
Teething can cause gum soreness, drooling, chewing and fussiness for a few days around eruption. Studies that tracked babies through eruption found it does not reliably cause high fever, diarrhea or weeks of sleep disruption. When a parent tells us a baby has been “teething” for a month, what we usually find is a sleep association that teething briefly disguised.
The medicines, from a pharmacist
Acetaminophen (Tylenol and generics) is a pain and fever reliever. It is the usual first choice in young infants. Dosing is by weight, and infant and children’s concentrations differ, so use the measuring device that came with the product and the dose your pediatrician or the label gives for your child. Never estimate.
Ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil and generics) also reduces inflammation. It is generally not used under 6 months, and should be given with food or milk. Again, by weight, as directed.
Neither is a sleep aid. They relieve pain for a few hours. If the baby sleeps better, the pain was real. If nothing changes, the waking has another cause.
Avoid: benzocaine gels (Orajel and similar) in children under 2 — the FDA warns of methemoglobinemia, a dangerous blood-oxygen problem; homeopathic teething tablets, which have had quality and belladonna-content problems; amber necklaces, which are a strangulation and choking hazard and have no mechanism.
Teething and your sleep plan
A genuinely uncomfortable baby gets comfort. Give pain relief if your pediatrician agrees, offer a cold teether before bed, then follow the same bedtime and response you always use. Changing the sleep routine for teething is how a three-day event becomes a three-month habit.
Frequently asked
Can I give Tylenol before bed every night for teething?No. Routine nightly dosing is not appropriate for teething and can mask other problems. Use it for clear discomfort, as your pediatrician directs, for a short period.
How long does teething disrupt sleep?Typically a few nights around a tooth breaking through. Longer than that points to a sleep pattern.
Do teething gels help at night?Benzocaine gels are not recommended for children under 2 and wash away quickly in any case. A chilled teether is safer and works about as well.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Acetaminophen for Fever and Pain.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Ibuprofen for Fever and Pain.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Safely Soothing Teething Pain and Sensory Needs in Babies and Older Children.

# Which over-the-counter medicines affect a baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/otc-medicines-and-infant-sleep/

Which over-the-counter medicines affect a baby’s sleep?
Fever and pain relievers can help a sick baby rest but do not cause sleep; antihistamines and cough-and-cold products should not be used for sleep in young children at all; gas drops and gripe water are largely inert for sleep. No over-the-counter product is a substitute for a sleep plan, and every one of them is a pediatrician decision in a baby.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
A pharmacist’s map of the medicine aisle
ProductWhat it doesEffect on sleepCautions
AcetaminophenPain and feverIndirect: a comfortable baby rests. Not sedating.Weight-based dosing; watch for duplicate acetaminophen in combination products.
IbuprofenPain, fever, inflammationIndirect, same as above.Generally not under 6 months; give with food.
Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)AntihistamineSedating in adults; in young children can cause agitation, and overdose is dangerous.Not for sleep in children. Not recommended under 2 without a physician.
Cough and cold productsDecongestants, cough suppressantsNone useful; decongestants can cause wakefulness.FDA: do not use in children under 2; manufacturers label 4+.
Simethicone (gas drops)Breaks up gas bubblesEssentially none in trials.Low risk, low benefit.
Gripe waterHerbal/sugar mixtureNo evidence.Unregulated; some products have had contamination issues. Avoid versions with alcohol.
Saline drops and suctionClears noseReal help for a congested baby who cannot feed or breathe well lying down.Use before feeds and sleep; do not overdo suction.
The pattern behind the aisle
Everything that helps does so by removing discomfort so the baby’s own sleep can happen. Nothing in the aisle teaches a baby to fall asleep or stay asleep. If your baby sleeps badly when well, the answer is in the routine, the schedule and the sleep association, not the pharmacy.
When to call the pediatrician instead
Fever in a baby under 3 months; trouble breathing; refusing feeds; fewer wet diapers; a baby who is hard to wake; any question about dose. Those are not sleep questions.
Frequently asked
Can Benadryl help my baby sleep on a flight?Pediatricians advise against it. It can cause the opposite reaction in young children and dosing errors are a real risk.
Do gas drops help a baby sleep?Trials have not shown simethicone to reduce crying or improve sleep. It is generally safe but rarely the fix.
Is it okay to give medicine ‘just in case’ before bed?No. Give a medicine for a reason, at the dose and interval your pediatrician or the label specifies.

# Do reflux medications help a baby sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/reflux-medication-and-baby-sleep/

Do reflux medications help a baby sleep?
Only when the baby has true acid-related disease (GERD), which is less common than the symptoms suggest. Most spitty, fussy babies have ordinary reflux that medication does not improve, and pediatric gastroenterology guidelines recommend feeding and positioning changes first. When a pediatrician does prescribe an acid suppressant, sleep usually improves only to the degree pain was the cause.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
Reflux versus GERD
Nearly all babies reflux: the valve at the top of the stomach is immature, they are on a liquid diet, and they lie flat. Spitting up without distress is normal and resolves with age. GERD is reflux that causes problems: poor weight gain, feeding refusal, pain with feeds, blood in spit-up, or breathing complications. Only the second group benefits from medication.
The medications
Famotidine (Pepcid) is an H2 blocker: it reduces acid production. Onset within an hour, modest effect, tolerance can develop within weeks.
Omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole are proton-pump inhibitors: stronger and longer acid suppression. They take days to reach full effect and are typically given before a feed. Guidelines recommend short, defined trials with a clear stopping point, because long-term acid suppression in infants is associated with higher rates of certain infections and other concerns.
What they do not do: reduce how often a baby spits up. They change the acidity of what comes up, not the volume. If the problem is volume or discomfort from a full stomach, feeding changes matter more.
What usually helps more
Smaller, more frequent feeds; thorough burping; 20–30 minutes upright after feeds.
For formula-fed babies, your pediatrician may trial a thickened or hydrolyzed formula; for breastfed babies, a time-limited maternal dairy elimination if cow’s-milk protein allergy is suspected.
Always flat and on the back for sleep. Inclined sleepers and wedges are not safe and are not an effective reflux treatment.
Where sleep coaching fits
Once reflux is managed and weight gain is on track, most reflux babies sleep poorly for the same reasons as other babies: how they fall asleep. They tend to have been (rightly) picked up at every sound, so the plan goes gently and rebuilds trust in the crib. That is coaching work, not pharmacy work.
Frequently asked
My baby is on omeprazole and still wakes a lot. Why?Acid suppression only helps the portion of waking that pain caused. Remaining wake-ups are usually sleep associations, which a plan addresses. Also ask your pediatrician whether the medication is still needed.
Should my reflux baby sleep on an incline?No. The AAP and CPSC advise against inclined sleep products for all infants. Flat, on the back, in a crib or bassinet.
When do babies outgrow reflux?Most improve substantially by 6–12 months as the valve matures, solids start and the baby spends more time upright.
ReferencesRosen R, et al. Pediatric Gastroesophageal Reflux Clinical Practice Guidelines: Joint Recommendations of NASPGHAN and ESPGHAN. J Pediatr Gastroenterol Nutr. 2018.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.

# Does my caffeine affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/caffeine-breastfeeding-and-baby-sleep/

Does my caffeine affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
A little. Caffeine passes into breast milk at low levels and peaks about one to two hours after you drink it, but a newborn clears caffeine extremely slowly — a half-life of days rather than hours — so it can accumulate in the first months. Moderate intake (commonly cited as up to about 300 mg a day, roughly two to three cups of coffee) is considered compatible with breastfeeding; if your young baby is unusually jittery or wakeful, cutting back is a reasonable experiment.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
The pharmacology in plain terms
Transfer is low. Roughly 1% of the mother’s dose reaches the baby through milk.
Clearance is slow in newborns. An adult clears half a dose of caffeine in about 4–6 hours. A newborn can take 2–4 days. By 4–6 months, clearance approaches adult speed. That is why a small daily amount can build up in a very young baby and why the effect fades with age.
Timing helps. Milk caffeine peaks 1–2 hours after you drink it. Having coffee right after a feed rather than right before one lowers what the baby gets.
What to watch for
Unusual jitteriness, wide-eyed wakefulness at odd hours, or fussiness that tracks with your intake. If you see that, cut back for a week and compare. If nothing changes, caffeine was not the driver — and in our experience it usually is not. Night waking in a 4-month-old is far more often a sleep-cycle and sleep-association story than a coffee story.
Other sources people forget
Energy drinks, pre-workout powders, some teas, dark chocolate, cola, and over-the-counter products that include caffeine (some headache remedies). Pre-workout products in particular can contain several hundred milligrams per serving.
Frequently asked
How much coffee can I drink while breastfeeding?Up to about 300 mg of caffeine a day is widely considered compatible with breastfeeding; many clinicians are comfortable somewhat higher. Discuss your situation with your pediatrician or lactation consultant.
Does caffeine lower milk supply?There is no good evidence that moderate caffeine reduces supply.
Should I pump and dump after coffee?No. Caffeine leaves milk as it leaves your blood; pumping does not speed that up.
ReferencesDrugs and Lactation Database (LactMed), National Library of Medicine. Caffeine.Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed), National Library of Medicine.

# Which of my medications could affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/medications-while-breastfeeding-and-infant-sleep/

Which of my medications could affect my breastfed baby’s sleep?
Most medications are compatible with breastfeeding, but a handful that reach milk can make a baby drowsier or more restless: sedating antihistamines, some sleep aids, certain antidepressants in the early weeks, opioid pain relievers after delivery, and decongestants. The authoritative free reference is LactMed from the National Library of Medicine; check it, and ask your pharmacist or pediatrician about anything you take regularly.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
Categories worth a conversation
Medication typePossible effect on baby’s sleepNotes
Sedating antihistamines (diphenhydramine, doxylamine — including in “PM” products)Drowsiness or, paradoxically, irritabilityNon-sedating options (loratadine, cetirizine) are generally preferred while nursing.
Opioid pain relievers (codeine, tramadol, oxycodone) after birthExcess sleepiness, poor feedingCodeine and tramadol are specifically cautioned against in nursing mothers. Short courses only, with monitoring.
SSRIs and other antidepressantsUsually minimal; some reports of irritability or sleep changes in early infancy with certain agentsUntreated postpartum depression harms infant sleep and development more. Sertraline and paroxetine have the most reassuring data. Do not stop a medication without your prescriber.
Decongestants (pseudoephedrine)Irritability; can also reduce milk supplySaline and steam are preferred.
Prescription sleep aids (zolpidem and similar)Low transfer, but caution with co-sleeping and night feeds because of maternal sedationDiscuss with prescriber; never bed-share while sedated.
Combined hormonal contraceptionNo direct sleep effect; may reduce supply if started earlyProgestin-only methods are usually preferred in the early months.
How to think about it
Three questions decide most cases: How much reaches milk? How well does a baby this age clear it? Is there a safer alternative that works as well? LactMed answers the first two for nearly every drug. Your pharmacist can answer the third in five minutes — that is literally what we are trained for.
The bigger point
Parents often look for a medication explanation for night waking. It is occasionally the answer in the first weeks. After about 3 months, with a mother on a standard, breastfeeding-compatible regimen, the medication is almost never why the baby wakes at 1, 3 and 5. The sleep association is.
Frequently asked
Where can I check if a medication is safe while breastfeeding?LactMed (free, National Library of Medicine) is the standard reference. InfantRisk Center also runs a helpline. Your pharmacist can look up anything on the spot.
Can I take something to help me sleep while breastfeeding?Talk to your prescriber. Some options are compatible; the main cautions are maternal sedation around night feeds and never bed-sharing while sedated.
Will my antidepressant make my baby sleepy?Usually not meaningfully. Keep taking it unless your prescriber says otherwise; treating postpartum depression protects your baby’s sleep and development.
ReferencesDrugs and Lactation Database (LactMed), National Library of Medicine.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Use Caution When Giving Cough and Cold Products to Kids.

# How do a baby’s sleep cycles and circadian rhythm develop?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-infant-sleep-cycles-develop/

How do a baby’s sleep cycles and circadian rhythm develop?
Newborns have no day–night rhythm and spend about half their sleep in active (REM-like) sleep in short cycles. Between roughly 6 weeks and 4 months the brain organizes sleep into distinct stages, consolidates it toward night, and begins a nightly melatonin rise. By 4 to 6 months most babies have adult-type 90-to-120-minute cycles — which is exactly when sleep associations start causing frequent night waking.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, not your baby’s physician. This guide explains how a medication relates to sleep. Whether and how your child takes any medication is a decision for your pediatrician.
The timeline
AgeWhat the brain is doingWhat you see
0–6 weeksNo circadian rhythm; ultradian cycles of 50–60 minutes; sleep onset through active sleepSleep spread evenly around the clock; day–night confusion
6–12 weeksCortisol and melatonin rhythms begin; longest sleep stretch starts to land at nightOne longer stretch (4–6 hours) emerging in the evening
3–5 monthsSleep reorganizes into NREM stages 1–3 plus REM; sleep onset shifts to NREM; cycles lengthen to 90–120 minutesThe “4-month regression”: more wakings between cycles, especially for babies with sleep associations
6–12 monthsDeep sleep concentrated in the first third of the night; most babies physiologically able to go 10–12 hours without feeding if growing wellNaps consolidate to 2–3; night feeds become habit more than need
12–36 monthsTotal sleep declines slowly; nap drops to 1 between 14–18 months; nighttime fears and bedtime negotiation appearBehavioral sleep problems dominate
Why this matters for sleep training
Every baby surfaces briefly between cycles. The difference between a baby who “sleeps through” and one who wakes four times is what happens in that moment. A baby who fell asleep alone resettles; a baby who fell asleep feeding or rocking calls for the same thing. The maturation at 3–5 months does not create the problem; it reveals it. That is also why 4–6 months is a good window to teach independent sleep onset: cycles are now adult-shaped and habits are shallow.
What supports the rhythm
Bright natural light in the morning and during awake time.
Dim light the hour before bed; a dark room overnight. Light suppresses melatonin, in babies as in adults.
A consistent bedtime in the 6:30–8 p.m. window once the night stretch has emerged.
Feeding and activity on a predictable daytime pattern.
Frequently asked
When do babies start producing melatonin?A measurable nighttime rise typically appears between about 6 and 12 weeks and strengthens over the following months.
Why does my baby wake exactly every 2 hours?Because that is roughly one sleep cycle at 4+ months. The waking is a cycle transition; the crying is the request for the bedtime method.
How much sleep does a baby need?AASM consensus: infants 4–12 months, 12–16 hours per 24 hours including naps; toddlers 1–2 years, 11–14 hours; children 3–5 years, 10–13 hours.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Melatonin and Children's Sleep.

# Is sleep training safe? What the AAP safe-sleep rules mean for a sleep plan
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/safe-sleep-and-sleep-training/

Is sleep training safe? What the AAP safe-sleep rules mean for a sleep plan
Yes, when the sleep plan follows the AAP safe-sleep guidance: baby on the back, on a firm flat surface in a crib or bassinet, with nothing else in the sleep space, in the parents’ room ideally for the first 6 months. Behavioral sleep training in babies over about 4–6 months has been studied in randomized trials and follow-ups to age 5 without evidence of harm to attachment, behavior or stress physiology.
The non-negotiables in every plan
Back to sleep, every sleep, until age 1. Once a baby can roll both ways independently, you do not need to reposition, but you still place them on the back.
Firm, flat surface that meets CPSC standards: crib, bassinet, play yard. Not an incline, not a swing, not a car seat, not an adult bed, not a couch.
Nothing in the sleep space: no bumpers, pillows, blankets, positioners, stuffed animals. Use a sleep sack for warmth.
Room-share, don’t bed-share, ideally for the first 6 months. A plan can teach independent sleep in a bassinet three feet from your bed.
No smoke exposure; offer a pacifier at sleep onset once breastfeeding is established; keep up vaccinations.
Swaddling stops at the first signs of rolling, usually by 8–12 weeks.
What the research says about sleep training itself
Randomized controlled trials of behavioral sleep interventions (graduated extinction, bedtime fading, parent-present methods) in infants over 6 months show improved infant sleep and maternal mood, with no measured differences in cortisol, attachment security or emotional and behavioral outcomes at follow-up, including a five-year follow-up of one of the largest trials. Reasonable people differ on method; the evidence does not support the claim that teaching independent sleep harms babies.
Where coaching adds safety
A written plan removes the 2 a.m. improvisation that leads to unsafe choices: the exhausted parent who brings the baby into bed, falls asleep on the couch holding them, or props a bottle. Families who are sleeping do not make those decisions.
When sleep training should wait
Under about 10–12 weeks adjusted age; during acute illness; when weight gain is a concern; when a pediatrician has flagged a medical sleep issue (for example suspected sleep-disordered breathing). Your pediatrician is the authority on readiness.
Frequently asked
Does cry-it-out cause harm?Studies of behavioral sleep methods, including extinction-based ones, have not found harm to attachment or stress physiology. Our own approach is not unmodified cry-it-out; the plan is designed to minimize crying, with daily coaching.
Can I sleep train while room-sharing?Yes. Many families do, following the AAP recommendation to room-share for the first 6 months.
When can my baby have a blanket or stuffed animal?Not before 12 months. After that, a small lovey is generally fine; discuss with your pediatrician.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Swaddling: Is it Safe for Your Baby?
