# Sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist: which does my baby need?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-vs-pediatric-sleep-specialist/

Sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist: which does my baby need?
A pediatric sleep specialist (a physician or psychologist in sleep medicine) diagnoses and treats medical and clinical sleep disorders: sleep apnea, restless legs, narcolepsy, severe insomnia in older children. A sleep consultant coaches behavioral sleep: how a healthy baby falls asleep and stays asleep. If your pediatrician suspects a medical cause — snoring, pauses in breathing, extreme daytime sleepiness, failure to thrive — see the specialist first. If your baby is healthy and the issue is habit and routine, a consultant is the right tool.
Signs that point to medical evaluation
Loud or regular snoring, gasping, or pauses in breathing during sleep.
Mouth breathing and restless, sweaty sleep in a toddler; very large tonsils.
Poor weight gain, feeding refusal, or pain behaviors with feeds.
Extreme daytime sleepiness beyond normal for age; unusual movements during sleep.
Sleep problems that began after a neurological diagnosis or alongside developmental concerns.
Your pediatrician screens for these at well visits and refers to ENT, pulmonology or a sleep clinic as needed. No sleep consultant should be treating these, and a good one will tell you so.
Signs that point to behavioral coaching
Baby falls asleep only while fed, rocked, held or with a pacifier replaced.
Wakes at roughly cycle intervals (every 1.5–2 hours) and settles immediately with the bedtime method.
Short naps, contact naps, bedtime battles, early waking, a toddler who leaves the bed.
Healthy, growing, happy when awake.
The credential question
“Sleep consultant” is not a regulated title; certifications are issued by private training programs. Judge a consultant by what they ask (medical screening questions), what they refuse to do (treat medical problems), and what they commit to (a written outcome). Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy, which informs the medication and physiology questions families ask; she is not a sleep-medicine physician and says so.
They are not either/or
A child treated for sleep apnea often still has the behavioral habits that formed while sleep was poor. Specialist first, then coaching, is a common and sensible sequence.
Frequently asked
Is a sleep consultant a medical professional?Usually not. Some have clinical backgrounds (nursing, pharmacy, psychology), but the role itself is coaching, not diagnosis or treatment.
Can a sleep consultant diagnose sleep apnea?No. That requires a physician and often a sleep study. A consultant should refer you back to your pediatrician if they hear snoring or breathing pauses.
My pediatrician said ‘they’ll grow out of it.’ Now what?Many do, eventually. If the waiting is costing your health or work, behavioral coaching is reasonable for a healthy baby over about 4 months.

# What is the best age to sleep train a baby?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/best-age-to-sleep-train/

What is the best age to sleep train a baby?
Between about 4 and 6 months is the sweet spot for most babies: sleep cycles have matured, most babies can go long stretches without feeding if growing well, and habits are still shallow. You can shape sleep from around 10–12 weeks with gentler steps, and you can successfully train at any age after that, including toddlers; it simply takes more consistency the longer a habit has existed.
By age
AgeWhat is realisticNotes
0–10 weeksShaping, not training: day–night differentiation, full feeds, putting down drowsy when it worksNo formal method. Feed on cue. Safe sleep above all.
10–16 weeksBegin separating feeding from falling asleep; consistent bedtime routine; practice putting down awakeExpect partial wins. Night feeds continue.
4–6 monthsFull independent sleep onset; most babies down to 0–1 night feeds with pediatrician agreementThe best window. Fastest results, least protest.
6–12 monthsFully trainable; separation anxiety (8–10 months) and mobility add some noiseStill typically 3–7 nights for nights.
12–24 monthsTrainable in a crib; toddler negotiation beginsConsistency matters more than ever.
2–3 yearsTrainable; bed vs crib is the big variableKeep the crib as long as safely possible; a bed adds freedom to leave.
Why 4–6 months works best
Sleep cycles are now adult-shaped, so what you teach at bedtime transfers to every cycle. Night feeding needs have dropped for most well-growing babies. The baby cannot yet stand, crawl or climb, so protest is vocal rather than physical. And the sleep association is only a few months old.
Starting earlier than 4 months
Starting young is the gentlest route, because there is no habit to undo. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage: the early work is foundations, night feeds are never dropped by the plan, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks. Feeding and weight gain stay with your pediatrician.
Corrected age for premature babies
Count from the due date, not the birth date, and get your pediatrician’s sign-off on night feeds. NICU graduates often do very well with coaching once weight gain is solid.
Frequently asked
Is 3 months too early to sleep train?Too early for formal methods; the right time to start shaping habits gently. Full training usually waits until about 4 months.
Is it too late to sleep train a 2 year old?No. Toddlers respond quickly to clear, consistent boundaries. It is harder in a bed than a crib.
Can I sleep train during a regression?Usually yes; the 4-month change is permanent, so there is nothing to wait out. For illness, pause and resume the same plan.

# What are the right wake windows by age?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/wake-windows-by-age/

What are the right wake windows by age?
Roughly 45–90 minutes for newborns, 1.5–2.5 hours at 4–6 months, 2–3.5 hours at 6–9 months, 3–4 hours at 9–12 months, and 4–6 hours once a toddler is on one nap. These are starting points, not rules: watch your baby’s cues and the quality of the sleep that follows, and adjust in 15-minute steps.
Starting points
AgeWake windowNaps per dayTotal sleep per 24 h (AASM)
0–4 weeks45–60 min5+14–17 h (NSF)
1–3 months60–90 min4–514–17 h (NSF)
3–4 months75 min–2 h3–412–16 h
4–6 months1.5–2.5 h312–16 h
6–9 months2–3.5 h2–312–16 h
9–12 months3–4 h212–16 h
12–18 months3–4.5 h (2 naps) / 4–5.5 h (1 nap)2 → 111–14 h
18–36 months5–6 h111–14 h
How to read your baby, not the chart
Too short a window: long time to fall asleep, playing or babbling in the crib, short nap, early waking.
Too long a window: fussy or wired before sleep, crying at put-down, short nap, frequent night waking, early waking.
Both produce short naps, which is why “my baby only naps 30 minutes” needs the schedule checked before the method is blamed.
Rules of thumb
The first window of the day is usually the shortest; the last before bed is usually the longest. Move one thing at a time, by 15 minutes, and hold it for three days before judging. Bedtime between 6:30 and 8 p.m. for most babies past the newborn stage.
Frequently asked
Are wake windows or sleepy cues more important?Use windows as the frame and cues to fine-tune. By 4–5 months many babies stop showing clear cues until they are already overtired, so the clock becomes the better guide.
Why are my baby’s naps only 30 minutes?One sleep cycle. Usually a schedule mismatch or a sleep association that prevents linking cycles. Fix nights first, then naps.
When do babies drop to one nap?Most between 14 and 18 months. Dropping earlier usually causes night waking.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.

# When do babies drop naps, and how do I handle the 3-to-2 and 2-to-1 transitions?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/nap-transitions-3-to-2-to-1/

When do babies drop naps, and how do I handle the 3-to-2 and 2-to-1 transitions?
Most babies go from 3 naps to 2 between 6 and 8 months, and from 2 naps to 1 between 14 and 18 months. The signs are consistent: the last nap is refused or pushes bedtime late for two weeks or more. Handle it by lengthening wake windows gradually and moving bedtime earlier for a few weeks, not by dropping the nap abruptly on one bad day.
Signs a transition is real (versus a bad week)
The last nap is consistently refused or takes 30+ minutes to happen, for 10–14 days.
Naps are fine but bedtime is being pushed past 8:30 p.m. to fit them.
Early morning waking appears with no other change.
One bad day, an illness or travel is not a transition. Hold the schedule and wait.
3 to 2 naps (about 6–8 months)
Stretch the first two wake windows by 15 minutes every few days until the day holds two naps of 1–2 hours.
Move bedtime earlier (even 6 p.m.) on days the second nap ends early. Early bedtime is the shock absorber.
Expect 1–2 weeks of some days with three naps and some with two.
2 to 1 nap (about 14–18 months)
Push the morning nap later by 15–30 minutes every few days, aiming for a single nap starting around 12–12:30.
Protect bedtime: move it to 6–6:30 p.m. during the transition.
Offer a quiet-time or a short late catnap if the day falls apart, then resume the push.
Give it 2–4 weeks. This is the longest transition.
The common mistake
Dropping the second nap at 12 months because of a few refusals. Twelve-month-olds are usually in a regression, not a transition; hold two naps and the refusals pass. A premature 2-to-1 transition produces weeks of night waking and early rising.
Frequently asked
My 12 month old refuses the second nap. Is it time for one nap?Usually not. Twelve months is a regression age; most toddlers still need two naps until 14–18 months. Hold the schedule for two weeks before deciding.
How long should the single nap be?Typically 2–3 hours once established, usually starting around midday.
When do toddlers stop napping entirely?Most between 3 and 5 years. Keep a quiet rest time after the nap goes.

# Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/early-morning-waking/

Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?
Early waking is almost always a schedule problem, a light problem, or a sleep-association problem — usually in that order. Check that bedtime is not too late (overtiredness causes early waking, counterintuitively), that the room is fully dark at 5 a.m., and that your baby can fall back asleep without your help. Then hold a firm “morning starts at 6” line for two weeks.
Work through the causes in order
Bedtime too late. An overtired baby produces more cortisol and sleeps lighter in the early morning. Try moving bedtime 30 minutes earlier for a week. This fixes more early waking than anything else.
Naps too long or too late. A late afternoon nap or too much total daytime sleep lowers sleep pressure for the end of the night. Cap the last nap so it ends by about 4 p.m.
Light. The sun is up, or a hallway light is on. Early morning sleep is the lightest of the night; any light becomes a cue to wake. Blackout the room properly — test it at 5 a.m.
Sleep association. The 5 a.m. waking is a cycle transition, and the baby cannot get back down without the bedtime method. Solving bedtime solves 5 a.m.
Reinforced waking. If 5 a.m. means milk, a parent’s bed or screen time, it becomes the best part of the day. Keep the morning boring until the set wake time.
Hunger is occasionally real in a baby under 6 months or one dropping a night feed. Offer more during the day.
The hold-the-line protocol
Choose a wake time (6 a.m. is realistic for most babies). Before that time, treat the waking exactly as you would a 2 a.m. waking: same response, no milk, no lights, no leaving the room for the day. At the set time, open the curtains, turn on lights, greet cheerfully. The contrast teaches the clock. Expect 1–2 weeks.
Frequently asked
Is 6 a.m. a normal wake time for a baby?Yes. Most babies wake between 6 and 7 a.m. Getting a baby to sleep until 8 is rarely realistic.
Will a later bedtime make my baby sleep later?Usually the opposite. Overtiredness causes earlier waking. Try earlier first.
Do toddler sleep-training clocks work?They help from about 2.5–3 years, once the child understands the color change. They do not work for babies.

# Why does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/short-naps-30-minutes/

Why does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?
A 30–45 minute nap is one sleep cycle; the baby wakes at the transition and cannot link to the next cycle. The usual causes are a wake window that is slightly off, a sleep association that worked at nap onset but is missing at the transition, or a room that is not dark enough. Fix the schedule first, teach independent sleep onset at bedtime, then give the nap a chance to extend by waiting a few minutes before intervening.
Why naps are the last thing to improve
Daytime sleep pressure is lower, naps are short by nature in the first months, and the body’s clock does not help as it does at night. Many babies under 5–6 months take short naps regardless of anything you do; it is developmental. Past that age, short naps are fixable.
The checklist
Schedule. Both too short and too long a wake window produce a 30-minute nap. Adjust by 15 minutes, hold for three days.
Onset. If the baby falls asleep being fed or rocked, the cycle transition reproduces the problem. Nap onset should look like bedtime onset: down awake.
Environment. Darker than you think. White noise continuous, not on a timer. Comfortable temperature.
The pause. When the baby stirs at 30 minutes, wait a set number of minutes before going in. Many babies resettle if given the chance; going in immediately ends the nap every time.
Crib hour. For babies over 5–6 months, keep the nap period to a consistent length in the crib even if the sleep is short, so the body learns the window. Do not leave a distressed baby; this is for a calm or grumbling baby.
Rescue the day. After a short nap, shorten the next wake window a little so overtiredness does not compound.
Realistic expectations
Nights usually improve in a week. Naps typically take 2–4 weeks after that to consolidate, and the first nap of the day lengthens first. Short afternoon catnaps are normal until the 3-to-2 transition.
Frequently asked
Are 30 minute naps normal?Under about 5 months, yes. Past 6 months, consistent 30-minute naps usually mean a schedule or sleep-association issue.
Should I wake my baby from a long nap?Cap naps that would push bedtime late, and wake a newborn for feeds if your pediatrician says so. Otherwise a long nap is fine.
Can I hold my baby for one nap a day?If you want to, yes — choose which one and keep it consistent so the baby knows what to expect at the others.

# My toddler won’t stay in bed. How do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed/

My toddler won’t stay in bed. How do I fix it?
First, if your child is under 3 and still fits safely in a crib, consider going back to it; most bed problems are a too-early crib exit. If a bed is where you are, the fix is a short consistent routine, a clear rule (“we stay in bed until the light turns green”), and a boring, silent, repeated return to bed every single time they get up — dozens of times the first night if needed, fewer each night after. Most toddlers stop within one to two weeks.
Before anything else: crib or bed?
The AAP suggests waiting until closer to 3 for a bed unless the child is climbing out dangerously. A 20-month-old in a bed has freedom with no impulse control. If you moved early, moving back is not a failure; it is often the fastest fix. If climbing is the issue, lower the mattress, use a sleep sack (it limits leg lift), and remove anything used as a step.
If the bed is staying
Make the room safe enough to be unsupervised. Anchored furniture, covered outlets, a gate or closed door, nothing climbable. Assume the child will be up alone.
A short routine with a clear ending. Same order nightly, 20–30 minutes, ending with one phrase that means “done.” No renegotiation after it.
State the rule once. “You stay in bed until the light is green.” A toddler clock helps from about 2.5 years.
The silent return. Every time the child gets up, walk them back without talking, without eye contact, without a cuddle, and leave. The first night may be 30–50 returns. It drops fast when the payoff is zero.
Pre-empt the requests. Water bottle in reach, last bathroom trip in the routine, one “bedtime pass” they can trade for one visit if that fits your child.
Morning reward, not bedtime bribes: a sticker or praise at wake-up for staying in bed.
What makes it worse
Lying down with them “just tonight.” Letting them fall asleep on the couch. Long explanations at 9 p.m. Getting angry (attention is attention). Inconsistency between parents. Each of these resets the count.
Frequently asked
Should I lock my toddler’s door?A gate at the door or a door knob cover is a common compromise; many families use a closed door for safety. Whatever you choose, the room itself must be fully childproofed.
How long will the silent return take to work?Typically a dramatic drop in 3–4 nights and near-zero in 1–2 weeks, if it is done every time.
My toddler is scared of the dark. Is that real?Fears emerge around 2–3 years and are real. A dim warm nightlight and a consistent, calm response help; staying in the room until they fall asleep tends to prolong it.

# Why is my 8, 9 or 10 month old suddenly waking at night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/8-to-10-month-sleep-regression/

Why is my 8, 9 or 10 month old suddenly waking at night?
The 8–10 month period stacks three things at once: new gross motor skills (crawling, pulling to stand) that get practiced in the crib, the peak of separation anxiety, and the 3-to-2 nap transition. Keep the response to night waking exactly what it was, practice the new skills in daylight, protect two solid naps, and expect 2–3 weeks. A previously independent sleeper usually returns to baseline in a few nights.
What is happening
Motor leaps. A baby who just learned to stand will stand up in the crib at 2 a.m. and may not know how to get down. Practice sitting down from standing during the day, many times. At night, lay them down once and leave; repeating it becomes a game.
Separation anxiety. Object permanence has arrived: the baby now knows you exist when you leave, and protests. A predictable routine and a brief, confident goodbye reassure more than lingering does.
Nap transition. The third nap is disappearing, and a day with too little daytime sleep produces a worse night. Move bedtime earlier on short-nap days.
Teething and illness ride along but rarely explain weeks of waking.
What to do
Do not introduce anything new at night: no return of night feeds, rocking to sleep or bed-sharing unless you plan to keep them.
Hold the nap schedule; two naps totaling 2.5–3.5 hours; bedtime 6:30–7:30 p.m.
Daytime practice for every new skill, especially getting down from standing.
If the baby never slept independently, this is a fine age to start; separation anxiety is not a reason to wait, and the plan accounts for it.
Frequently asked
How long does the 8 month sleep regression last?Typically 2–3 weeks with a consistent response; longer if new habits are introduced during it.
Should I feed my 9 month old at night during the regression?If your baby was not feeding at night before, do not restart. Offer more during the day.
My baby stands in the crib and cries. What do I do?Lay them down once, calmly, and leave. Then practice sitting down from standing during the day until they can do it alone.

# Is the 18 month sleep regression real, and what do I do about it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/18-month-sleep-regression/

Is the 18 month sleep regression real, and what do I do about it?
Yes, and it is mostly a toddler-development story: new independence and testing, language exploding faster than self-control, separation anxiety returning, molars, and the 2-to-1 nap transition. The fix is boundaries, not new comforts: a tight routine, the same response every night, two naps held until they are clearly done, and patience for 2–6 weeks.
Why 18 months is different
Earlier regressions are about sleep physiology. This one is about a person: an 18-month-old wants control, has opinions, and has discovered that bedtime protest gets a reaction. It overlaps with molars (real but brief), the nap transition (real and long), and a second wave of separation anxiety.
What works
Routine with limited choices. “Red pajamas or blue?” gives control where it is harmless. The order and the ending do not change.
Same response at night. Brief, boring, consistent. Toddlers are expert at finding the one thing that works on you.
Nap schedule. If still on two naps, hold them until the second is refused for two weeks. If transitioning, one nap around midday and an early bedtime.
Keep the crib. This is not the moment to move to a bed. Regressions and transitions compound.
Daytime connection. Twenty minutes of undivided attention before the routine reduces bedtime stalling more than most tricks.
Molars and medicine
First molars often arrive around 13–19 months and can hurt. Pain relief for a clearly uncomfortable toddler, as your pediatrician directs, is reasonable for a night or two. A new sleep habit started during those nights will outlast the tooth by months.
Frequently asked
How long does the 18 month regression last?Two to six weeks is typical. It runs longer when new habits are introduced during it.
Should I move my 18 month old to a toddler bed?No. Most experts suggest waiting until closer to 3 unless there is a safety reason.
Is my toddler manipulating me?Testing, not manipulating. Toddlers learn what works. A calm, consistent response teaches them that protest does not change the outcome.

# How do you sleep train twins?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-twins/

How do you sleep train twins?
The same way as one baby, on the same schedule, in the same room, with the expectation that one will wake the other less often than you fear. Synchronize feeds and naps from the start, put both down awake at the same time, respond to each by the plan rather than rushing to prevent noise, and accept that the first week is louder. Most twin families see both babies sleeping through within the same two weeks.
Principles that matter more with twins
Same schedule, always. If one wakes to feed, feed both (or wake the other within 15–20 minutes). Staggered twins mean no sleep for anyone.
Same room. Twins habituate to each other’s noise faster than you expect. Separating them for training usually just postpones the problem. White noise helps.
Do not referee. Rushing in to keep one from waking the other teaches both that crying brings you fast. Follow the plan for each baby individually.
Treat them as individuals within the plan. One may be a faster learner; the plan accounts for temperament. Do not hold the easier sleeper to the harder one’s pace.
Two adults, one method. Decide in advance who handles which baby and that both respond identically.
Premature twins
Many twins arrive early. Use corrected age for readiness, get the pediatrician’s sign-off on night feeds for each baby separately, and expect that weight gain, not the calendar, decides when night feeds go.
Why coaching helps disproportionately for twins
There is twice as much data every night and half as much parental capacity to interpret it. A coach reading both babies’ logs each morning and telling you which adjustment to make is the difference between a hard week and a hard season.
Frequently asked
Will one twin wake the other?Occasionally in the first days, then rarely. Babies habituate to a roommate quickly; adults are usually the ones who cannot sleep through it.
Should twins sleep in the same crib?No. The AAP recommends a separate sleep surface for each baby.
Can twins be on different schedules?They can, but it doubles the work and is rarely sustainable. Synchronize feeds and naps as early as possible.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# How do I sleep train my baby? A step-by-step guide
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-sleep-train-a-baby/

How do I sleep train my baby? A step-by-step guide
Sleep training means teaching a baby to fall asleep in the crib without being fed, rocked or held to sleep, so they can link sleep cycles on their own overnight. Many families start between 4 and 6 months. Spend a week fixing schedule, routine and room, then hold one method consistently for 2 weeks. Nights often improve within a week; naps take longer.
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
Step 1: Check readiness
Start when every line below is true. If one is not, fix that first.
Age: at least 4 months (corrected age for babies born early). The AAP’s parent site notes that babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months, and from that age suggests putting babies down before they are asleep so they learn to fall asleep on their own. Before that, shape habits gently rather than train; see the best age to sleep train.
Health: growing well, no current illness, and your pediatrician has told you how many night feeds your baby still needs.
Safe sleep space: on the back, on a firm, flat mattress in an empty crib or bassinet. No inclines, wedges, positioners, bumpers or loose blankets. Swaddle off once there are signs of rolling.
Calendar: 2 weeks with no travel, house move, new childcare or visitors sleeping in the baby’s room.
Adults: everyone who does bedtime agrees on the plan and will respond the same way at 2 a.m.
Step 2: Prep week
Most failed attempts skip this. Spend 5 to 7 days on the foundations before you change how your baby falls asleep.
Log 3 days. Write down wake time, naps, feeds, bedtime and every night waking. The pattern usually shows the cause.
Fix the schedule. Set a wake time within the same 30 minutes daily and age-appropriate wake windows. A baby who is under-tired or badly overtired will protest any method.
Move the feed. Put the last feed at the start of the bedtime routine, with lights on, so your baby finishes it awake. This loosens the feed-to-sleep association before night one.
Build a 20–30 minute routine. Same steps, same order: feed, bath or wash, diaper, sleep sack, book, song, crib.
Set the room. Dark enough that you cannot read, continuous white noise at a moderate volume placed away from the crib, comfortably cool.
Decide night feeds in advance. Write down which feeds stay, roughly when, and how you will respond to every other waking.
Step 3: Choose a method
All of these teach the same skill. They differ in how much you are present and how fast they work. The method you can carry out consistently is the right one.
MethodWhat you doTypical time for nightsSuits
Timed checks (Ferber)Leave awake; return for brief checks at lengthening intervals3–7 nightsBabies 5–6 months and up; parents who want a clear script
Extinction (cry it out)Leave awake; do not return except for planned feeds and safety3–5 nightsBabies who escalate when they see a parent
Chair methodSit beside the crib and move the chair out over about 2 weeks1–3 weeksParents who want to stay in the room; older babies and toddlers
Pick up, put downPick up to calm, put down awake, repeat1–3 weeksYounger babies, roughly 3–6 months
Bedtime fadingMove bedtime later to match real sleep onset, then walk it earlier1–3 weeksLong bedtime battles; often paired with another method
The times in this table are typical ranges from practice when a method is applied consistently, not results from a trial. A side-by-side view is in methods compared.
Step 4: Night by night
This is a common pattern, not a research finding. Your baby may move faster or slower.
Night 1. Routine, then into the crib fully awake. Expect the longest protest of the process, commonly 30 to 60 minutes and sometimes longer. Respond exactly as your method says. Treat night wakings the same way, apart from planned feeds.
Night 2. Often similar or a little shorter. Occasionally worse than night 1.
Night 3. Usually a clear drop in time to fall asleep. Some babies have a late surge here (an “extinction burst”) just before things settle.
Nights 4–7. Most babies fall asleep within 5 to 15 minutes with little or no crying, and night wakings shrink to the planned feeds.
Week 2. Consolidation. Early mornings and naps are still improving. A brief relapse around days 10–14 is common and passes if your response stays the same.
More detail by method is in how long sleep training takes.
Step 5: Naps
Daytime sleep pressure is lower, so naps lag behind nights. Many families start with bedtime and add naps on day 2 or 3. Use the same method, give each nap attempt up to about an hour in the crib, and if no sleep happens, get the baby up and try again at the next window. Keep one consistent approach for at least a week before judging it. Thirty-minute naps are usually the last thing to lengthen.
Common mistakes
Drowsy instead of awake. A baby put down nearly asleep has not practiced falling asleep.
Inconsistent responses. Holding out for 40 minutes and then rocking to sleep teaches a baby to cry for 40 minutes.
Switching methods every night or two. Give one method 7 nights.
A bedtime that is too late. Overtired babies fight sleep harder and wake earlier.
Bedtime only. Training bedtime but feeding or rocking back to sleep at every waking keeps the old habit alive.
Starting during illness or travel. Pause, then restart cleanly.
When to get help
Stop and call your pediatrician if your baby snores or gasps in sleep, seems to be in pain, is feeding poorly, or is not gaining weight. If your baby is healthy and you have been fully consistent for 7 to 10 nights without clear progress, the plan needs changing, not more effort; see what to do when sleep training is not working. That is also the point where 1:1 coaching earns its place. At Actually Sleeping, Dr. Sam writes a custom plan for your baby, is on live support on Night 1, checks in daily, and coaches naps until they are solid. The approach is not cry it out and not wait it out. See how it works.
Frequently asked
What is the easiest sleep training method?There is no single easiest method. Timed checks are the simplest to follow because the script is clear; the chair method feels easier emotionally for many parents but takes longer and demands more patience. The easiest one is the one both caregivers can repeat the same way every night.
How long does it take to sleep train a baby?As a rule of thumb from practice, nights often improve within about a week with check-based methods and over 1 to 3 weeks with gradual, parent-present methods. Naps usually take longer. Plan on 2 weeks of consistency.
Do I have to stop night feeds to sleep train?No. Sleep training teaches falling asleep independently; night weaning is a separate decision. Keep the feeds your pediatrician says your baby needs and apply your method to the other wakings.
Can I sleep train without letting my baby cry?You can choose methods where you stay with your baby and respond throughout, which usually means less intense crying. No method can promise zero protest, because any change to how a baby falls asleep is frustrating at first.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Paruthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.Mindell JA, et al. A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.

# How do I get my baby to sleep through the night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-get-baby-to-sleep-through-the-night/

How do I get my baby to sleep through the night?
Babies sleep through the night when three things line up: they fall asleep at bedtime on their own, their daytime schedule and calories suit their age, and they no longer need night feeds. Timing varies widely. In one study of 388 babies, 28 to 57 percent of healthy 6- and 12-month-olds were not yet sleeping 6 or 8 hours straight. Before about 4 months, night waking to feed is normal.
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
What “through the night” means
Researchers often define it as 6 or 8 hours of uninterrupted sleep. Parents usually mean 10 to 12 hours. In a Canadian study of 388 babies, 28 to 57 percent of 6- and 12-month-olds did not sleep through by those definitions, and sleeping through was not linked to their later development. Every baby wakes briefly between sleep cycles all night long; a baby who “sleeps through” wakes too, and goes back to sleep without help. See how infant sleep cycles develop.
What is realistic by age
AgeRealistic nightNight feeds
0–3 monthsStretches of 2–5 hoursOn cue; this is normal
4–6 monthsLongest stretch lengthening, often to about 6 hours by 6 months; 10–12 hours in the crib overallCommonly 1–2; some babies need none
6–9 months10–12 hours0–1 for most well-growing babies
9 months–3 years10–12 hoursUsually none, with your pediatrician’s agreement
These are typical ranges from practice, not deadlines, and many healthy babies fall outside them. Your pediatrician decides when night feeds can stop for your baby.
The five things that make it happen
Falling asleep independently at bedtime. This is the largest factor. A baby who is fed or rocked to sleep expects the same at each brief waking between sleep cycles, which in infancy last about 50 minutes. Put your baby down fully awake after the routine.
The right schedule. A consistent morning wake time, age-appropriate wake windows, enough daytime sleep, and a bedtime usually between 6:30 and 8:00 p.m.
Daytime calories. Full feeds every 2.5 to 4 hours in the day, plus solids from around 6 months as your pediatrician advises. Babies who snack all day tend to make it up at night.
A consistent response to night wakings. Decide which wakings are feeds and treat every other waking the same way each time, using one sleep training method.
A sleep space that helps. Dark, cool, white noise, and safe: back, firm flat mattress, empty crib.
What does not work
Cereal in the bottle. The AAP advises against it because it can increase gagging or inhaling the thickened mix. Solids are started at about 6 months, as your pediatrician advises, for nutrition rather than as a sleep tool.
Keeping the baby up later. Overtired babies wake more often and earlier.
Dropping naps. Less daytime sleep usually makes nights worse.
Inclined sleepers, wedges or positioners. These are unsafe for sleep at any age.
Waiting past 6 months for a baby with a strong sleep association. Habits tend to deepen, not fade.
If your baby used to sleep through and stopped
Look for a cause: illness, a new skill such as rolling or standing, a nap transition, or a regression at 4 months, 8 to 10 months or 12 months. Keep your response consistent for 1 to 2 weeks. If new habits crept in during the disruption, a few nights of your original method usually restores sleep.
When it is not behavioral
Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, persistent mouth breathing, poor weight gain, eczema that itches at night or frequent painful spit-up are reasons to see your pediatrician before any sleep plan.
Frequently asked
At what age do babies sleep through the night?It varies widely. The longest stretch often reaches about 6 hours by 6 months, but in one study 28 to 57 percent of healthy 6- and 12-month-olds were not yet sleeping 6 or 8 hours straight. Babies fed or rocked to sleep at bedtime often take longer.
Will a dream feed help my baby sleep through the night?Sometimes. A feed given around 10 to 11 p.m. while the baby stays drowsy can push the long stretch into the parents’ sleeping hours for babies under about 6 months. If it does not reduce later wakings within a week, drop it.
Why does my baby wake at the same time every night?Wakings at predictable times usually fall at sleep-cycle transitions. A baby who needs help to fall asleep at bedtime needs the same help at those transitions. Habitual feeds at a fixed time can also set an internal hunger alarm.
Is it normal for a 1 year old not to sleep through the night?It is common, and it is usually fixable. Many healthy 1-year-olds no longer need night feeds, so waking is often a sleep association or a schedule problem. Confirm feeding needs with your pediatrician, then address the habit.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Paruthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.Pennestri MH, et al. Uninterrupted Infant Sleep, Development, and Maternal Mood. Pediatrics. 2018.Patel AK, et al. Physiology, Sleep Stages. StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf (NIH).HealthyChildren.org (AAP). # What is the Ferber method, and does it work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/ferber-method-explained/

What is the Ferber method, and does it work?
The Ferber method, also called graduated extinction or timed checks, means putting your baby down awake, leaving the room, and returning for brief checks at gradually longer intervals until they fall asleep. It has randomized-trial support, mostly in babies 6 months and older, and nights often improve within a week. It is not cry it out, because you keep checking.
How it works
Finish a calm bedtime routine with the feed at the start, not the end.
Put your baby in the crib awake, say a short goodnight phrase, and leave.
If your baby cries, wait a set interval, then go in for 1 to 2 minutes. Use a calm voice and perhaps a brief pat. Do not pick up, feed or stay until asleep.
Leave again while your baby is still awake and wait a longer interval.
Repeat until your baby is asleep. Do the same at night wakings, apart from planned feeds.
Lengthen the intervals each night.
A typical interval schedule
The chart below is an example of a lengthening-wait pattern, not a fixed rule. You can adjust the numbers. What matters is that the waits grow and that checks stay short.
NightFirst checkSecond checkLater checks
13 minutes5 minutes10 minutes
25 minutes10 minutes12 minutes
310 minutes12 minutes15 minutes
4 and afterKeep adding a few minutes to each interval per night
What to expect
A common course in practice, not a research finding:
Night 1: commonly 30 to 60 minutes of protest crying, sometimes more.
Nights 2–3: shorter, though one of these nights can be worse than the first.
Nights 4–7: most babies settle within 10 to 15 minutes or less.
Naps: slower, usually 1 to 2 weeks.
Does it work? What the research says
Yes, for most families who apply it consistently. A 2006 review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found support for graduated extinction; its strongest evidence was for unmodified extinction and preventive parent education. In a 2016 randomized trial of 43 babies aged 6 to 16 months, the graduated extinction group fell asleep faster and woke less than the control group. Their cortisol (a stress hormone) showed small-to-moderate declines compared with controls, and there were no differences in attachment or in emotional and behavioral problems 12 months later. The full picture, including the limits of these studies, is in what the research says.
Who it suits, and who it does not
Suits: healthy babies from about 5 to 6 months through the toddler years in a crib; parents who want a clear script and a fast result.
Less suited: babies who become more upset each time a parent appears and leaves (shorter, less frequent checks or a different method may fit better); parents who know they will end up picking the baby up after a long cry; babies under 4 months; any baby who is ill or whose night-feed needs are unclear.
Common mistakes
Checks that turn into 10 minutes of soothing, or rocking to sleep “just this once.”
Feeding at a waking that was not a planned feed.
Using it at bedtime but not at 2 a.m.
Stopping on night 2 or 3, which is often the hardest point and just before improvement.
The method is a general script. It does not tell you whether your baby’s schedule, feeds or room are working against you; those matter as much as the intervals. See the step-by-step guide for the preparation that makes it work.
Frequently asked
What age can you start the Ferber method?Many families start around 5 to 6 months, when night-feed needs have dropped for many babies. The trial evidence comes mostly from babies 6 months and older, and some families start from 4 months. Ask your pediatrician about your baby’s feeds first.
Is the Ferber method the same as cry it out?No. In Ferber you return for brief, timed checks. In cry it out, or unmodified extinction, you do not return until morning apart from planned feeds and safety needs.
How long does the Ferber method take?As a rule of thumb from practice, often 3 to 7 nights for bedtime and night wakings when applied consistently, and 1 to 2 weeks for naps.
What if the checks make my baby cry harder?That happens with some babies, often older ones. Options are to make checks shorter and less frequent, or to use a different method. Do not switch back and forth night to night.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Gradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# What is cry it out (extinction), and is it safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/cry-it-out-extinction-method/

What is cry it out (extinction), and is it safe?
Cry it out, called unmodified extinction in research, means putting a healthy baby down awake after a full bedtime routine and not returning until a planned feed or morning. Studies have not found lasting harm to children’s emotional health, stress regulation or attachment from behavioral sleep training. It often works within a week, is commonly used from about 6 months, and only suits healthy babies in a safe sleep space.
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
What it is, and what it is not
Extinction is a structured method: a loving routine, a fed and dry baby, a safe crib, a set bedtime, planned night feeds if your pediatrician wants them, and a parent who is watching a monitor. It is not ignoring a baby all day, leaving a sick or hungry baby, or closing the door for 12 hours regardless of what happens. You always go in for illness, vomiting, a limb stuck in the crib slats, or anything that sounds wrong.
How it works
Confirm with your pediatrician that your baby is healthy and how many night feeds are needed.
Do the bedtime routine, with the feed first.
Put your baby down awake, say goodnight, leave.
Do not go back in for crying alone. Feed at the planned times, then put down awake again.
Start the day at a set time, at least 10 to 11 hours after bedtime.
Is it safe? What the evidence says
A 2006 review of 52 studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found strong support for unmodified extinction, alongside preventive parent education.
A five-year follow-up of a randomized trial of behavioral sleep techniques found no differences at age 6 in emotional or behavioral problems, stress regulation, or the parent–child relationship. Families in that trial were taught behavioral techniques by nurses; it was not a test of unmodified extinction.
A 2016 randomized trial of graduated extinction found small-to-moderate declines in cortisol compared with controls, and no differences in attachment at 12 months.
The honest limits: samples are modest, most participants were 6 months or older, and pure extinction has less long-term follow-up than check-based methods. The research supports “no lasting harm found,” which is not the same as proof for every child. See what the research says.
What to expect
A common course in practice, not a research finding:
Night 1: often 45 to 90 minutes of crying, sometimes longer.
Night 2: usually shorter; occasionally longer.
Nights 3–5: most babies fall asleep within about 10 minutes.
Later: a brief return of crying a week or two in is common and fades if you respond the same way.
Who should not use it
Babies under 4 months, and usually not before 6 months.
Babies who are ill, in pain, or have unresolved feeding, weight or breathing concerns. See sleep training a baby with reflux.
Any baby not in a safe sleep space: back, firm flat mattress, empty crib. See safe sleep and sleep training.
Families who are not sure they can see it through. Crying for an hour and then being rocked to sleep is harder on everyone than a method with more parental presence, done consistently.
Alternatives
If extinction is not for you, timed checks, the chair method, pick-up-put-down and bedtime fading all teach the same skill with more parental presence; they are compared in methods compared. For transparency, Actually Sleeping does not use cry it out. Plans are built around the individual baby with daily 1:1 support.
Frequently asked
How long is too long to let a baby cry it out?There is no research-defined limit. Many families set their own ceiling in advance, and in practice many babies fall asleep within 45 to 90 minutes on the first night. If crying sounds different from protest, or your baby may be ill or unsafe, go in.
Does cry it out cause attachment problems?Studies that measured attachment and the parent–child relationship after behavioral sleep training, including a five-year follow-up, found no differences from children who were not sleep trained.
Can I do cry it out at 4 months?Many families wait until about 6 months for extinction, because many 4-month-olds still need night feeds and most of the research involved babies 6 months and older. Gentler shaping and gradual methods fit better at 4 months. Ask your pediatrician.
What if my baby vomits from crying?Go in, clean up calmly with the lights low, offer comfort briefly, and put your baby back down awake. If it happens more than once, pause and talk to your pediatrician, and consider a method with more parental presence.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Price AM, et al. Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention: randomized trial. Pediatrics. 2012.Gradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# What is the chair method of sleep training?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/chair-method-sleep-training/

What is the chair method of sleep training?
In the chair method you put your baby down awake and sit in a chair beside the crib until they fall asleep, then move the chair farther away every 2 to 3 nights until you are out of the room. It usually takes 10 to 14 nights and often up to 3 weeks. It works best from about 6 months through the toddler years and suits parents who want to stay present, but it is not tear-free.
How it works, step by step
NightsChair positionWhat you do
1–3Beside the cribQuiet voice, occasional touch or pat; no picking up to sleep
4–6Halfway to the doorVoice only; go to the crib briefly if truly needed, then back to the chair
7–9In the doorwayOccasional quiet reassurance
10–12In the hall, in viewMinimal voice
13–14Out of sightBrief verbal check-ins from the door if needed
At night wakings, return to wherever the chair is that night and do the same thing. The method is also known as camping out or gradual withdrawal.
Rules that make it work
Be boring. Sit, stay calm, keep words few and repetitive. Eye contact and conversation keep babies awake.
Fade your help within each stage. Less touching on night 3 than on night 1.
Move the chair on schedule, even if the last position has not become easy. Staying in one spot for a week creates a new habit: needing you in the chair.
Stay until asleep in the early stages, then leave quietly. Later, leave while your baby is drowsy but awake.
One adult per night. Swapping mid-bedtime restarts the protest.
What to expect
In practice, crying is usually less intense than with leave-the-room methods, but it can last as long or longer on the first nights, because some babies are frustrated that you are right there and not picking them up. Many families see 20 to 60 minutes on night 1, and a fresh protest on each night the chair moves. Most families see clear improvement by the end of week 1 and finish in 2 to 3 weeks.
Does it work?
The chair method has less direct trial evidence than extinction, graduated extinction or bedtime fading, which are the approaches the 2006 American Academy of Sleep Medicine review lists with support. It rests on the same principle: the child does the final step of falling asleep while your help is reduced. A large Australian randomized trial in which nurses taught parents behavioral settling techniques found fewer infant sleep problems and fewer maternal depression symptoms at 10 and 12 months, and no differences in children’s emotional health or the parent–child relationship at age 6.
Pros and cons
Pros: you are present throughout; changes are gradual; works well for toddlers and for children with separation anxiety; easy to adapt when room-sharing.
Cons: slow; demands patience at 2 a.m.; your presence stimulates some babies, especially under about 6 months; easy to stall at one position.
If it stalls
The usual causes are staying too long at one position, doing too much from the chair (picking up, lying down next to the crib, holding hands through the slats), or a schedule problem that makes falling asleep hard in the first place. Check wake windows, then tighten the steps. If your baby is more upset with you in the room than out of it, a check-based method may suit them better.
Frequently asked
How long does the chair method take?As a rule of thumb, 10 to 14 nights to move the chair out of the room, and up to 3 weeks for sleep to be fully settled. Naps can take a similar time.
Is the chair method the same as camping out?Yes. Camping out, gradual withdrawal and the chair method describe the same approach: a parent sits near the crib and moves away every few nights until they are out of the room.
Does the chair method work for toddlers?Yes. It is one of the more useful methods from about 12 months to 3 years, including for toddlers in a bed, where the parent can calmly return the child and sit back down.
Can I touch my baby during the chair method?In the first 2 to 3 nights, brief patting or a hand on the chest is fine. Reduce it each night so that your touch does not become the new way your baby falls asleep.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Hiscock H, et al. Improving infant sleep and maternal mental health: a cluster randomised trial. Arch Dis Child. 2007.Price AM, et al. Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention: randomized trial. Pediatrics. 2012.
Related guidesWhich sleep training method is gentlest? Methods comparedCan I sleep train while room-sharing?Can I sleep train and keep breastfeeding?Sleep training isn’t working. What should I do?Does the pick-up-put-down method work?

# Does the pick-up-put-down method work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/pick-up-put-down-method/

Does the pick-up-put-down method work?
It can, mainly for younger babies of about 3 to 6 months, and it is slow: in practice it often takes 1 to 3 weeks and many repetitions each night. You pick your baby up when they cry, calm them, and put them back down awake, repeating until they fall asleep in the crib. After about 6 to 7 months it often backfires, because being picked up and put down repeatedly stimulates and frustrates older babies more than it calms them.
How it works
After the bedtime routine, put your baby down awake.
If your baby fusses, pause for a minute or two. Try your voice and a hand on the chest first.
If fussing becomes crying, pick your baby up and hold them until calm. Calm, not asleep.
Put your baby back down as soon as the crying stops, even if they are wide awake.
Repeat until your baby falls asleep in the crib.
On the first nights that can mean 20, 30 or more pick-ups over 45 to 90 minutes. The number should fall night by night.
Who it suits
AgeHow it tends to go
Under 3 monthsToo early for a method; soothe and feed on cue
3–6 monthsThe best fit: babies are light, calm quickly when held, and are not yet strongly stimulated by the up-and-down
6–8 monthsMixed; many babies cry harder at each put-down
8 months and upOften counterproductive; the chair method or timed checks usually fit better
What the evidence says
We found no controlled trial that tests pick-up-put-down on its own, so there is no direct research on how well it works compared with other methods. It rests on the same principle as the studied methods: the baby does the final step of falling asleep in the crib while your help is gradually reduced. That principle is well supported; this particular technique is supported mostly by clinical and parent experience.
Pros and cons
Pros: very responsive; you never leave a crying baby; usable from about 3 months; fits room-sharing.
Cons: physically tiring; slow; easy to slide into holding the baby to sleep; stimulating for older babies; hard to keep up at 3 a.m.
Making it work
Put your baby down the moment they are calm. The longer you hold, the closer you are to rocking to sleep.
Stretch the pause before each pick-up a little every night.
Replace pick-ups with crib-side soothing as the nights go on: voice, then a hand, then nothing.
Get the schedule right first. An overtired 4-month-old will not settle with any method; see wake windows by age.
Always put your baby down on the back in an empty crib, however many times you repeat it.
Signs it is not the right method
Switch if, after 5 to 7 consistent nights, the number of pick-ups is not falling; if your baby cries harder each time they are put down; or if your baby falls asleep in your arms nearly every time. Good next steps are the chair method or timed checks, depending on your baby’s age. Babies around 4 months are also going through a permanent change in sleep structure, covered in the 4-month sleep regression.
Frequently asked
What age is pick-up-put-down best for?About 3 to 6 months. Younger babies need soothing and feeding on cue rather than a method, and older babies are often stimulated or frustrated by repeated picking up.
How long does pick-up-put-down take to work?Typically 1 to 3 weeks. You should see the number of pick-ups per bedtime dropping within the first 5 to 7 nights; if not, the method or the schedule needs to change.
How many times should I pick my baby up?As many as it takes on the first nights, which can be 20 to 30 or more. The goal is fewer each night, with crib-side soothing gradually replacing the pick-ups.
Is pick-up-put-down a no-cry method?No. There is usually crying between pick-ups, and total crying time can be similar to other methods, spread over more nights. The difference is that you respond every time.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# Which sleep training method is gentlest? Methods compared
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/gentle-sleep-training-methods-compared/

Which sleep training method is gentlest? Methods compared
Measured by crying per night, bedtime fading and the parent-present methods (the chair method and pick-up-put-down) are the gentlest, and they take the longest, often 1 to 3 weeks. Timed checks and extinction involve more crying at first but often finish within a week. Research has not shown any one method is better or worse for a child’s wellbeing, so choose the one you can apply consistently.
Methods compared
MethodHow it worksTypical time to resultsCryingBest for
Bedtime fadingTemporarily move bedtime later to when the baby actually falls asleep, then shift it earlier in 15-minute steps1–3 weeksLowestBabies and toddlers who take 45+ minutes to fall asleep; a first step before another method
Pick up, put downPick up to calm when crying, put down awake, repeat1–3 weeksLow to moderate, in short burstsAbout 3–6 months
Chair methodSit by the crib until asleep; move the chair away every 2–3 nights2–3 weeksModerate, with a parent present6 months to 3 years; separation anxiety; toddlers
Timed checks (Ferber)Leave the room; brief checks at lengthening intervals3–7 nightsModerate to high for 2–3 nights5–6 months and up; parents who want a clear script
Extinction (cry it out)Leave the room; no checks apart from planned feeds and safety3–5 nightsHighest on nights 1–2, then drops quickly6 months and up; babies who escalate with checks
Times are typical ranges from practice for nights when a method is applied consistently, not trial results. Naps usually take longer with every method.
What “gentle” means
Parents use the word in three different ways, and they point to different methods:
Least crying on any one night: bedtime fading, then pick-up-put-down and the chair method.
Least crying in total: not clearly any of them. Gradual methods spread protest over more nights, and no study has shown that total crying is lower.
Most parental presence: the chair method and pick-up-put-down.
No method is cry-free. Changing how a baby falls asleep is frustrating for the baby, and crying is how babies express frustration. What you can choose is how you respond to it.
What the research says about gentleness
The 2016 randomized trial that compared graduated extinction, bedtime fading and a control group found that both active methods improved sleep, that infant cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines in both method groups compared with controls, and that attachment did not differ a year later. The five-year follow-up of an Australian trial in which nurses taught behavioral settling techniques found no lasting differences in children’s emotional health. In short, the evidence does not show that a faster method harms a baby or that a slower one protects them. Details are in what the research says.
How to choose
Start with age. Under 4 months: no formal method. At 4 to 6 months: fading, pick-up-put-down or gentle checks. From 6 months: any method. Toddlers in a bed: the chair method with clear limits; see when a toddler won’t stay in bed.
Watch your baby’s reaction to you. If your presence calms them, a parent-present method fits. If seeing you and not being picked up makes them more upset, leaving the room is often kinder.
Be honest about your own stamina. Three hard nights or three slower weeks? Pick the one you will finish.
Agree with the other caregiver before night one.
What matters more than the method
Schedule, feeding plan and consistency account for most of the result. A well-timed bedtime with a gradual method beats a badly timed bedtime with any method. Much of the crying parents fear is avoidable with the right preparation, which is the main thing an individual plan adds. Actually Sleeping builds custom plans with daily 1:1 support, and the approach is not cry it out and not wait it out.
Frequently asked
Is there a no-cry sleep training method?No method can promise no crying. Bedtime fading and parent-present methods usually involve the least intense crying, and good preparation of schedule and routine reduces it further.
Is gentle sleep training as effective as Ferber?Gradual methods can reach the same result but in practice take longer, often 1 to 3 weeks compared with about a week. In the one trial that compared them directly, both shortened the time to fall asleep; only graduated extinction clearly reduced night waking.
Which sleep training method is fastest?In practice, extinction is usually fastest, often within a week, followed closely by timed checks. Both involve more crying on the first nights than gradual methods.
Can I combine sleep training methods?Yes, if you plan the combination in advance, for example bedtime fading for a week and then the chair method. What does not work is changing methods in the middle of a night or every other night.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Gradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.Price AM, et al. Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention: randomized trial. Pediatrics. 2012.

# What is bedtime fading?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/bedtime-fading/

What is bedtime fading?
Bedtime fading means temporarily moving bedtime later, to the time your child actually falls asleep, so they fall asleep quickly, and then shifting it earlier by about 15 minutes every 2 to 3 nights until you reach the bedtime you want. It usually takes 1 to 3 weeks and involves little crying. It is best for babies from about 6 months and toddlers who take 45 minutes or more to fall asleep, and it has randomized-trial support.
Why it works
Sleep pressure builds the longer a child is awake. If bedtime is earlier than the child’s body is ready for, they lie awake, protest, and learn that bed is a place for struggling. Fading lines bedtime up with real sleepiness, so the child falls asleep fast and bed becomes linked with sleep again. Then you move the body clock earlier in small steps.
How to do it
Track for 3 to 5 nights. Note the time your child actually falls asleep, not the time you put them down.
Set a temporary bedtime at the average sleep-onset time, or 15 minutes after it. If your 9-month-old goes down at 7:00 and falls asleep around 8:15, the temporary bedtime is 8:15 to 8:30.
Move the routine to match, starting 20 to 30 minutes before the new bedtime. Keep the time before it calm and dim, not in the crib.
Fix the morning wake time. Wake your child at the same time every day, even after a late night. This is what makes the method work.
Keep naps normal. Do not let extra daytime sleep replace the lost night sleep, and do not cut naps either.
Shift earlier. Once your child falls asleep within about 15 minutes for 2 to 3 nights in a row, move bedtime 15 minutes earlier. Repeat until you reach your target.
If a step fails, go back to the last bedtime that worked for 2 more nights.
What to expect
StageTypical timingWhat happens
Tracking3–5 nightsNo change yet; you collect sleep-onset times
Late bedtime2–4 nightsFalls asleep quickly; evenings feel long
Shifting earlier1–2 weeks15 minutes earlier every 2–3 nights
Target bedtimeBy week 2–3Asleep within about 15 minutes at the time you want
What the research says
Bedtime fading was one of two methods tested in a 2016 randomized controlled trial of 43 infants aged 6 to 16 months. Babies in the fading group fell asleep faster than the control group, their cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines compared with controls, and there were no differences in attachment or emotional and behavioral problems 12 months later. The earlier American Academy of Sleep Medicine review also lists bedtime fading with positive routines among the behavioral treatments with supporting evidence.
What it does and does not fix
It fixes: long bedtime battles, a bedtime set too early for the child’s body clock, and bed that has become linked with being awake.
It does not fix by itself: needing to be fed or rocked to sleep. If your baby is still helped to sleep at the later bedtime, night wakings will continue. Pair fading with putting down awake, or with another method.
It is not a fix for early morning waking; a later bedtime rarely produces a later morning.
Cautions
Do not leave the late bedtime in place for weeks. Total sleep still matters: the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12 to 16 hours in 24 for babies of 4 to 12 months and 11 to 14 hours for toddlers of 1 to 2 years, naps included. If your child becomes clearly overtired, with more night waking or earlier mornings, move bedtime earlier faster. The trial evidence for fading is in babies 6 months and older, so most families use it from then.
Frequently asked
How long does bedtime fading take?In practice, usually 1 to 3 weeks: a few nights of tracking, a few nights at the later bedtime, then 15-minute shifts earlier every 2 to 3 nights.
Is bedtime fading a no-cry method?It usually involves little crying, because the child is put down when truly sleepy. Some protest is still possible, especially if the child is used to being helped to sleep.
Does bedtime fading help with night wakings?Only partly. In the 2016 trial it shortened the time to fall asleep more clearly than it reduced night wakings. Night wakings improve most when the child also learns to fall asleep without help.
Can I use bedtime fading with a toddler?Yes. It works well for toddlers who stall, call out or leave the room for an hour at bedtime. Combine it with a consistent routine and a clear response to getting out of bed.
ReferencesGradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.Mindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Paruthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.

# Can I sleep train and keep breastfeeding?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-while-breastfeeding/

Can I sleep train and keep breastfeeding?
Yes. Sleep training changes how your baby falls asleep, not whether they are breastfed, and you do not have to night wean to do it. Most families move the bedtime feed to the start of the routine, keep the night feeds the pediatrician recommends, and use their chosen method for the other wakings. Ideally breastfeeding is well established and your baby is at least 4 months old and growing well.
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
Sleep training and night weaning are separate
Sleep trainingNight weaning
What changesHow your baby falls asleepWhether your baby eats overnight
WhenFrom about 4 monthsWhen your pediatrician agrees; timing varies widely from baby to baby
Required for the other?NoNo
A baby can fall asleep independently and still have one or two night feeds. Many breastfed babies do exactly that for months.
How to do both
Feed at the start of the bedtime routine, in a lit room, and keep your baby awake through it. Then bath, sleep sack, book, song, crib.
Offer full feeds in the day, about every 2.5 to 3.5 hours, in a calm spot if your baby is distractible.
Decide the night feeds with your pediatrician. A common rule is to feed if it has been at least 3 to 4 hours since the last feed, and to use your method for wakings before that.
Keep night feeds plain. Dim light, a full feed, then back into the crib awake or lightly drowsy. Feeding fully to sleep now and then at 3 a.m. is not a disaster; doing it at bedtime is what maintains the feed-to-sleep association.
Use one method at bedtime and non-feed wakings. See the step-by-step guide.
Protecting your milk supply
Reduce feeds gradually. If you are dropping a night feed, shorten it by a few minutes every night or two, or stretch the time before it, so your supply adjusts slowly.
Do not stay painfully full. If you wake engorged, express just enough for comfort, and call your doctor or a lactation consultant if you develop a painful lump, redness or fever.
Expect calories to shift to the day. Babies usually feed more in the morning and daytime when night feeds fall. Offer an extra daytime feed during the change.
Watch diapers and weight. If wet diapers drop or you are worried about intake, pause and call your pediatrician or a lactation consultant.
If you pump at work or have had supply concerns, involve a lactation consultant before removing night feeds.
Does sleep training reduce breastfeeding?
The evidence is limited. The randomized trials of sleep interventions focused on sleep and maternal mood, and their long-term follow-up found no harms, but they were not designed to measure breastfeeding duration. One observational study found that babies who slept 6 to 8 hours straight were much less likely to be breastfed; that shows an association, not that one causes the other. Keep an eye on your own supply. The AAP notes that human milk reduces the risk of SIDS, which is a good reason to protect breastfeeding while you improve sleep.
Who settles the baby?
A breastfed baby often smells milk and protests harder when the nursing parent responds. For the first few nights it can help if the other caregiver handles non-feed wakings. If you are on your own, a consistent response still works; it may take a night or two longer.
When to wait
Hold off if your baby is under 4 months, has slow weight gain, has latch or supply problems that are still being worked on, or is ill. At Actually Sleeping, feeding plans are written around the family’s breastfeeding goals and the pediatrician’s guidance, and night feeds stay in the plan for as long as the baby needs them.
Frequently asked
Do I have to night wean to sleep train?No. You can keep one or more night feeds and still teach your baby to fall asleep independently at bedtime and at other wakings.
Will sleep training hurt my milk supply?Not if night feeds are reduced gradually and daytime feeds increase to match. Supply follows demand, so drop feeds slowly and express for comfort if you become engorged.
How do I know if my baby is hungry or just waking from habit?Clues for hunger: a long gap since the last feed, a full active feed, and going straight back to sleep. Clues for habit: waking every 1 to 2 hours, sucking briefly and dozing off. Your pediatrician can tell you how many feeds are needed at your baby’s age and weight.
Can I still nurse my baby to sleep for naps?It is your choice, but mixed messages slow progress. Most babies learn faster when they fall asleep the same way at naps and at night, so try to feed after naps instead of before them.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.Hiscock H, et al. Improving infant sleep and maternal mental health: a cluster randomised trial. Arch Dis Child. 2007.Price AM, et al. # Can I sleep train while room-sharing?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-while-room-sharing/

Can I sleep train while room-sharing?
Yes. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that babies sleep in the parents’ room, on their own separate sleep surface, ideally for at least the first 6 months, and you can teach independent sleep in that arrangement. It usually takes a few nights longer, because your baby can see, hear and smell you. Blocking the line of sight, using white noise and choosing a parent-present method make it workable.
Room-sharing is not bed-sharing
Room-sharing means your baby sleeps in a crib or bassinet in your room: on the back, on a firm, flat mattress, with nothing else in the sleep space. The AAP recommends it and recommends against sharing a bed. Never let your baby sleep on a sofa or armchair, and do not use inclined sleepers, wedges or positioners.
Why it is harder
Babies stir between sleep cycles, see or smell a parent, and call for the usual help.
Parents hear every grunt and respond before the baby has fully woken. Babies are noisy in light sleep.
Parents’ coughing, phones and movement wake the baby, particularly in the early morning hours.
Set up the room
Distance. Put the crib as far from your bed as the room allows.
Break the line of sight. Use a freestanding room divider or screen placed well away from the crib, or position the crib around a corner. Never drape fabric over or on the crib.
White noise. Continuous, moderate volume, placed between your bed and the crib and not inside or right beside it.
Darkness. Blackout the window; no screens in bed.
Methods that fit
MethodHow it adapts to a shared room
Chair methodThe most natural fit: sit by the crib, then move toward your bed, then to the door
Pick up, put downWorks for babies of about 3–6 months; settle from beside the crib
Timed checksAt bedtime, leave the room and check as usual. Overnight, give brief verbal reassurance from your bed at the same intervals, without getting up
Bedtime fadingUnchanged; it depends on timing, not on where the crib is
Night by night
Bedtime: do the routine, put your baby down awake, and apply your method. Stay out of the room afterwards until you go to bed yourself.
Coming to bed: enter quietly in the dark. No lights, no checking the crib up close.
Night wakings: pause for a few minutes before doing anything; many wakings end without you. Then respond as your method says, and feed at planned feed times.
Early morning: the hardest stretch. Treat anything before your set wake time as night. See early morning waking.
Some parents sleep in another room for the first 3 to 5 nights so the baby can practice without an audience. Under 6 months, weigh that against the AAP recommendation to room-share and talk to your pediatrician.
After 6 months
Moving a baby to their own room after 6 months is a family decision. Many babies sleep longer stretches once they are no longer woken by their parents, and many families room-share far longer by choice or necessity. Both can work. If you share one room for the long term, as in a studio or one-bedroom home, the setup above matters more, and the timeline is usually 1 to 2 weeks.
The same principles apply to siblings sharing a room; see sleep training twins. General safety points are in safe sleep and sleep training.
Frequently asked
Can you sleep train a baby in the same room as you?Yes. Use a parent-present method or adapted timed checks, block the line of sight between your bed and the crib, and run white noise. Expect it to take a few nights longer than in a separate room.
Should I move my baby to their own room to sleep train?Not before 6 months unless you have discussed it with your pediatrician; the AAP recommends room-sharing ideally for at least the first 6 months. After that it is your choice, and it often makes training simpler.
Does room-sharing cause more night wakings?It can after the first few months, because babies and parents disturb each other. Good room setup and independent sleep skills reduce this considerably.
Can I sleep train in a one-bedroom apartment?Yes. Put the crib as far from the bed as possible, use a divider placed away from the crib and white noise, and consider sleeping in the living room for the first few nights if your baby is over 6 months.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.
