# Does sleep training work? What the research says
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/does-sleep-training-work-evidence/

Does sleep training work? What the research says
Yes. A 2006 review of 52 studies found that 94 percent reported behavioral sleep interventions were effective, and more than 80 percent of treated children improved, with gains lasting 3 to 6 months. Randomized trials also show lower rates of maternal depression symptoms, and a five-year follow-up found no lasting harm to children’s emotional health, stress regulation or relationship with their parents. The studies are modest in size and mostly involve babies of 6 months and older.
The key studies
StudyDesignMain findings
Mindell et al., 2006 (Sleep)Review of 52 treatment studies for the American Academy of Sleep Medicine94% of studies reported that the intervention worked; over 80% of treated children showed clinically significant improvement, maintained for 3–6 months. Strongest evidence for unmodified extinction and for preventive parent education; support also for graduated extinction, bedtime fading with positive routines, and scheduled awakenings
Hiscock et al., 2007 (Arch Dis Child)Cluster randomized trial in Melbourne, Australia; 328 mothers who reported an infant sleep problem at 7 months; nurses taught behavioral strategies in structured consultationsFewer sleep problems at 10 months (56% vs 68%) and 12 months (39% vs 55%), and fewer maternal depression symptoms, than usual care
Hiscock et al., 2008 (Pediatrics)Follow-up of the same trial at age 2Mothers in the intervention group were less likely to report clinical depression symptoms (15.4% vs 26.4%); no evidence of adverse effects on children’s mental health or on parenting. Sleep problems: 27.3% vs 32.6%
Price et al., 2012 (Pediatrics)Five-year follow-up of the same trial; 225 of 326 families (69%) assessed at age 6No differences, positive or negative, in emotional and behavioral health, sleep, stress regulation, parent–child closeness or maternal mental health
Gradisar et al., 2016 (Pediatrics)Randomized trial of 43 infants aged 6–16 months: graduated extinction, bedtime fading or sleep education onlyBoth methods shortened the time to fall asleep; graduated extinction also reduced night waking. Cortisol showed small-to-moderate declines in both method groups compared with controls. No differences in attachment or in emotional and behavioral problems 12 months later
What the evidence supports
It works for most families. Babies fall asleep faster and wake their parents less.
Parents benefit. Improved maternal mood is among the most consistent findings.
No lasting harm has been found in the studies that looked, up to age 6.
More than one method works. Check-based, parent-present and fading approaches all have support.
What the evidence does not show
It is not permanent. By age 6, sleep in the trained and untrained groups looked the same. Sleep training brings relief months or years sooner; it does not create a lifelong advantage, and some children need a refresher after illness, travel or a regression.
It does not work for everyone. A minority of families in every study did not improve.
Babies still wake. In a 2015 Canadian trial of 235 families, movement sensors showed nearly all babies in both groups still woke 2 or more times a night 6 weeks later, while parents in the intervention group reported far fewer severe sleep problems. The change is largely in how babies resettle and how much they need a parent.
Evidence under 6 months is thin. Most trial participants were 6 months or older.
Methods without trials. Pick-up-put-down and many branded approaches have not been tested directly.
The criticisms, fairly stated
Small samples and parent report. The 2016 trial had 43 babies, and many outcomes rely on parents’ diaries.
Loss to follow-up. The five-year study assessed 225 of the 326 families in that analysis (69%).
Mixed methods. Families in the Australian trial were taught behavioral techniques over 1 to 3 nurse consultations, so results reflect being offered sleep help, not one specific method.
Stress during the process. One small study of 25 babies aged 4 to 10 months in a 5-day inpatient sleep program reported that on the third day infants no longer showed distress at bedtime but their cortisol was raised. It had no control group and drew published criticism; the randomized trial that measured cortisol found small declines, not rises. This question is not fully closed.
Absence of evidence. “No harm found” in studies of a few hundred children is reassuring but cannot rule out small effects or effects in particular children.
What this means for your decision
The research supports sleep training as an effective and, as far as has been measured, safe option for healthy babies from about 6 months. It does not say that you must do it. Families who are coping well with night waking are not harming their baby by waiting. The choice turns on how sleep loss is affecting your family. Whatever you choose, safe sleep rules apply every night, and your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health.
For how the individual methods work, see methods compared and the step-by-step guide.
Frequently asked
Is sleep training harmful to babies?Studies have not found harm. A randomized trial with five-year follow-up found no differences in emotional health, behavior, stress regulation or parent–child closeness at age 6, and a 2016 trial found no differences in attachment a year later, with cortisol slightly lower, not higher, in trained babies.
Does sleep training raise cortisol?The randomized trial that measured cortisol found small-to-moderate declines in sleep-trained babies compared with controls. One small uncontrolled study reported raised cortisol during an inpatient program; it drew published criticism and its finding has not been confirmed in a controlled trial.
Do the effects of sleep training last?A review found improvements maintained for 3 to 6 months, and one trial found fewer sleep problems at 10 and 12 months. By age 2 the gap had narrowed, and by age 6 sleep in both groups looked the same, so the benefit is earlier relief for the family, not a permanent difference.
Does the AAP recommend sleep training?The AAP’s safe sleep policy does not address sleep training methods, and its rules apply whatever you choose. Its parent site suggests that from about 4 months you put babies down before they are asleep so they learn to fall asleep on their own. Ask your own pediatrician about timing.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Hiscock H, et al. Improving infant sleep and maternal mental health: a cluster randomised trial. Arch Dis Child. 2007.Hiscock H, et al. Long-term mother and child mental health effects of a population-based infant sleep intervention: cluster-randomized, controlled trial. Pediatrics. 2008.Price AM, et al. Five-year follow-up of harms and benefits of behavioral infant sleep intervention: randomized trial. Pediatrics. 2012.Gradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.Hall WA, et al. A randomized controlled trial of an intervention for infants' behavioral sleep problems. BMC Pediatr. 2015.Middlemiss W, et al. Early Hum Dev. 2012.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. # Sleep training isn’t working. What should I do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-not-working/

Sleep training isn’t working. What should I do?
First check how long you have been fully consistent: as a rule of thumb, check-based methods need 5 to 7 nights and gradual methods 10 to 14. If you are past that with no clear progress, the cause is nearly always one of five things: inconsistent responses, a baby who is put down drowsy or still fed to sleep, a schedule that does not fit, night feeds without a plan, or a medical issue. Find which one applies and fix it before changing methods.
Your pediatrician is the authority on your child’s health. Confirm growth, night-feed needs and any medical concerns with them before changing how your baby sleeps.
Is it really not working?
Progress is rarely a straight line. These are normal and do not mean failure:
Night 2 or 3 worse than night 1.
A burst of crying around nights 3 to 5, just before things settle.
Nights improving while naps and early mornings lag by 1 to 2 weeks.
A short relapse around days 10 to 14.
Signs of real progress: less time to fall asleep, fewer or shorter wakings, or crying that is less intense. If any of these is trending the right way, keep going. Typical timelines are in how long sleep training takes.
The five usual causes
What you seeLikely causeFix
Crying is as long or longer after a weekInconsistent response: sometimes rocked, fed or brought into your bed after a long cryOne response, every waking, every caregiver, for 7 nights
Falls asleep easily at bedtime, then wakes every 2–3 hoursPut down drowsy or nearly asleep, or the feed is still the last stepMove the feed to the start of the routine; into the crib wide awake
Takes over 45 minutes to fall asleep, or wakes before 6 a.m.Schedule mismatch: bedtime too early or too late, too much or too little daytime sleepRecheck wake windows and nap totals; consider a nap transition
Wakes at varying times and feeds a little each timeNo feeding plan; feeds are being used to settleAgree set feeds with your pediatrician; use your method for the rest
Screams as if in pain, snores, arches, or was doing well and suddenly is notIllness, ear infection, reflux, teething pain, breathing problemSee your pediatrician before continuing
Other things to check
The room: light leaking in at 5 a.m., white noise on a timer that switches off, a room that is too warm.
New skills: rolling, sitting, pulling to stand. Give plenty of daytime practice; see the 8 to 10 month regression.
Checks that stimulate: if your baby cries harder after each visit, make checks shorter and less frequent.
Different rules by day and night, or between caregivers.
Too many crutches at once: a pacifier that needs replacing eight times a night is a sleep association too.
Should I switch methods?
Only after one method has had a fair trial with the foundations in place: 7 consistent nights for check-based methods, 14 for gradual ones. If you switch, switch once, to a method chosen for a reason, and hold it for a week. Changing methods every two nights teaches a baby that persistence changes the rules.
Should I stop?
Pause if your baby is ill, if your pediatrician has concerns, or if a major disruption is under way. Wait until things are stable, then restart from night one. A clean restart works better than a half-continued plan. If the constant waking is the main problem, waking every 2 hours covers the common causes by age.
When to get help
If you have been consistent for 7 to 10 nights, the checks above have not revealed the cause, and your pediatrician has ruled out a medical issue, the problem is usually in the details of the plan: timing that is off by 20 minutes, a feed in the wrong place, a response that works against this baby’s temperament. Those are hard to see from inside the house at 3 a.m. This is the situation most families are in when they contact Actually Sleeping. Dr. Sam reviews what you have tried, writes a custom plan, and adjusts it daily through 1:1 check-ins. We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Full refund if not; details are on the guarantee page. Deciding whether that is right for you is covered in should I hire a baby sleep consultant.
Frequently asked
How long should I try sleep training before giving up?Give check-based methods 5 to 7 fully consistent nights and gradual methods 10 to 14. If nothing has improved by then, look for the cause before either giving up or switching methods.
Why is sleep training getting worse instead of better?A temporary worsening around nights 2 to 5 is common and usually comes just before improvement. If it keeps getting worse beyond a week, the usual reasons are inconsistent responses, an overtired or under-tired schedule, or illness.
Why did sleep training work and then stop?Illness, travel, teething, a developmental leap or a nap transition can disrupt sleep, and the old habits can return if the response changes during that time. Going back to your original method usually restores sleep within a few nights.
Can some babies not be sleep trained?Nearly all healthy babies can learn to fall asleep independently, but not every baby responds to every method, and a small number have medical causes for waking. If a consistent, well-prepared attempt fails, see your pediatrician and get the plan reviewed.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Paruthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.Mindell JA, et al. # What is a realistic newborn sleep schedule (0–8 weeks)?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/newborn-sleep-schedule-0-to-8-weeks/

What is a realistic newborn sleep schedule (0–8 weeks)?
There is no clock schedule for a newborn, only a rhythm: feed on cue, stay awake briefly (a common rule of thumb is 45–60 minutes, rising toward 60–90 minutes by 6–8 weeks), sleep, repeat. Expect 5 or more naps, sleep spread across day and night, often only 1–2 hours at a time at first, a total the AAP puts at about 16–17 hours, and a late “bedtime”.
A sample day at about 6 weeks
This is an illustration of the rhythm, not a timetable to enforce. Feeding on cue always comes first, and a younger newborn will be awake for less time than shown.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, feed, curtains open, daylight
8:00 a.m.Nap 1 (after about 60 minutes awake)
9:30 a.m.Wake, feed, a few minutes of tummy time
10:30 a.m.Nap 2
12:00 p.m.Wake, feed
1:00 p.m.Nap 3
2:30 p.m.Wake, feed, time outside if you can
3:30 p.m.Nap 4
5:00 p.m.Wake, feed; the fussy evening stretch often starts here
6:15 p.m.Catnap, often short
7:00–9:30 p.m.Cluster feeds with one more short doze
10:00 p.m.Feed, swaddle, down on the back in the bassinet
OvernightFeeds on cue, usually every 2–4 hours; lights low, little talking
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hoursVaries widely; the AAP’s parent site describes about 16–17 hours a day, and healthy newborns fall on both sides of it
Night sleepBroken stretches, often only 1–2 hours at a time in the early weeks, lengthening over the following weeks
Naps5 or more, from 20 minutes to 2–3 hours, with no pattern yet
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)45–60 minutes at 0–4 weeks; 60–90 minutes by 6–8 weeks, including the feed
Night feedsEvery 2–4 hours on cue. Some newborns need to be woken to feed until weight gain is established. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
A newborn has no settled body clock. Circadian rhythms develop around 2 to 3 months, and by about 3 months melatonin and cortisol follow a day–night cycle, which is why newborn sleep is scattered across 24 hours and why day–night confusion is normal. Newborns fall asleep through active (REM-like) sleep, and much of their sleep is light and active, so grunting, twitching and brief cries during sleep do not always mean the baby is awake. Fussing typically peaks at about 6 weeks and eases by 3 to 4 months.
The AASM consensus on sleep duration deliberately gives no recommendation under 4 months, because normal sleep varies so widely at that age and there is too little evidence linking it to health outcomes. See how infant sleep cycles develop for what comes next.
Common problems at this age
Day–night confusion: bright, busy days and dark, boring nights. Do not let a single daytime nap run much past 2–3 hours without offering a feed.
Only sleeps when held: expected in these weeks. Hold your baby while you are fully awake, and try one put-down a day in the bassinet for practice. Later, contact napping can be phased out.
Overtired by evening: watch the clock as well as the baby; see wake windows by age.
Safe sleep: on the back, on a flat, firm surface, in an empty bassinet or crib, in your room. Stop swaddling at the first signs of rolling.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Not with any method that drops feeds or leaves a newborn to cry; those are not for this age. What can start now is the foundation: feeding well, safe sleep and a simple, repeatable wind-down. Gentle shaping can begin around 10–12 weeks and formal sleep training generally from about 4 months; Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage (foundations first, night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks). More in the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Should I wake my newborn to feed?Follow your pediatrician’s guidance. Newborns are often woken to feed until weight gain is established. Once a baby is healthy and growing well, the AAP’s parent site says they usually do not need to be woken to feed.
When do newborns start sleeping longer at night?As the body clock develops around 2 to 3 months, many babies begin to produce one longer stretch, usually the first of the night. The range is wide and depends on feeding and growth.
What time should a newborn go to bed?Late is normal in the first weeks, often 9 to 11 p.m. as a rough guide. Bedtime tends to drift earlier on its own as the body clock develops, often toward 7–8 p.m. by 3–4 months.
Can a newborn be on a schedule?Not a clock schedule. A repeating pattern of feed, short awake time and sleep is realistic. Fixed feeding or nap times are not, and feeds should never be delayed to fit a timetable.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Swaddling: Is it Safe for Your Baby?Paruthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. # What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/2-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 month old?
At 2 months most babies take 4–5 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 60–90 minutes at a time. Total sleep varies widely; there is no official hour target under 4 months. Bedtime is still on the late side, around 8–9:30 p.m., and night feeds on cue are normal and expected.
Sample day for a 2 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, feed, daylight
8:15 a.m.Nap 1
9:45 a.m.Wake, feed, tummy time
11:00 a.m.Nap 2
12:30 p.m.Wake, feed
1:45 p.m.Nap 3
3:00 p.m.Wake, feed, time outside
4:30 p.m.Nap 4
5:15 p.m.Wake, feed
6:45 p.m.Nap 5, a 30-minute catnap
7:15 p.m.Wake; evening feeds, bath, short routine
8:30 p.m.Final feed, swaddle or sleep sack, down on the back
OvernightFeeds on cue, commonly every 3–5 hours
Naps will not land at the same times every day yet. Hold the wake window steady and let the clock times float. Feed whenever your baby is hungry, including in the middle of a wake window.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hoursVaries widely; the AASM gives no recommendation under 4 months
Night sleepBroken by feeds; often one longer first stretch of the night begins to appear
Naps4–5, anywhere from 30 minutes to 2 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)60–90 minutes, including feeding time
Night feedsTypically 2–4 a night, on cue. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
The body clock is starting to work: circadian rhythms develop around 2 to 3 months. Night sleep begins to consolidate into one longer stretch, usually the first of the night, while daytime naps stay irregular for another couple of months. Social smiling arrives, awake time becomes more alert, and the fussing that typically peaks at about 6 weeks starts to ease, usually by 3 to 4 months. Bedtime drifts earlier week by week; follow it rather than forcing it.
The AASM consensus gives no sleep-duration recommendation under 4 months because normal variation is so wide, so judge by your baby’s mood, feeding and growth rather than by an hour count.
Common problems at this age
Short naps: 30–45 minute naps are developmentally normal at 2 months and are not something to fix yet. See why naps are only 30 minutes.
Naps only in arms: common. Practice the first nap of the day in the bassinet, where sleep pressure helps most. Later steps are in how to stop contact napping.
Overtired evenings: a window stretched past 90 minutes usually shows up as a hard bedtime. Check wake windows by age.
Swaddle safety: some babies show the first signs of rolling around now. Stop swaddling at the first sign and move to an arms-free sleep sack. Sleep stays on the back, on a flat, firm surface, in an empty crib or bassinet.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Not formal sleep training; that generally starts from about 4 months. From roughly 10–12 weeks you can begin gentle shaping: a consistent wind-down, a dark room, and putting your baby down drowsy or calm for one sleep a day, always responding and feeding on cue. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage using exactly this kind of gentle approach: night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
How long should a 2 month old sleep at night without feeding?It varies widely. Many begin to manage one longer stretch early in the night, and some go longer. How long your baby may go between night feeds depends on weight gain and feeding, so confirm with your pediatrician.
What time should a 2 month old go to bed?Usually between 8 and 9:30 p.m. Bedtime moves earlier over the next two months as night sleep consolidates.
How long can a 2 month old stay awake?A common rule of thumb is about 60–90 minutes, counting the feed. Past that, many 2 month olds become overtired and harder to settle. Watch your own baby’s cues too.
Is it too early for a routine?No. A 5–10 minute wind-down in the same order before sleep is helpful at any age. A fixed clock schedule is what is still too early.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 3 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/3-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 3 month old?
At 3 months most babies take 4 naps (some 3) and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake about 75 minutes to 2 hours. Total sleep varies widely; there is no official hour target under 4 months. Bedtime moves earlier, to roughly 7:30–8:30 p.m., and many babies still feed 1–3 times overnight.
Sample day for a 3 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, feed, daylight
8:20 a.m.Nap 1
9:50 a.m.Wake, feed, floor play
11:20 a.m.Nap 2
12:50 p.m.Wake, feed
2:30 p.m.Nap 3
3:45 p.m.Wake, feed, time outside
5:30 p.m.Nap 4, a 30-minute catnap
6:00 p.m.Wake, feed
7:15 p.m.Bath, feed, short routine
7:45 p.m.Down on the back, in a sleep sack
OvernightFeeds on cue, commonly 1–3
The first window of the day is the shortest (about 75–80 minutes) and the last is the longest (up to about 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours). Feed on cue throughout; the feed times shown are only typical.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hoursVaries widely; the AASM gives no recommendation under 4 months
Night sleep10–12 hours, usually with feeds
Naps3–4, totalling about 4–5 hours; the last is a catnap
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)75 minutes to 2 hours, lengthening through the day
Night feedsCommonly 1–3 a night. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
By about 3 months, melatonin and cortisol follow a day–night rhythm, so nights lengthen and bedtime settles earlier. Naps are the last piece to organize and are often still short and unpredictable. Many babies begin working on rolling, and hands come free as a self-soothing tool. Around 3 to 4 months sleep becomes more adult-like: babies start falling asleep through quiet sleep rather than active sleep, and regular sleep cycles develop, which is what parents often experience as the 4-month regression. How infant sleep cycles develop explains the change.
Common problems at this age
The swaddle transition: stop swaddling at the first signs of rolling, even if sleep gets worse for a few nights. Use an arms-free sleep sack; no loose blankets.
30-minute naps: still within normal. Protect the wake windows and offer a short rescue in arms if the day falls apart. See short naps.
Feeding to sleep for every sleep: normal now, and a common root of waking later. Begin moving the feed to the start of the routine for one sleep a day. See the feed-to-sleep association.
Sudden frequent waking: it may be the early edge of the 4-month sleep regression.
Is this age right for sleep training?
For gentle shaping, yes. From about 10–12 weeks a baby can practice falling asleep in the crib with your support: consistent routine, dark room, drowsy or calm put-downs, feeds on cue. Formal sleep training generally waits until about 4 months and your pediatrician’s agreement. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage (foundations first, night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks), with a plan written for the individual baby by Dr. Sam. See the best age to sleep train and safe sleep and sleep training.
Frequently asked
How many naps should a 3 month old take?Usually 4, sometimes 3 if naps run long. Total daytime sleep is typically 4–5 hours.
What is a good bedtime for a 3 month old?Between about 7:30 and 8:30 p.m. for most. If the last catnap ends early, move bedtime earlier rather than stretching the final window past 2 hours.
Can a 3 month old sleep through the night?A few sleep a long stretch; many still need 1–3 feeds. Both are normal. Night-feed decisions depend on growth and belong to your pediatrician.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 4 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/4-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 4 month old?
At 4 months most babies take 3–4 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 1.5–2 hours at a time. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24 from 4 months, including naps. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m., with 10–12 hours in the crib overnight and often 1–2 night feeds.
Sample day for a 4 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, feed, daylight
8:30 a.m.Nap 1
9:45 a.m.Wake, feed, floor play
11:30 a.m.Nap 2
1:00 p.m.Wake, feed
2:45 p.m.Nap 3
3:30 p.m.Wake, feed
5:15 p.m.Nap 4, a 30-minute catnap
5:45 p.m.Wake, feed
7:00 p.m.Bath, feed, book, song
7:30 p.m.Into the crib awake, on the back
OvernightOften 1–2 feeds
When naps start running longer than an hour, the day naturally compresses to 3 naps with windows closer to 2 hours. Until then, a fourth catnap keeps the last window from overshooting.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep10–12 hours
Naps3–4, totalling about 3.5–4.5 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)1.5–2 hours; shortest in the morning, longest before bed
Night feedsCommonly 1–2 a night. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Sleep matures into more regular cycles of light and deep sleep, each lasting about 50 minutes in infancy, with a brief arousal between them. This change is permanent. A baby who falls asleep with help now notices that the help is gone at each arousal and calls for it. Rolling arrives for many babies, and feeds get distractible in daylight.
Common problems at this age
Waking every 1–2 hours: see 4-month sleep regression or sleep problem for how to tell a passing phase from a pattern.
Short naps: one sleep cycle and done. Usually the same cause as the night waking; see 30-minute naps.
Feeding back to sleep at every waking: see the feed-to-sleep association.
Rolling in the crib: the swaddle must be gone. Keep placing your baby on the back in an empty crib; a baby who rolls both ways on their own can stay as they land.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Generally yes. Many families start formal sleep training from about 4 months with healthy, full-term babies, once the pediatrician is happy with growth and feeding. The AAP’s parent site suggests that from 4 months you put babies down before they are asleep so they learn to fall asleep on their own. Teaching independent sleep does not require dropping night feeds; those are separate decisions. Actually Sleeping builds a custom plan with live support on the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins, and it is not cry it out and not wait it out. Read the best age to sleep train first.
Frequently asked
Should a 4 month old take 3 or 4 naps?Either. Four short naps or three longer ones can both add up to about 4 hours. Let nap length decide: if the third nap ends before 4:30 p.m., a catnap usually helps.
What time should a 4 month old go to bed?Between 7 and 8 p.m. for most, about 1.75–2 hours after the last nap ends.
How long does the 4-month regression last?The change in sleep cycles is permanent. There is no research-defined length for the disruption; in practice it often settles within a few weeks for babies who can already fall asleep on their own, and lasts longer for babies who depend on feeding, rocking or holding.
Does a 4 month old still need night feeds?Many do, often 1–2. Ask your pediatrician what is appropriate for your baby’s growth; do not cut feeds on your own.

J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.Patel AK, et al. Physiology, Sleep Stages. StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf (NIH).HealthyChildren.org (AAP). # What is a good sleep schedule for a 5 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/5-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 5 month old?
At 5 months most babies take 3 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 2–2.5 hours at a time. The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, naps included. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 7:45 p.m., with 11–12 hours overnight and often 0–2 night feeds.
Sample day for a 5 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, feed, daylight
9:00 a.m.Nap 1 (aim for 1–1.5 hours)
10:30 a.m.Wake, feed, floor play
12:45 p.m.Nap 2 (aim for 1–1.5 hours)
2:15 p.m.Wake, feed
4:30 p.m.Nap 3, a 30-minute catnap
5:00 p.m.Wake, feed
6:45 p.m.Bath, feed, book, song
7:15 p.m.Into the crib awake, on the back
OvernightOften 0–2 feeds
If naps are still short, keep a fourth catnap for now or bring bedtime forward to as early as 6:30 p.m. An early bedtime does not cause early waking; an overtired bedtime often does.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps3, totalling about 3–4 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)2–2.5 hours; shortest first, longest before bed
Night feedsCommonly 0–2 a night. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
The new sleep cycles from the 4-month change have settled, and naps become capable of lengthening past one cycle, though many babies need to learn how. Rolling in both directions, grabbing feet and early sitting practice often show up in the crib at 2 a.m. Daytime feeds get more efficient and more distracted, which can shift calories toward the night if feeds are rushed.
Common problems at this age
Naps stuck at 30–45 minutes: at 5 months this is the most common complaint. Check the window first, then how your baby falls asleep. See why naps are only 30 minutes.
The regression never ended: as a rule of thumb, if frequent waking has lasted more than about 6 weeks, it is a pattern rather than a phase. See regression or sleep problem.
Early waking: usually a too-late bedtime, a too-long last window, or light in the room. See early morning waking.
Rolling onto the tummy: always start on the back in an empty crib with no positioners. Give plenty of floor time to practice in the day.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes, 5 months is a very workable age for most healthy babies: old enough for formal sleep training, young enough that habits are not deeply set. Confirm with your pediatrician that growth is on track and ask how many night feeds make sense. Actually Sleeping coaches nights first and then naps until they are solid, with a plan written for your baby. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Can a 5 month old be on 2 naps?Rarely. Most 5 month olds cannot comfortably stay awake the 2.5–3.5 hours a two-nap day requires. In practice the move to 2 naps commonly happens between 6 and 8 months.
How long should a 5 month old nap?About 3–4 hours in total: ideally two naps of 1–1.5 hours and one catnap of 30–45 minutes.
What time should a 5 month old go to bed?Between 7 and 7:45 p.m. for most, 2–2.5 hours after the last nap ends. Use 6:30 p.m. on days with poor naps.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 6 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/6-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 6 month old?
At 6 months most babies take 3 naps, with some starting the move to 2. Wake windows of 2–3 hours are a common rule of thumb, the AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, and bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m. with 11–12 hours overnight.
Sample day for a 6 month old (3 naps)
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, milk feed, daylight
8:15 a.m.Solids, if your pediatrician has cleared them
9:15 a.m.Nap 1
10:30 a.m.Wake, milk feed, floor play
1:00 p.m.Nap 2
2:30 p.m.Wake, milk feed
4:45 p.m.Nap 3, a 30-minute catnap
5:15 p.m.Wake, milk feed
7:15 p.m.Bath, feed, book, song
7:45 p.m.Into the crib awake, on the back
OvernightOften 0–1 feeds
Breast milk or formula remains the main source of nutrition; solids at this age are practice and are not a sleep tool. The AAP suggests starting solids at about 6 months. In one large UK trial, babies started on solids from 3 months slept about 17 minutes longer a night at 6 months: a small difference, and not a reason to start early without your pediatrician’s advice.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps3 (some days 2), totalling about 3–3.5 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)2–3 hours; about 2.25 in the morning, 2.5–3 before bed
Night feedsCommonly 0–1 a night; some babies still have 2. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Sitting, rolling freely and reaching for everything. Many babies start solids around 6 months. The third nap begins to be resisted on some days, the first sign of the 3-to-2 transition that, in practice, many babies complete between 6 and 8 months. By about 6 months the longest stretch of sleep typically lengthens to around 6 hours, which is why continued waking every 2 hours at this age is often about how the baby falls asleep rather than hunger.
Common problems at this age
Waking every 2 hours: see why a 6 month old wakes every 2 hours.
Third nap refused: if it is refused for 10–14 days, start the transition. Until then, use an early bedtime on refusal days. See nap transitions.
Feeding to sleep at every waking: see the feed-to-sleep association.
5 a.m. starts: see early morning waking.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. Formal sleep training is generally appropriate from about 4 months, and 6 months is one of the most common ages to start. Ask your pediatrician whether your baby still needs a night feed; a plan can keep one feed and still teach independent sleep. Actually Sleeping works one-to-one with families on this, with live support on Night 1. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Should a 6 month old have 2 or 3 naps?Most still need 3. Move to 2 when the third nap has been refused, or has pushed bedtime past 8:30 p.m., for about two weeks.
Do solids help a 6 month old sleep through the night?Not in any way that matters much. In one large trial, earlier solids were linked to about 17 more minutes of sleep a night at 6 months. Milk remains the main nutrition. Follow your pediatrician on when and how to begin.
How long should a 6 month old sleep at night?About 11–12 hours in the crib. Whether that includes a feed is individual and a question for your pediatrician.
What time is bedtime for a 6 month old?Between 7 and 8 p.m., roughly 2.5–3 hours after the last nap ends.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 7 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/7-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 7 month old?
At 7 months most babies are on 2 naps or finishing the move from 3. Wake windows of about 2.5–3.25 hours are a common rule of thumb, the AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, and bedtime usually falls between 6:30 and 7:30 p.m. with 11–12 hours overnight.
Sample day for a 7 month old (2 naps)
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, milk feed
8:15 a.m.Breakfast solids
9:45 a.m.Nap 1 (about 1.5 hours)
11:15 a.m.Wake, milk feed
12:30 p.m.Lunch solids
2:15 p.m.Nap 2 (about 1.5 hours)
3:45 p.m.Wake, milk feed
5:15 p.m.Dinner solids
6:30 p.m.Bath, milk feed, book, song
7:00 p.m.Into the crib awake
OvernightOften 0–1 feeds
Still on 3 naps? Keep windows near 2.25–2.75 hours with a catnap ending by 5:30 p.m. and bedtime around 7:30–8 p.m. Expect a week or two of mixed days during the switch.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps2–3, totalling about 2.5–3.5 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)2.5–3.25 hours; shortest first, longest before bed
Night feedsCommonly 0–1 a night. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Sitting steadily, starting to scoot or crawl, and babbling in strings. Your baby is beginning to understand that people and objects still exist out of sight, which is the root of the separation anxiety that commonly starts between 8 and 12 months. Solids become real meals, and the third nap disappears for most babies.
Common problems at this age
The 3-to-2 transition: overtired late afternoons and a rough week of bedtimes. Use a bedtime as early as 6 p.m. as the shock absorber. See nap transitions.
Early waking after dropping the nap: usually a last window stretched too far. See early morning waking.
Still waking every 2–3 hours: the cause is usually the same as at 6 months; see waking every 2 hours.
Practicing skills in the crib: sitting up and getting stuck. Practice getting back down during the day; at night, keep responses brief and boring.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. A 7 month old is well within the age for formal sleep training, and doing it before separation anxiety builds (it usually peaks between 10 and 18 months) is often easier. Check night-feed needs with your pediatrician first. Actually Sleeping writes a custom plan and checks in 1:1 every day while it runs. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Is 7 months too early for 2 naps?No. In practice many babies move to 2 naps between 6 and 8 months. The test is whether your baby can handle windows of about 2.5–3 hours without falling apart.
How long should a 7 month old’s naps be?On 2 naps, about 1–1.5 hours each, for 2.5–3 hours in total.
What time should a 7 month old go to bed?Between 6:30 and 7:30 p.m. on a two-nap day. Go earlier while the third nap is being dropped.

# What is a good sleep schedule for an 8 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/8-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for an 8 month old?
At 8 months most babies take 2 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 2.5–3.5 hours at a time. The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, naps included. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 7:45 p.m., with 11–12 hours overnight.
Sample day for an 8 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, milk feed
8:00 a.m.Breakfast solids
9:45 a.m.Nap 1 (about 1.5 hours)
11:15 a.m.Wake, milk feed
12:15 p.m.Lunch solids
2:30 p.m.Nap 2 (about 1.5 hours)
4:00 p.m.Wake, milk feed
5:30 p.m.Dinner solids
7:00 p.m.Bath, milk feed, book, song
7:30 p.m.Into the crib awake
OvernightOften 0–1 feeds
The windows here are 2.75, 3.25 and 3.5 hours. If your baby takes a long time to fall asleep, add 15 minutes to the window before that sleep; if they melt down before it, take 15 away.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps2, totalling about 2.5–3 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)2.5–3.5 hours; shortest first, longest before bed
Night feedsCommonly 0–1 a night. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
A burst of motor skills: crawling, pulling to stand, sometimes cruising. Separation anxiety commonly starts between 8 and 12 months, and your baby may cry when you leave the room at bedtime even if they never did before. Language comprehension is growing fast. These changes often arrive together and can disrupt sleep for a few weeks.
Common problems at this age
Sudden night waking or nap refusal: see the 8-to-10-month sleep regression.
Standing in the crib and unable to get down: practice squatting down from standing many times a day. The mattress should be at its lowest setting before your baby can stand.
Crying at separation: play peekaboo and short leave-and-return games in daylight, keep the bedtime routine identical, and say a brief, confident goodnight.
New habits from the regression: extra rocking or feeding for two weeks easily becomes the new requirement. See the feed-to-sleep association.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. Formal sleep training is appropriate at 8 months, and a consistent response matters more now because babies this age learn patterns quickly, in both directions. Separation anxiety is a reason to choose a method with a parent present and responsive, which is how Actually Sleeping works: not cry it out, not wait it out. Confirm night-feed needs with your pediatrician. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Does an 8 month old still need 3 naps?Almost never. By 8 months most babies do best on 2 naps with windows of about 2.5–3.5 hours.
How long does the 8-month sleep regression last?There is no research-defined length. In practice it often passes within a few weeks when the response stays consistent, and lasts longer when new sleep habits are introduced to get through it.
What time should an 8 month old go to bed?Between 7 and 7:45 p.m., about 3–3.5 hours after the second nap ends.
Should I drop night feeds at 8 months?That is your pediatrician’s call, based on growth and daytime intake. Many 8 month olds no longer need one, and some still do.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 9 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/9-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 9 month old?
At 9 months babies take 2 naps and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake about 3–3.5 hours at a time. The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, naps included. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 7:45 p.m., with 11–12 hours overnight and 2–3 hours of daytime sleep.
Sample day for a 9 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, milk feed
8:00 a.m.Breakfast
10:00 a.m.Nap 1 (about 1.25 hours)
11:15 a.m.Wake, milk feed
12:15 p.m.Lunch
2:30 p.m.Nap 2 (about 1.25 hours)
3:45 p.m.Wake, milk feed
5:30 p.m.Dinner
6:45 p.m.Bath, milk feed, book, song
7:15 p.m.Into the crib awake
OvernightOften no feeds; some babies still have 1
A simple pattern that suits many 9 month olds is 3 hours, then 3.25, then 3.5 hours awake. Cap daytime sleep at about 3 hours so it does not borrow from the night.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps2, totalling about 2–3 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)3–3.5 hours; shortest first, longest before bed
Night feedsCommonly 0–1 a night. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Pulling to stand and cruising along furniture, pincer grasp, waving, and understanding simple words like “no” and “bye-bye.” Separation anxiety is often building toward its peak, which usually falls between 10 and 18 months. Three solid meals are established for most babies, which changes the feeding picture overnight. Your baby also now remembers and anticipates routines, which makes a consistent bedtime sequence especially effective.
Common problems at this age
Regression in full swing: standing, crying at the door, fighting the second nap. See the 8-to-10-month sleep regression.
Early waking: at 9 months often a first nap that is too early or too long, which turns the early wake-up into a habit. See early morning waking.
Second nap refused: lengthen the middle window by 15 minutes before assuming the nap is going. Babies this age are not ready for one nap; see nap transitions.
Naps only on a parent: see how to stop contact napping.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. Nine months is well past the roughly 4-month starting point for formal sleep training, and it is not too late: older babies often learn in fewer nights because they recognize patterns quickly. Expect more protest about standing and separation than a younger baby would show, and plan your response in advance. Actually Sleeping supports families through this with a custom plan and daily 1:1 check-ins. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
How many naps does a 9 month old need?Two. Total daytime sleep is usually 2–3 hours.
How long should a 9 month old be awake before bed?About 3.25–3.5 hours after the second nap ends. Much longer tends to cause night waking and early rising.
Why is my 9 month old suddenly waking at night?Most often the 8-to-10-month regression: new motor skills plus separation anxiety. Keep the schedule and your response steady; in practice it often passes within a few weeks.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 10 or 11 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/10-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 10 or 11 month old?
At 10–11 months babies still need 2 naps, with wake windows of 3–4 hours as a common rule of thumb. The AASM recommends 12–16 hours of sleep in 24, naps included. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m., with 11–12 hours overnight and 2–3 hours of naps.
Sample day for a 10–11 month old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, milk feed
8:00 a.m.Breakfast
10:00 a.m.Nap 1 (about 1.25 hours)
11:15 a.m.Wake, milk feed
12:15 p.m.Lunch
2:45 p.m.Nap 2 (about 1.25 hours)
4:00 p.m.Wake, milk feed or snack
5:30 p.m.Dinner
7:15 p.m.Bath, milk feed, book, song
7:45 p.m.Into the crib awake
OvernightUsually no feeds
The windows here are 3, 3.5 and 3.75 hours. If naps are long, wake your baby by 4 p.m. to protect bedtime.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours12–16 hours (AASM, ages 4–12 months)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps2, totalling about 2–3 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)3–4 hours; shortest first, longest before bed
Night feedsMost babies this age have none; some still have 1. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Cruising, standing alone and, for some, first steps. First words appear and comprehension runs far ahead of speech. Babies this age test cause and effect on purpose, including what happens when they throw the pacifier out of the crib or stand and shout. Separation anxiety is still present but usually easing.
Common problems at this age
The false one-nap transition: many babies refuse a nap for a week or two around 10–12 months. It is usually temporary. In practice most babies are not ready for one nap until somewhere around 14–18 months, and dropping early often causes night waking. See nap transitions.
Lingering regression: see the 8-to-10-month sleep regression, and what is coming in the 12-month sleep regression.
Early waking: check that the first nap is not before about 9:45 a.m. See early morning waking.
Still fed or rocked to sleep: see the feed-to-sleep association.
Crib safety: mattress at the lowest setting, and still nothing loose in the crib; the AAP’s safe sleep guidance, which keeps blankets, pillows, toys and bumpers out, covers the whole first year.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. Formal sleep training is appropriate at any point from about 4 months, and 10–11 month olds usually respond quickly to a consistent plan because they understand routines. Most no longer need night feeds, but confirm that with your pediatrician rather than assuming. Actually Sleeping coaches both nights and naps, continuing with naps until they are solid. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Can a 10 month old switch to one nap?It is rarely a good idea. In practice few babies can handle the long windows a one-nap day needs this early, and in a large review fewer than 2.5% of children had stopped napping altogether before age 2. Nap refusal at 10–11 months is usually a schedule tweak or a phase.
How long should a 10 month old nap?About 2–3 hours in total across two naps of 1–1.5 hours each.
What time should an 11 month old go to bed?Between 7 and 8 p.m., about 3.5–4 hours after the second nap ends.
Is the schedule different at 11 months than 10?Only slightly. Windows stretch by about 15 minutes, typically toward 3.25, 3.5 and 4 hours.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 12 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/12-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 12 month old?
From 12 to 14 months most toddlers still do best on 2 naps, with wake windows of 3–4.5 hours as a common rule of thumb. The AASM recommends 11–14 hours of sleep in 24 for ages 1–2, naps included. Bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m., with 11–12 hours overnight and 2–2.5 hours of naps.
Sample day for a 12–14 month old (2 naps)
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake, milk
7:30 a.m.Breakfast
10:00 a.m.Nap 1 (about 1.25 hours)
11:15 a.m.Wake
12:00 p.m.Lunch
3:00 p.m.Nap 2 (about 1 hour)
4:00 p.m.Wake, snack
5:45 p.m.Dinner
7:15 p.m.Bath, milk, teeth, book, song
7:45 p.m.Into the crib awake
OvernightUsually no feeds
The windows here are 3, 3.75 and 3.75 hours. If the second nap starts being refused, cap the first nap at 1 hour before changing anything else.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours11–14 hours (AASM, ages 1–2 years)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps2, totalling about 2–2.5 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)3–4.5 hours on two naps; shortest first, longest before bed
Night feedsMost toddlers have none. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Walking, or very nearly. First words, pointing and strong opinions. Around the first birthday many families also change milk and move from bottles to cups; make those changes on your pediatrician’s advice, and keep milk at the start of the bedtime routine rather than as the last step. Daily sleep need drops slightly, which is why a schedule that worked at 10 months can suddenly produce nap refusal or early waking.
Common problems at this age
Nap strikes and new night waking: see the 12-month sleep regression.
Dropping to one nap too soon: in practice many toddlers make the 2-to-1 move between 14 and 18 months. Signs it is real: a nap refused for 10–14 days, or bedtime pushed past 8:30 p.m. See nap transitions.
Early waking: often too much daytime sleep for the new, lower total. See early morning waking.
Bottle or nursing to sleep: see the feed-to-sleep association.
Bedding: the AAP’s safe sleep recommendations, including keeping soft and loose bedding out of the sleep space, cover babies up to 1 year. After 12 months a wearable blanket is still the simplest choice, since most toddlers cannot keep a blanket on.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. A 12–14 month old is fully able to learn independent sleep, and formal sleep training has been appropriate since about 4 months. Toddlers protest with more stamina and more skill than babies, so consistency between caregivers matters most. Actually Sleeping works with children up to 3 years, with a plan written by Dr. Sam for the individual child. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Should a 12 month old be on one nap?Usually not. In practice many are not ready until around 14–18 months. A 12 month old pushed to one nap often starts waking at night or before 6 a.m.
How much should a 12 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 11–14 hours per 24 hours for ages 1–2 years, including naps. A typical split is 11–12 hours at night and 2–2.5 hours of naps.
Can my 1 year old have a blanket or pillow?The AAP’s guidance keeps soft bedding out of the crib for at least the first year. After that, ask your pediatrician; a wearable blanket remains the easy option and pillows are generally left until later in toddlerhood.
What time should a 12 month old go to bed?Between 7 and 8 p.m., about 3.5–4 hours after the second nap ends.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.

# What is a good sleep schedule for an 18 month old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/18-month-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for an 18 month old?
Between 15 and 23 months most toddlers settle on one midday nap of 1.5–3 hours. As a rule of thumb, wake windows are about 4.5–5.5 hours just after the switch and 5–6 hours from 18 months. The AASM recommends 11–14 hours of sleep in 24, and bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m.
Sample day for an 18 month old (1 nap)
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake
7:30 a.m.Breakfast
9:30 a.m.Snack, active play outside
11:30 a.m.Lunch
12:15 p.m.Nap (about 2–2.25 hours)
2:30 p.m.Wake, snack
5:30 p.m.Dinner
7:00 p.m.Bath, teeth, two books, song
7:30 p.m.Into the crib awake
OvernightNo feeds for most toddlers
Newly on one nap at 15–16 months? Start the nap around 11:30 a.m. and use a 6:30–7 p.m. bedtime, then push the nap later by 15 minutes every few days until it starts between 12 and 12:30 p.m.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours11–14 hours (AASM, ages 1–2 years)
Night sleep11–12 hours
Naps1, lasting 1.5–3 hours, starting around midday
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)4.5–5.5 hours just after the transition; 5–6 hours from about 18 months
Night feedsMost toddlers have none. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
The 2-to-1 nap transition, which in practice many toddlers complete between 14 and 18 months. A language burst, and with it the word “no.” A strong drive for independence alongside separation anxiety, which often peaks between 10 and 18 months before easing in the second half of the second year. First molars (about 13–19 months) and canines (about 16–23 months) come through in this window. Toddlers also begin to understand rules and to test whether they hold.
Common problems at this age
A messy nap transition: some days need two naps and some one for 2–4 weeks. See nap transitions.
Bedtime battles and night waking around 18 months: see the 18-month sleep regression.
Short single nap: a nap under an hour usually means it started too early or too late. See short naps.
Early waking: see early morning waking.
Climbing: keep the mattress at its lowest setting and use a sleep sack. Stay in the crib as long as it is safe; moving to a bed this young usually adds problems.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes. It is not too late, and it is not a different process in principle: a predictable routine, a clear and calm response, and the same answer every night. What changes is that toddlers negotiate, so the plan needs firm, kind limits and words your child understands. Actually Sleeping works with toddlers up to 3 years with a responsive approach that is not cry it out and not wait it out. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
When should my toddler drop to one nap?In practice, many between 14 and 18 months. Look for 10–14 days of a refused nap or a bedtime pushed past 8:30 p.m., not one bad day.
How long should an 18 month old nap?Usually 1.5–3 hours in a single nap. Wake your toddler by about 3 p.m. to protect bedtime.
What time should an 18 month old go to bed?Between 7 and 8 p.m., about 5 hours after the nap ends. Use an earlier bedtime during the nap transition.
How long does the 18-month sleep regression last?There is no research-defined length. In practice it often passes within a few weeks when limits and routine stay consistent.

# What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 year old?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/2-year-old-sleep-schedule/

What is a good sleep schedule for a 2 year old?
Between 2 and 3 years most children take one nap of 1–2 hours and, as a rule of thumb, stay awake 5–6 hours on either side of it. The AASM recommends 11–14 hours of sleep in 24 at ages 1–2 and 10–13 hours at ages 3–5, naps included, and bedtime usually falls between 7 and 8 p.m.
Sample day for a 2 year old
Treat every time below as a starting point. Shift the whole day to match your baby’s actual wake-up time, then adjust one thing at a time in 15-minute steps and hold it for three days before judging.
TimeWhat happens
7:00 a.m.Wake
7:30 a.m.Breakfast
9:30 a.m.Snack, active play outside
11:45 a.m.Lunch
12:30 p.m.Nap (about 1.75 hours)
2:15 p.m.Wake, snack
5:30 p.m.Dinner
7:15 p.m.Bath, teeth, toilet or diaper, two books, song
8:00 p.m.Lights out
OvernightSleep; no feeds
If bedtime turns into an hour of chatting in the dark, shorten the nap in 15-minute steps (wake by 2:30, then 2:15) before you consider dropping it.
Numbers at a glance
MeasureTypical range
Total sleep per 24 hours11–14 hours at ages 1–2 years; 10–13 hours at ages 3–5 years (AASM)
Night sleep10.5–12 hours
Naps1, lasting 1–2 hours
Wake windows (rule of thumb, not a research finding)5–6 hours before and after the nap
Night feedsNone expected at this age; raise any ongoing night feeding at your next visit. Whether to keep, reduce or drop night feeds is your pediatrician’s decision.
Total sleep figures marked AASM are the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommendation. The other rows are common practice ranges, not research findings; healthy babies vary.
What is changing developmentally
Sentences, imagination and a strong sense of self. Imagination brings the first real fears of the dark or of “monsters.” Two year olds are skilled at stalling: one more book, water, a different blanket. Many families also face toilet learning, a new sibling, or the move from crib to bed in this year, and each can disturb sleep for a couple of weeks.
Common problems at this age
Getting out of bed repeatedly: see toddler won’t stay in bed. If your child is safe in the crib and not climbing out, there is no need to rush the move; closer to 3 is easier.
Nap refusal: common around age 2 and usually temporary. Keep offering a daily rest in the dark room. In a large review, fewer than 2.5% of children had stopped napping before age 2, and most stopped somewhere between 3 and 5.
Bedtime stalling: build the requests into the routine (one drink, two books, one song) and end it the same way every night.
Early waking: see early morning waking. A color-changing clock gives a 2 year old a rule they can see.
Night fears: a dim, warm-colored night light is fine. Acknowledge the fear briefly and keep the response short and the same.
Is this age right for sleep training?
Yes, though at this age it is better described as sleep coaching: clear expectations explained in daylight, a visual routine, limits that hold, and a calm, repeatable response. Children of 2 and 3 learn quickly when every caregiver gives the same answer. Actually Sleeping works with children up to 3 years, with a custom plan and daily 1:1 check-ins. See the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
Does a 2 year old still need a nap?Almost always. A large review found fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before 2, while 94% have stopped by 5. A 2 year old who refuses the nap for a week or two usually returns to it if you keep offering.
How much sleep does a 2 year old need?The AASM recommends 11–14 hours per 24 hours at ages 1–2 years and 10–13 hours at ages 3–5 years, naps included.
What time should a 2 year old go to bed?Between 7 and 8 p.m. for most, about 5.5–6 hours after the nap ends.
When should I move my toddler from a crib to a bed?When the crib is no longer safe because your child is climbing out or has reached 35 inches (89 cm), the height at which MedlinePlus says children should no longer use a crib, or when your child is close to 3 and ready. Moving earlier often means more night-time visits, not better sleep.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Staton S, et al. Many naps, one nap, none: A systematic review and meta-analysis of napping patterns in children 0-12 years. Sleep Med Rev. 2020.MedlinePlus (NIH). Cribs and crib safety.

# When and how do I night wean my baby?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/night-weaning-how-and-when/

When and how do I night wean my baby?
Timing varies widely: many healthy, well-growing babies are able to drop night feeds at some point in the second half of the first year, and some need them longer. The timing is your pediatrician’s call, not a calendar’s. Once you have that sign-off, a common approach is to wean gradually over 5–10 nights: move the feed away from falling asleep, shrink it a little every night or two, and add the calories back during the day.
First: is it a hunger feed or a habit feed?
Young babies need to eat at night, and nothing here applies to them. Never restrict or stretch feeds for a newborn or a young baby, and never night wean a baby whose weight gain is in question. For an older baby, these clues separate the two:
Looks like hungerLooks like habit
A full, active feed, then straight back to sleepA few minutes of sucking, then asleep at the breast or bottle
One or two feeds at fairly predictable timesFeeds every 1.5–3 hours, close to sleep-cycle intervals
Daytime intake is steadyDaytime feeds are small or distracted because calories arrive at night
Baby under about 4–6 months, or pediatrician wants night feeds keptBaby is growing well and the pediatrician has said night feeds are optional
Rough expectations by age
These are common patterns from practice, not rules. Healthy babies vary a lot.
Under 4 months: feed on cue, day and night. No weaning.
4–6 months: many babies do well with 1–2 night feeds. Some pediatricians are comfortable with none; many prefer to keep one.
6–9 months: many well-growing babies on established solids can go 10–12 hours, with pediatrician agreement, though plenty still wake.
9 months and up: night feeds are usually habit, but ask anyway, especially for babies who were premature or have had feeding or growth concerns.
How to wean, step by step
Get the sign-off. Ask your pediatrician directly: “Is my baby growing well enough to go all night without a feed?”
Fix bedtime first. If your baby falls asleep feeding at bedtime, every night waking asks for the same thing. Move the bedtime feed to the start of the routine and put your baby down awake. See the feed-to-sleep guide.
Reduce gradually. Bottle: take a small, equal amount out of each night feed every night or two. Breast: shorten each feed by a couple of minutes every night or two. When a feed is down to a token amount, drop it.
One feed at a time, if there are several. Keep the feed that follows the longest stretch; let the others go first.
Respond without feeding. When a dropped feed’s time comes, comfort by your plan instead. Many families send the non-feeding parent.
Move the calories. Offer an extra daytime feed or fuller feeds. In practice appetite often shifts to the day within a few days.
If you are breastfeeding
Dropping feeds gradually also protects you from engorgement and plugged ducts. If you are uncomfortable, express just enough for relief. If supply is a worry, a lactation consultant can help you keep it while your baby sleeps longer; some parents keep a pump session before their own bedtime for a few weeks.
When to pause
Illness, a growth concern, fewer wet diapers, or a baby who is clearly hungry during the day despite extra offers. Feed, call the pediatrician, and resume later. At Actually Sleeping, night feeds stay in a baby’s plan until the family’s pediatrician says otherwise.
Frequently asked
Can I night wean a 4 month old?Only if your pediatrician agrees. Many 4-month-olds still need one or two night feeds. You can teach independent sleep at bedtime and keep the feeds; the two are separate.
Is it better to night wean cold turkey or gradually?Gradually for most babies. Shrinking feeds over 5–10 nights lets daytime intake catch up and is more comfortable for a breastfeeding parent.
Will night weaning make my baby sleep through the night?Not on its own. A baby who needs help falling asleep will still wake between cycles. Weaning works when it is paired with falling asleep independently at bedtime.
Will night weaning hurt my milk supply?A gradual reduction usually lets supply adjust. If you have supply concerns, talk with a lactation consultant before you start.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Sleeping Through the Night.

# Does a dream feed help a baby sleep longer?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/dream-feed-does-it-work/

Does a dream feed help a baby sleep longer?
Sometimes. A dream feed — feeding your baby around 10–11 p.m. without fully waking them — helps some babies between about 2 and 6 months shift their longest stretch to line up with yours, and does nothing or causes extra waking in others. Try it for 5–7 nights; if the first waking does not move later, drop it.
What a dream feed is
You lift your sleeping baby roughly 2–3 hours after bedtime, usually just before you go to bed, feed them while they stay drowsy, and lay them back down. The idea is simple: a baby whose longest stretch runs 7 p.m. to midnight has spent it while you were awake. Topping up at 10:30 may move the next waking to 3 or 4 a.m.
What the evidence says
Not much. One small 1993 randomized study of 26 breastfed newborns combined a “focal feed” between 10 p.m. and midnight with gradually stretching middle-of-the-night feeds and strong day–night cues. By 8 weeks, all 13 babies in that group slept from midnight to 5 a.m., compared with 23% of controls, with no difference in 24-hour milk intake. The late feed was never tested alone. In practice it is an experiment you run on your own baby, not a proven technique.
Who it tends to help, and who it does not
More likely to helpLess likely to help
Babies about 2–6 months who still need a night feedBabies over about 6–7 months who no longer need night calories
Babies who feed well while drowsyBabies who will not latch or suck while asleep, or who wake fully and stay up
Babies who fall asleep independently at bedtimeBabies who wake every 2 hours because of a sleep association
That last row matters most. A dream feed addresses hunger. It does not address a baby who cannot link sleep cycles, which is the more common reason for frequent waking after 4 months. See why a 6 month old wakes every 2 hours.
How to do it safely
Time it 2–3 hours after bedtime, between about 10 and 11 p.m.
Keep lights off and the room quiet. Lift your baby gently; most will root and feed with eyes closed.
Hold your baby in your arms, semi-upright, for the whole feed. Never prop a bottle and never feed a baby lying flat in the crib.
If your baby is swaddled and will not rouse enough to feed well, loosen the swaddle.
Burp briefly, then place your baby on their back in their own crib or bassinet.
Stay awake yourself. If you might doze off, do the feed sitting up in a lit room rather than in bed or on a sofa.
Signs it is backfiring
Your baby now wakes at the dream-feed time on their own, plus the old times.
The feed wakes them fully and resettling takes 30 minutes or more.
Night waking after the feed is no later than before.
When and how to drop it
Many families drop it somewhere between 6 and 9 months, once the pediatrician agrees night feeds are no longer needed. Either move it 15 minutes earlier every few nights until it merges with bedtime, or reduce the amount gradually as you would any night feed. The full process is in when and how to night wean.
In the plans Dr. Sam writes at Actually Sleeping, a dream feed is used when it clearly earns its place for that baby and removed when it does not.
Frequently asked
What time should I do a dream feed?About 2–3 hours after bedtime, typically between 10 and 11 p.m., ideally right before you go to sleep yourself.
Should I burp or change my baby after a dream feed?A brief burp, yes. Change the diaper only if it is dirty or leaking; a full change tends to wake the baby completely.
Does a dream feed cause a feeding habit?It can if it continues long after the baby stops needing night calories. Used for a few months and then phased out, it rarely causes a problem.
My baby will not wake enough to eat. Should I keep trying?No. Some babies sleep too deeply in the first part of the night to feed well. If a few attempts fail, skip the dream feed and feed when your baby wakes.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Pinilla T, Birch LL. Help me make it through the night: behavioral entrainment of breast-fed infants' sleep patterns. Pediatrics. 1993.
