# Is the pacifier helping or hurting my baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/pacifier-and-baby-sleep/

Is the pacifier helping or hurting my baby’s sleep?
It is helping if your baby takes it at bedtime and sleeps; the AAP recommends offering a pacifier at sleep onset because it is associated with a lower risk of SIDS. It is hurting if you are getting up several times a night to put it back in. Many babies can learn to find and replace it themselves once their hand control allows, often in the second half of the first year; before that, your choices are to keep replacing it or to teach your baby to fall asleep without it.
What the AAP says
Offer a pacifier when placing your baby down for naps and at night. The protective association holds even if it falls out after the baby is asleep.
You do not need to put it back in once your baby is asleep, and you should not force it if your baby refuses.
If you are breastfeeding, wait until feeding is well established before introducing one.
Nothing attached: do not hang a pacifier around the neck or attach it to clothing, blankets or stuffed toys during sleep. Those are strangulation, suffocation and choking hazards.
Help or hindrance? A quick test
HelpingHurting
Baby takes it at sleep onset, it falls out, baby stays asleepBaby wakes crying each time it falls out
Zero to one replacement per nightThree or more replacements a night, often every 45–120 minutes
Naps are a reasonable lengthNaps end at 30–40 minutes when the pacifier drops
The second column is a sleep association: your baby fell asleep sucking, surfaced between cycles, and needs the same condition back. It works exactly like feeding to sleep, just faster to fix.
Option 1: keep it and teach your baby to manage it (often from about 7 months)
During the day, practice: put the pacifier in your baby’s hand instead of their mouth and let them bring it up.
At bedtime, offer a plain pacifier with nothing attached. Some families leave a spare within reach in the crib; check with your pediatrician that this suits your baby, and keep everything else out of the sleep space.
At night, guide your baby’s hand to a pacifier rather than inserting it. After a few nights, just point or tap the mattress.
Expect about a week before the night wakings for it stop.
Option 2: fall asleep without it
For a baby under about 7 months who cannot yet replace it, or a family tired of the nightly search, the cleaner route is to stop using it for sleep. Babies typically protest for two to four nights, then settle. Because of the AAP guidance, this is a trade-off worth raising with your pediatrician for a baby under 6 months: most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, and more than 90% before 6 months. A middle path: offer it at put-down and do not replace it afterwards, while your baby learns to resettle another way.
Toddlers
Many families phase the pacifier out in the toddler years; ask your pediatrician or dentist about timing for your child. Limit it to the crib first, then pick a day, tell your child plainly, and expect a few rough bedtimes.
When Actually Sleeping builds a plan for a pacifier baby, the decision to keep or drop it is made with the parents and written into the plan, so nobody is deciding at 3 a.m.
Frequently asked
Do I need to put the pacifier back in after my baby falls asleep?No. The AAP says it does not need to be reinserted once the baby is asleep.
At what age can a baby replace their own pacifier?In practice many learn from around 7 to 8 months, once they have the hand control to pick it up and turn it around. There is no research-defined age, and daytime practice helps.
Can I use a pacifier attached to a stuffed animal for sleep?Not for sleep. AAP and NIH safe sleep guidance says not to attach pacifiers to clothing, blankets or stuffed toys during sleep. Use a plain pacifier.
Will taking the pacifier away ruin my baby’s sleep?Usually only for a few nights. Babies adapt quickly when the change is consistent and they have another way to fall asleep.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). How to Keep Your Sleeping Baby Safe: Preventing SIDS.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). SIDS by Baby's Age.

# When and how do I stop swaddling?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/swaddle-transition/

When and how do I stop swaddling?
Stop swaddling at the first signs your baby is trying to roll; that is the AAP’s guidance. Rolling usually happens around 3 to 4 months, but some babies start working on it as early as 2 months. If rolling attempts have started, stop immediately and go straight to an arms-free wearable blanket. If they have not, you can take a few nights to transition, one arm at a time.
Why the timing is not flexible
Once a baby starts to roll, swaddling increases the risk of suffocation and strangulation; a swaddled baby who ends up on their stomach cannot use their arms to push up or turn. The AAP therefore says to stop when a baby looks like they are trying to roll, not once they have managed it.
Signs of rolling to watch for
Rolling to the side, or rocking side to side on the back.
Lifting head and shoulders high during tummy time, or pushing up on the arms.
Kicking the legs up and over, twisting the hips.
Regularly breaking out of the swaddle.
Any roll in either direction, even once, even by accident.
How to transition
SituationMethodWhat to expect
Rolling signs have appearedStop tonight. Both arms out, in a regular wearable blanket (sleep sack).2–5 unsettled nights, then sleep returns to baseline.
No rolling signs yet, baby about 6–8 weeks or olderOne arm out for 2–3 nights, then both arms out, then into a sleep sack.Milder disruption spread over about a week.
Rolling signs appear mid-transitionSkip the remaining steps; arms fully out now.Same as stopping at once.
Making the first nights easier
Start at bedtime, when sleep pressure is highest, then carry it through to naps the next day.
Keep everything else the same: routine, dark room, continuous white noise, a pacifier at sleep onset if your baby uses one.
Expect the startle reflex. It starts to fade after about 2 months. Arms will flail for a few nights. That is normal, not a sign the change was too early.
Give a moment before responding. A baby with free hands often finds them and sucks or settles. This is the beginning of self-soothing.
Lots of floor time by day, so rolling both ways arrives sooner and your baby is comfortable moving at night.
What not to use
Weighted swaddles or weighted sleep sacks. The AAP advises against them; they can place too much pressure on a baby’s chest and lungs.
Positioners, wedges or rolled towels to keep a baby on their back. Nothing goes in the sleep space.
Any product that restrains the arms once rolling attempts have started. An arms-free sleep sack only.
Loose blankets as a substitute.
Keep placing your baby on their back for every sleep. Once your baby rolls both ways on their own, you do not have to turn them back over. More in safe sleep and sleep training.
The opportunity in it
Dropping the swaddle often lands near the 4-month sleep change. It is a natural moment to start putting your baby down awake. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage (foundations first, night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks), and the swaddle exit is frequently the first step in the plan.
Frequently asked
Can I swaddle with one arm out long term?No. One arm out is a short bridge of a few nights for a baby who is not yet showing rolling signs. Once rolling attempts begin, both arms must be free.
My baby is 8 weeks and not rolling. Do I have to stop?Not yet, but watch closely from here. Some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months, and the swaddle stops the day they show signs.
Are weighted sleep sacks a good swaddle replacement?No. The AAP advises against weighted swaddles and weighted sleep sacks for infants. Use a regular, non-weighted wearable blanket.
How long does the swaddle transition take?In practice most babies adjust within 2–5 nights when it is done all at once, or about a week with the one-arm approach.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Swaddling: Is it Safe for Your Baby?HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Newborn Reflexes.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.

# Why does my baby wake 30–45 minutes after bedtime?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/false-starts-at-bedtime/

Why does my baby wake 30–45 minutes after bedtime?
A waking 30–45 minutes after bedtime is called a false start: your baby reached the end of the first sleep cycle and could not move into the next. The usual causes are falling asleep with help (feeding, rocking, a replaced pacifier), a last wake window that is too long or too short, or a bedtime early enough that the body treats it as a nap. Fix how your baby falls asleep first, then adjust the last wake window by 15 minutes at a time.
Why it happens at exactly that time
A baby’s sleep cycle is typically about 50 minutes, compared with about 90 minutes in adults. At the end of the first one, every baby surfaces briefly. If conditions match what they were at sleep onset and sleep pressure is high, the baby slides into deep sleep. If something has changed, or the drive to sleep is weak, they wake fully. How infant sleep cycles develop covers the mechanics.
Find your cause
CauseCluesFix
Sleep associationBaby was fed, rocked or held to sleep; wakes crying and settles quickly with the same helpPut down awake at bedtime. Move the feed to the start of the routine.
OvertiredFussy or wired before bed, asleep within a minute or two, wakes screamingShorten the last wake window by 15–30 minutes or bring bedtime earlier.
UndertiredTook 20+ minutes to fall asleep, or wakes happy and chattyLengthen the last wake window by 15 minutes; cap the last nap.
Bedtime treated as a napBedtime before about 6–6:30 p.m., or a late nap ending within 90 minutes of bedShift the day so bedtime lands between 6:30 and 8 p.m.
DiscomfortGas, a burp, reflux symptoms, illness, too warmFeed earlier in the routine, burp well, check the room temperature. Raise ongoing symptoms with your pediatrician.
EnvironmentEvening light, household noise, white noise on a timerBlackout the room; run white noise continuously.
What to do in the moment
Pause. Give your baby a few minutes. Some false starts end on their own.
Respond the way you do at bedtime. If your baby normally falls asleep on their own, use the same brief reassurance you would use then.
Avoid adding a new feed if your baby ate well at bedtime. A top-up 40 minutes later becomes an expected second course. For a young baby who is cluster feeding in the evening, feed; that is normal in the early months.
Do not get them up. Lights on and playtime tell the body that was a nap.
How to test the schedule
Change one variable, by 15 minutes, and hold it for three nights before judging. Starting points are in wake windows by age. As a rule, the last window of the day is the longest, and total daytime sleep should fit your baby’s age.
When false starts mean something else
Under about 3–4 months, evening waking is common and developmental; nothing needs fixing. During a nap transition, expect a week or two of false starts while the day reshuffles. And if your baby also snores, struggles to breathe or seems in pain lying down, that is a pediatrician question, not a schedule one.
False starts are among the first things to disappear in a Actually Sleeping plan, because the first skill taught is falling asleep independently at bedtime.
Frequently asked
Are false starts a sign of overtiredness or undertiredness?Either. A baby who falls asleep instantly and wakes crying is usually overtired; one who takes a long time to fall asleep or wakes cheerful is usually undertired.
How long do false starts last?With the right fix, usually less than a week. If they continue beyond two weeks, the cause is almost always how the baby falls asleep.
Should I feed my baby after a false start?If your baby had a full feed at bedtime, generally no. A young baby who cluster feeds in the evening is a different case; feed them.
ReferencesPatel AK, et al. Physiology, Sleep Stages. StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf (NIH).
Related guidesWhy does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?How do I handle separation anxiety at bedtime?Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?My baby’s sleep fell apart after being sick. How do I get back on track?Why does my 6 month old wake every 2 hours, and how do I fix it?

# Why is my baby awake for hours in the middle of the night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/split-nights/

Why is my baby awake for hours in the middle of the night?
A baby who is wide awake and often cheerful for 1–3 hours in the middle of the night is having a split night. It almost always means more time is being offered for sleep than your baby can fill: too much daytime sleep, a bedtime that is too early, or 13–14 hours in the crib for a baby who sleeps 11. Trim the schedule so time in bed matches actual sleep need, hold a fixed morning wake time, and in practice it often resolves in 1–2 weeks.
How to recognize one
Awake for an hour or more, typically somewhere between midnight and 4 a.m.
Often calm: babbling, rolling around, practicing skills. Crying usually starts only once boredom sets in.
Feeding, rocking or holding does not bring sleep back quickly.
It happens most nights, at a similar time.
This is different from frequent brief wakings every 1.5–2 hours, which point to a sleep association instead. See waking every 2 hours.
Why it happens
Two systems keep a baby asleep: sleep pressure, which builds while awake and is spent in the first half of the night, and the body clock, which carries the second half. When a baby has slept a lot by day or gone to bed very early, pressure runs out before the clock takes over. The gap is the split.
Do the arithmetic
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 12–16 hours per 24 for babies 4–12 months and 11–14 hours for ages 1–2, naps included. Individual babies sit at different points in that range. Log three days: total nap hours plus actual night sleep, not time in the crib.
ExampleOfferedActually sleepsResult
9-month-old, 3.5 h of naps, bed 6:30 p.m. to 7 a.m.16 hAbout 13.5 h2+ hours awake overnight
Same baby, 3 h of naps, bed 7:30 p.m. to 6:45 a.m.14.25 hAbout 13.5 hNight fills in
The fix
Set a fixed wake time and keep it even after a bad night. Sleeping in to recover is what keeps the split going.
Cap daytime sleep to an age-appropriate total and end the last nap early enough to protect the final wake window. Use wake windows by age.
Move bedtime later in 15-minute steps if time in bed exceeds what your baby sleeps. Aim for about 10.5–12 hours in the crib overnight, depending on age and nap total.
Keep the night boring. Dark room, no play, no screens, minimal talk. Check in by your plan and leave. Do not start the day.
Do not add a feed for an older baby whose pediatrician has said night feeds are optional. A feed can anchor the waking in place.
Morning light. Open the curtains and get outside early; daylight sets the clock.
Hold the new schedule for at least a week. The first few days may look worse while your baby runs slightly short of sleep; that deficit is what closes the gap.
Other triggers
Nap transitions. Hanging onto a nap your baby has outgrown is a classic cause. See nap transitions.
New motor skills. Crawling and standing get rehearsed at 2 a.m. for a week or two. Practice hard by day.
Jet lag or a clock change, which shift the body clock directly.
Catch-up sleep after illness, when long recovery naps linger after the illness is over.
Split nights are a schedule puzzle more than a behavior problem, which is why Dr. Sam reviews the daily log each morning during a Actually Sleeping plan and adjusts the timings as the pattern changes.
Frequently asked
Is a split night the same as a sleep regression?No. A regression is a burst of waking around a developmental change. A split night is one long wakeful period caused by more sleep opportunity than the baby needs.
Should I get my baby up and play during a split night?No. Keep the room dark and interaction minimal. Treating it as daytime teaches the body clock to expect it.
How long does it take to fix split nights?Usually 1–2 weeks after the schedule is corrected and the morning wake time is held.
Can an early bedtime cause split nights?Yes, when it adds up to more time in bed than your baby can sleep. An early bedtime helps an overtired baby and hurts one who is already getting enough.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.

# My baby will only sleep on me, not in the crib or bassinet. What do I do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-wont-sleep-in-crib-or-bassinet/

My baby will only sleep on me, not in the crib or bassinet. What do I do?
This is normal in the first weeks and fixable after. In the newborn period, practice one or two put-downs a day and take shifts so that whoever is holding the baby is fully awake. From about 10–12 weeks, and reliably from 4 months, teach your baby to fall asleep in the crib itself, starting at bedtime, because a baby who falls asleep on you and wakes somewhere else will keep protesting the transfer.
Safety first
Holding a sleeping baby while you are awake and alert is fine. The danger is you falling asleep. The AAP’s parent site says the risk is up to 67 times higher when infants sleep with someone on a couch, soft armchair or cushion. If you feel yourself fading, put the baby down on their back in the crib or bassinet, even if they cry, or hand them to another adult. A crying baby in a safe space is safe.
Do not solve the problem with inclined sleepers, loungers, nests, positioners, wedges, weighted sacks, or a swing for sleep. None is a safe sleep surface. The surface should be firm, flat and empty.
Why your baby objects to the crib
You are warm, moving and familiar; the crib is still, flat and cool. That contrast is biggest in the first 8–12 weeks.
The transfer wakes them. Newborns fall asleep through light, active (REM-like) sleep until about 3 months, so a put-down in the first 15–20 minutes often fails.
From about 4 months, it is a sleep association. Your baby fell asleep in your arms, surfaced between cycles, found the conditions changed and called for you.
Newborn to about 10 weeks: practice, without pressure
Try one put-down a day, usually the first nap, when sleep comes easiest.
Swaddle if your baby is not showing signs of rolling, use continuous white noise, and keep the room dark.
For transfers, wait about 15–20 minutes until limbs are heavy, then lower feet first, then bottom, then head, keeping a hand on the chest for a moment.
Split the night with a partner or helper so each of you gets a protected block of sleep.
From about 10–12 weeks: teach the skill
Start at bedtime. Sleep drive is strongest and the body clock helps.
Feed at the beginning of the routine, not the end, so your baby goes into the crib awake.
Put down awake and stay close. Your voice and touch in the crib do the settling that your arms used to do. Then reduce your help over several nights.
Respond to night wakings the same way, keeping any feeds your pediatrician wants.
Naps next. Begin with the first nap of the day. Hold the others if you need to, for now. The stepwise approach is in how to stop contact napping.
AgeRealistic goal
0–10 weeksSome crib or bassinet sleep each day; safe shifts for the rest
10–16 weeksBedtime in the crib, put down awake; some naps still held
4 months and upAll night sleep in the crib within about a week; naps follow over 2–4 weeks
These goals are typical from practice, not research findings.
Rule out discomfort
A baby who arches, screams when laid flat, feeds poorly or is not gaining well needs a pediatrician visit before a sleep plan. If reflux is part of the picture, see sleep training a baby with reflux.
This is the most common reason families contact Actually Sleeping: Dr. Sam writes the plan for the specific baby and is on the line for Night 1, when the first awake put-down happens.
Frequently asked
Is it normal for a newborn to only sleep when held?Yes, very common in the first weeks. The goal then is safe shifts and a little daily practice in the bassinet, not independence.
Can I let my baby sleep on my chest if I stay awake?Yes, if you are fully alert. If there is any chance you will fall asleep, place your baby on their back in the crib or bassinet first.
Will a lounger or nest help my baby sleep in the bassinet?No. Loungers, nests and positioners are not safe for sleep and should not be placed in a crib or bassinet.
Bassinet or crib: does it matter?Not for sleep quality. Both are safe if they meet current safety standards. Move to a crib when your baby reaches the bassinet’s weight limit or starts to push up or roll.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). # Why does my overtired baby fight sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/overtired-baby-fights-sleep/

Why does my overtired baby fight sleep?
When a baby stays awake well past the point their body was ready for sleep, many become more wired and harder to settle, not sleepier. The result looks backwards: the more tired the baby, the harder they fight. The fix is prevention — age-appropriate wake windows, an earlier bedtime on bad nap days — plus a calm, low-stimulation reset when you have already missed the window.
What “overtired” means
Sleep pressure builds the longer a baby is awake. Past a certain point, many babies get a second wind instead of settling. For parents the practical version is simple: a tired baby settles; an overtired one is wired, frantic and hard to console.
Tired versus overtired
Tired (act now)Overtired (window missed)
Staring into space, quieter, less interested in toysCrying that escalates quickly, arching, stiffening
First yawn, slower movementsFrantic or jerky movements; pulling ears, rubbing eyes hard
Pink eyebrows, turning away from stimulationA burst of giddy energy in an older baby or toddler
Falls asleep in 5–15 minutesFights the put-down, or crashes in under 2 minutes and wakes 30–45 minutes later
From about 4–5 months, many babies skip the early cues entirely, so the clock is a better guide than the yawn. Use wake windows by age as your frame.
What overtiredness does to the rest of the day
Short naps, which create more overtiredness. See 30-minute naps.
Waking soon after bedtime. See false starts.
More night waking and early morning waking.
Resetting an overtired baby right now
Cut stimulation. Dark room, white noise, no screens, one calm adult.
Shorten the routine to a few minutes: diaper, sleep sack, one song.
Help more than usual, once. Rocking or holding an overtired baby to get one decent sleep is reasonable. One rescued nap does not create a habit; a pattern does.
Bring bedtime forward by 30–60 minutes that evening. Bedtime as early as 6 p.m. is fine after a poor nap day.
Start fresh tomorrow. Wake at the normal time and watch the first window closely.
Preventing it
Start the wind-down 10–15 minutes before the end of the wake window, not at it.
After a short nap, shorten the next window by 15–30 minutes.
Keep a consistent morning wake time so the day’s naps land predictably.
Protect naps during transitions with a temporary earlier bedtime.
When it is not overtiredness
“Overtired” gets blamed for nearly everything. Check the alternatives:
Undertired. A baby put down too soon also fights sleep, but is usually happy about it: playing, babbling, rolling.
Sleep association. If your baby only fights when put down awake and sleeps easily when fed or rocked, the issue is how they fall asleep, at any level of tiredness.
Evening fussiness in the first months. Fussing that typically peaks at about 3 hours a day around 6 weeks and declines by 3–4 months is common and not caused by the schedule. Long, inconsolable crying deserves a pediatrician’s opinion.
Pain or illness. A sudden change in a baby who normally settles well.
Sorting out which of these is in play is most of the intake work at Actually Sleeping; the schedule in each plan is set by Dr. Sam for that baby’s age and actual sleep totals.
Frequently asked
Can a baby be too tired to sleep?Often, yes. Past a certain point many babies get a second wind and settling becomes harder, so an overtired baby often fights sleep more than a merely tired one.
How do I break the overtired cycle?One or two days of rescued naps by any safe means, an earlier bedtime, and then age-appropriate wake windows from a consistent morning wake time.
Does keeping a baby awake longer make them sleep better at night?Rarely. Stretching a baby past their window usually produces a harder bedtime, more night waking and an earlier morning.
How early is too early for bedtime?For most babies past the newborn stage, 6 p.m. is the practical floor, used temporarily after poor naps. A much earlier bedtime tends to be treated as a nap.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Colic Relief Tips for Parents.

# How do I handle daycare naps when sleep training?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/daycare-naps-and-sleep-training/

How do I handle daycare naps when sleep training?
Start sleep training on a Friday night if you can, so bedtime and the first two days of naps happen at home, then keep going at daycare with one page of clear instructions. Daycare naps are often shorter and that is workable: babies learn that different places have different rules. Protect the night with an earlier bedtime on short-nap days, usually 30–60 minutes earlier.
Why daycare does not undo your work
In practice, babies distinguish settings well. A baby who is rocked by a caregiver at daycare can still fall asleep independently at home, as long as home stays consistent. Nights carry the most weight; get those solid and imperfect daycare naps are survivable.
Timing the start
Best: begin Friday night, giving three nights and two full nap days at home before Monday.
Better still: a long weekend, or a parent at home for a couple of extra days.
New to daycare? Avoid starting both in the same week. Train two or more weeks before the start date, or wait until your baby has had two or three weeks to settle in.
What to ask the daycare
AskWhy
Where and how do babies nap? What is your safe-sleep policy?Every nap should be on the back, on a firm, flat surface in a crib or play yard, with nothing but a fitted sheet. This one is not negotiable.
Can naps follow my baby’s wake windows, or is there a fixed room schedule?Infant rooms are often flexible; toddler rooms usually run one group nap around midday.
Will you put my baby down awake and give a few minutes to settle?Many will try for 5–10 minutes before helping. That is enough to practice.
Is white noise or a darker corner available? Can I send a sleep sack?Familiar cues carry over from home.
Will you log nap start and end times?You need them to set bedtime.
A one-page handout for caregivers
Target nap times or wake windows for this week.
The wind-down: diaper, sleep sack, the same short phrase, into the crib awake.
What to do if the baby fusses: wait the agreed few minutes, then soothe however works for the room.
What to avoid: napping in swings, bouncers or car seats. Safe sleep guidance says sitting devices are not for routine sleep; if a baby falls asleep in one, move them to a flat sleep space.
Keep it short and appreciative. Caregivers manage several babies at once and cannot run a one-to-one plan; a reasonable request gets followed, a three-page protocol does not.
Managing the evenings
Short-nap day: bedtime 30–60 minutes earlier, as early as 6 p.m.
Car nap on the way home: keep your baby awake if it is within about 90 minutes of bedtime, or cap it at 10–15 minutes.
Weekends: hold your home schedule and let naps run to their full length. Many daycare babies catch up on Saturday and Sunday.
One-nap rooms: if your toddler is moved to a single nap before they are ready, use an early bedtime for a few weeks and offer two naps at home on weekends until about 14–15 months. See nap transitions.
Realistic expectations
Night sleep usually improves on the same timeline as for any baby (see how long sleep training takes). Daycare naps tend to lengthen over 2–4 weeks as the baby becomes better at linking cycles, though a bright, busy room may always produce shorter naps than a dark nursery.
In a Actually Sleeping plan, Dr. Sam sets the home schedule around the daycare’s actual routine and adjusts bedtime from the daily nap log, with naps coached until they are solid.
Frequently asked
Will daycare ruin sleep training?No. Babies learn that settings differ. Keep bedtime, nights and weekend naps consistent at home and the skill holds.
My baby only naps 30 minutes at daycare. What should I do?Move bedtime earlier on those days, ask for a darker or quieter crib spot if one exists, and give it a few weeks. Naps often lengthen as night sleep consolidates.
Should I ask daycare to let my baby cry?No. Most centers cannot and will not. Ask instead for an awake put-down and a few minutes to settle before they help.
What day of the week should I start sleep training with daycare?Friday night, so the first two days of naps happen at home before the daycare week begins.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.

# How do I keep my baby sleeping while traveling or changing time zones?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-travel-and-time-zones/

How do I keep my baby sleeping while traveling or changing time zones?
Bring the sleep environment with you — dark, white noise, the usual sleep sack and routine — and keep the same way of falling asleep. For a change of 1–2 time zones or a trip of only a few days, staying on home time is often easiest; for 3 or more zones, switch to local time on arrival and use daylight, meals and capped naps to shift the body clock. In adults it adjusts about 1 hour a day after flying east and 1.5 hours after flying west.
Safe sleep away from home
Same rules as home: on the back, on a firm, flat surface, alone, nothing else in the sleep space.
Bring or request a crib or play yard that meets current safety standards. Inspect a hotel or rental crib: firm, snug-fitting mattress, no broken or missing parts, no added padding. Use a play yard as the manufacturer supplied it, with no extra mattress or padding added.
Not an adult bed, sofa, or cushion nest, even for one night. Couches and armchairs are never safe places for babies to sleep.
Car seats and strollers are for travel. Sleeping in a car seat while riding is expected; when you arrive, move your baby to a firm, flat sleep surface as soon as you can.
Scan the room: blind cords, loose cables, anything a baby can reach from the crib.
Packing list for sleep
Sleep sack and a crib sheet from home, unwashed, for a familiar smell.
Portable white-noise machine.
Portable blackout: travel blinds or paper shades and painter’s tape.
Pacifiers, if used. For toddlers over 12 months, the usual small lovey.
Sharing a room
Put the crib as far from your bed as the room allows, out of your baby’s line of sight if you can, for example around a corner. Never drape a cover over the crib. White noise between you and the baby helps everyone.
Time zones
TripApproach
1–2 hours’ difference, any lengthStay on home time if it suits the trip (a later local bedtime going west can be convenient), or split the difference.
3+ hours, trip under about 4 daysStay close to home time; partial shifts of an hour or two only.
3+ hours, longer tripSwitch to local time on day one. Adult data suggest about one day per hour of change going east, a little faster going west.
Shifting the clock
Wake at a normal local morning time, even after a rough night, and get into daylight straight away.
Eat on local time. Meals are a clock signal.
Cap naps at their usual length so daytime sleep does not replace the night. Wake a baby from a nap that runs long.
Dim the hour before local bedtime; keep the room dark overnight.
Night wakings: keep them dark and quiet. A hungry young baby gets fed; an older baby awake from jet lag gets calm company, not playtime.
Eastward travel (bedtime arrives before the body is ready) is usually harder than westward (early mornings for a few days), because the body clock shifts later more easily than earlier. Morning light helps after flying east.
In transit
On planes and long drives, take whatever sleep you can get: feeding, holding and motion are all fine. Sedating medicines are not a travel tool; see over-the-counter medicines and infant sleep.
Coming home
Return to the usual rules on the first night back. In practice, most babies who slept independently before a trip are back to baseline within 2–4 nights, or about a week after a large time change. If travel is coming soon after sleep training, try to leave 2 weeks between the two. Families working with Actually Sleeping plan upcoming trips with their coach.
Frequently asked
Should I keep my baby on home time when traveling?For a 1–2 hour difference or a short trip, often yes. For 3 or more hours and a longer stay, switching to local time is easier in the end.
How long does jet lag last in babies?There is little research in babies. Adult data suggest the body clock shifts about 1 hour a day after flying east and 1.5 hours after flying west, and strong morning light and consistent local mealtimes help.
Can my baby sleep in my bed just for the trip?The AAP advises against bed-sharing, and unfamiliar adult beds and soft bedding add risk. Use a crib or play yard in your room.
Will travel undo sleep training?It can cause a few off nights. Returning to the usual routine as soon as you are home typically restores sleep within several nights.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.CDC Yellow Book. Jet Lag Disorder.

# How do I adjust my baby’s sleep for daylight saving time?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/daylight-saving-time-baby-sleep/

How do I adjust my baby’s sleep for daylight saving time?
Either shift the whole schedule by 15 minutes a day for the four days before the clock change, or change nothing in advance, move straight to the new clock time and let your baby adjust over about a week. In spring, bedtime needs to move earlier by the body clock; in fall, later. Light is the main tool: bright mornings, dim evenings and a dark bedroom.
What the clock change does
Your baby’s body clock does not read the wall clock. After the spring change, a 7 p.m. bedtime feels like 6 p.m. to the body, so falling asleep is harder and mornings run later. After the fall change, 7 p.m. feels like 8 p.m., so your baby is tired early and up an hour early. Fall is the one parents dread, because nobody wants a 5 a.m. start.
Spring forward
DayWake, naps, meals and bedtime
Wednesday15 minutes earlier than usual
Thursday30 minutes earlier
Friday45 minutes earlier
Saturday60 minutes earlier
SundayNormal schedule on the new clock
The do-nothing version: on Sunday, wake your baby at the usual clock time and run the normal day. Bedtime may take longer for a few nights. If your baby has been waking too early, spring is a gift: a 5:30 a.m. waker becomes a 6:30 a.m. waker. Keep the room very dark in the mornings to hold onto it.
Fall back
DayWake, naps, meals and bedtime
Wednesday15 minutes later than usual
Thursday30 minutes later
Friday45 minutes later
Saturday60 minutes later
SundayNormal schedule on the new clock
The split-the-difference version: on Sunday, put your baby to bed 30 minutes early by the new clock (which feels 30 minutes late to them) for three nights, then move to the normal time.
Tools that move the clock
Morning light at the target wake time; outdoors if possible. Morning light shifts the body clock earlier and evening light shifts it later.
Dim light for the hour before bed. In spring it will still be bright outside at bedtime, so close the blinds early.
Blackout the bedroom, especially for brighter spring evenings and for mornings year-round.
Meals move with the schedule; they are a time cue too.
Hold the wake time. In fall, treat a waking before the target time like any night waking: dark, quiet, boring, until morning officially begins. See early morning waking.
Which approach suits which child
Young babies under about 4 months: schedules are loose anyway. Follow wake windows and ignore the clock.
Adaptable babies and families with fixed daycare times: do nothing in advance and adjust afterwards.
Sensitive sleepers and early risers in fall: the gradual four-day shift is worth the effort.
Toddlers with a wake-up light: move the light’s time in the same 15-minute steps.
What to expect
In practice most babies settle within 3–7 days by either method. Naps may be slightly off; use an earlier bedtime if the day goes badly. Do not add new sleep help during the adjustment week. A baby who can fall asleep independently handles a one-hour shift with far less fuss, which is the core skill Actually Sleeping teaches.
Frequently asked
Should I wake my baby at the normal time after the clocks change?Yes. A consistent morning wake time, with bright light, is the fastest way to move the body clock.
How long does it take a baby to adjust to daylight saving time?In practice, usually 3–7 days. Babies who are sensitive to schedule changes may take up to two weeks.
My baby is waking at 5 a.m. after the fall time change. What do I do?Keep the room dark and treat it as night until your target wake time, moving that target 10–15 minutes later every day or two. Shift naps, meals and bedtime later to match.
Is spring or fall harder for babies?Fall is usually harder because it produces early mornings. Spring mostly causes a few slow bedtimes.
ReferencesCDC Yellow Book. Jet Lag Disorder.

# My baby’s sleep fell apart after being sick. How do I get back on track?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/baby-sleep-after-illness/

My baby’s sleep fell apart after being sick. How do I get back on track?
While your baby is sick, comfort comes first: hold, feed and respond as much as needed. Once your baby is fever-free (a day without fever is a common rule of thumb), eating and drinking normally and back to their usual self by day, return to your normal bedtime routine and night response that same night. In practice, a baby who slept independently before often returns to baseline in 2–4 nights.
During the illness
Respond freely. Extra feeds, cuddles and night checks are appropriate. Sick babies need fluids and may eat less by day and more at night.
Keep the frame if you can: same bedtime, same routine, same room. Add comfort inside that frame.
Go to them rather than bringing them to you. If you want to be close, sleep on a mattress in your baby’s room instead of bringing a sick baby into an adult bed.
Keep sleep safe. Congested babies still sleep flat on their back in an empty crib. Inclined or tilted sleep surfaces are not safe, so do not prop the mattress, use a wedge or pillow, or let your baby sleep in a car seat or swing. Saline drops and gentle suction with a bulb syringe, plus a humidifier if the air is dry, are the usual comfort measures.
Medicines: fever and pain relievers only as your pediatrician directs for your baby’s age and weight. The AAP does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children under 4. More in over-the-counter medicines and infant sleep.
Let them sleep more. Extra and longer naps are part of recovery.
Call the pediatrician
Call right away for a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby 3 months or younger, even with no other symptoms. Also call for trouble breathing or fast, labored breathing; refusing feeds or far fewer wet diapers; a baby who is hard to wake or unusually limp; ear pulling with fever; or symptoms that are getting worse rather than better. Ear infections often cause pain and trouble sleeping, and only an examination can confirm one.
How to know your baby is ready to reset
ReadyNot yet
No fever for about a day without fever medicine (a common rule of thumb; ask your pediatrician)Fever within the last day
Eating and drinking close to normalPoor intake or fewer wet diapers
Playing and alert during the dayClingy, listless or clearly uncomfortable
A lingering mild cough or runny nose onlyBreathing that looks like work; untreated ear infection
If you are unsure, ask the pediatrician: “Is there any medical reason not to go back to our normal sleep routine?”
The reset
Pick the night and go back fully. Same routine, down awake, your usual response. A slow fade tends to drag things out.
Drop the extra night feeds that crept in, if your baby was not feeding overnight before and your pediatrician has no concerns. Offer more by day; appetite rebounds after illness.
Trim the recovery naps back to the usual schedule over two or three days so daytime sleep stops borrowing from the night.
Expect protest for 2–4 nights. It is usually shorter than the first time, because the skill is still there.
Both adults respond the same way.
If illnesses keep coming
In the first daycare winter, colds can arrive every few weeks. Reset after each one; the resets get quicker. If your baby never slept independently before the illness, this is not a reset but a first attempt, and waiting until a fully healthy week is sensible. See the best age to sleep train.
Families in an active Actually Sleeping plan pause during illness and pick up the same plan when the baby is well, with Dr. Sam confirming the restart in the daily check-in.
Frequently asked
Should I keep sleep training while my baby is sick?No. Pause, comfort your baby and resume the same plan once they are well. Keep the bedtime and routine consistent in the meantime if possible.
How long after an illness can I restart sleep training?A common rule of thumb is once your baby has gone about a day without fever, is feeding normally and is acting like themselves. Check with your pediatrician if in doubt.
Can I raise the crib mattress to help with congestion?No. Safe sleep guidance from the AAP and NIH says inclined or tilted sleep surfaces are not safe. Use saline, gentle suction and a humidifier if the air is dry instead.
My baby started waking to feed again when sick. Will that stop?Usually, once you stop offering the extra feeds after recovery and add calories back during the day. If your baby lost weight during the illness, ask your pediatrician first.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Fever and Your Baby.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Coughs and Colds: Medicines or Home Remedies?HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Ear Infection Symptoms.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Use Caution When Giving Cough and Cold Products to Kids.

# How do I handle separation anxiety at bedtime?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/separation-anxiety-at-bedtime/

How do I handle separation anxiety at bedtime?
Separation anxiety is a normal stage that usually starts between 8 and 12 months, peaks between 10 and 18 months, and tapers off in the second half of the second year. Handle it with extra connection during the day, a predictable bedtime routine, and a short, confident goodnight; then check in briefly and consistently rather than staying until your child is asleep.
Why it shows up at bedtime
Somewhere between 8 and 12 months, babies grasp that you still exist when you are out of sight, but not yet when, or whether, you will come back. Bedtime is the longest separation of the day, so that is where the protest lands. It is a sign of healthy attachment, not a sleep problem in itself.
AgeWhat it looks likeWhat helps most
8–12 months (onset)Crying when you leave the room, clinging at put-down, new night wakingPeekaboo and short daytime separations; a brief, steady goodnight
Up to about 18 months (peak window)Loud protest, “one more” requests, standing and callingLimited choices in the routine; the same words every night
2–3 yearsStalling, fears, leaving the room if in a bedExtra one-to-one time before the routine; a clear rule and calm follow-through
By day: build the idea that you come back
Peekaboo and hiding games. They are practice for exactly this.
Short separations. Step out of the room, say where you are going, return cheerfully. Lengthen gradually.
Always say goodbye. Sneaking out teaches a child to watch you constantly.
Play in the bedroom at happy times so the crib is not only the place where you leave.
Fill the tank. Ten to twenty minutes of undivided attention before the routine reduces protest more than any trick.
At bedtime
Same routine, same order, 20–30 minutes, ending in the bedroom.
One goodnight phrase, said warmly and once. Then leave while your child is awake.
If they cry, check in briefly: a calm voice, a quick touch, the same phrase, and out. The message is “you are safe and I come back,” not “I will stay until you sleep.”
Do not lengthen the goodbye. Hesitation reads as a signal that something really is wrong.
A comfort object can help, but only after 12 months. The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations cover the first year, and until then the crib stays empty.
What prolongs it
Staying until your child is asleep, or lying down with them, as a new habit.
Bringing back night feeds or rocking that had already ended.
Bed-sharing as a response, which the AAP advises against for infants.
Responding differently each night, so your child keeps testing which version they will get.
Moving to a bed. A crib is containing and reassuring at this stage.
One or two hard nights during illness or a big change are a different matter; comfort freely and return to normal afterwards.
Is this a reason to delay sleep training?
No. If your baby does not yet fall asleep independently, a plan built around this stage, with a parent close by at first and predictable returns, tends to lower bedtime distress because your child learns exactly what happens next. At Actually Sleeping the approach is “not cry it out, not wait it out”: a custom plan with live support on Night 1. Related: the 8–10 month regression and the 18 month regression.
When to talk to the pediatrician
If the anxiety is extreme throughout the day, lasts many weeks without easing, follows a major upheaval, or comes with signs of illness or pain at night.
Frequently asked
At what age does separation anxiety peak?According to the AAP’s parent site, it usually starts between 8 and 12 months, peaks between 10 and 18 months, and tapers off in the second half of the second year. Bedtime protests can resurface later at times of change.
Should I stay in the room until my baby falls asleep?As a short, planned step that you fade over several nights, it can be part of a plan. As an open-ended response, it usually becomes a new sleep association.
Can I give my baby a lovey for separation anxiety?After 12 months, a small lovey is generally fine. Before 12 months, the AAP advises keeping soft objects out of the sleep space.
How long does separation anxiety at bedtime last?The stage as a whole runs for months. In practice, an intense bedtime phase often eases within a few weeks with a consistent response, though it can resurface at later stages.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Emotional and Social Development: 8 to 12 Months.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.

# When should I move my toddler from a crib to a bed?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/crib-to-toddler-bed-when/

When should I move my toddler from a crib to a bed?
As late as you safely can: ideally close to age 3, when a child can understand and follow a “stay in bed” rule. Move sooner only if your toddler is climbing out and the usual fixes have failed, or they have outgrown the crib’s height limit. A new sibling, an 18-month or 2-year regression, or bedtime resistance are not reasons to switch, and usually get worse in a bed.
Why waiting helps
A crib does the job of impulse control for a child who does not yet have it. In practice, many children under about 2.5–3 cannot reliably stay in an open bed because they have been told to, however well they understand the words. Families who switch at 18–24 months often trade one problem for a bigger one: see my toddler won’t stay in bed.
Good reasons and poor reasons
Good reasons to movePoor reasons to move
Repeatedly climbing out despite the fixes belowA new baby needs the crib (use a second crib or a bassinet for the newborn)
Taller than the limit in the crib’s manual, or about 35 inches (89 cm), the height by which MedlinePlus says children should no longer use a cribTurning 2
Close to 3, asking for a bed, following simple rules by dayFighting bedtime or waking at night
Night toilet training that requires getting to the bathroomA regression, a move or a new daycare in the same month
If your toddler is climbing out
Lower the mattress to its lowest setting.
Use a regular sleep sack. It limits how high a leg can lift. Not a weighted one.
Remove footholds: bumpers, large toys, anything inside or beside the crib that works as a step.
Respond flatly. A calm “we stay in the crib,” back in, no drama. A big reaction makes climbing a game.
Do not use crib tents or homemade covers. The CPSC has recalled crib tents over strangulation and entrapment hazards and told parents to stop using them.
If your child still gets out, the crib is no longer safe. Move to a bed or a mattress on the floor that same day.
Make the room the crib
Once a child can leave the bed, the whole bedroom has to be safe to be in alone:
Anchor dressers, shelves and televisions to the wall.
Secure blind cords and electrical cords; cover outlets.
Remove small objects, medicines, toiletries and anything climbable.
Put a gate at the bedroom door or the top of the stairs; lock windows or fit guards.
Choose a low bed or toddler bed, with guardrails made for the purpose, away from windows.
Making the switch
Pick a calm stretch. No travel, illness, new sibling or toilet-training push within a few weeks.
Involve your child a little: choosing sheets is enough. Keep the build-up low-key.
Same routine, same bedtime, same spot in the room if possible.
State one rule: “You stay in bed until your light turns green.” In practice a wake-up light tends to work from about 2.5 years.
Return them silently every time they get up, starting on the first night. The honeymoon week often ends around night 5–10; be ready.
Praise in the morning for staying in bed.
If you moved too early
Going back to the crib is allowed, and for a child under about 2.5 who is not climbing it is often the quickest fix. Present it plainly and without blame.
Actually Sleeping works with children up to age 3, in cribs and in beds; where a family has a choice, the plan Dr. Sam writes usually keeps the crib until sleep is solid.
Frequently asked
What is the best age to switch from a crib to a bed?For most children, close to 3. Earlier only for safety reasons such as climbing out or outgrowing the crib.
Should I move my toddler to a bed before the new baby arrives?Preferably not for that reason. If the move is truly needed, do it at least 2–3 months before the birth, or wait until a few months after.
Is a toddler bed or a twin bed better?Either works. What matters is that it is low, has appropriate guardrails and sits in a fully childproofed room.
My 2 year old climbed out of the crib once. Do I have to switch?Not necessarily. Lower the mattress, use a sleep sack, remove footholds and respond calmly. If climbing continues, move to a bed for safety.
ReferencesU.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Safe Sleep – Cribs and Infant Products.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Five Retailers Agree to Stop Sale and Recall Tots in Mind Crib Tents Due to Strangulation and Entrapment Hazard. 2012.MedlinePlus (NIH). Cribs and crib safety.American Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.

# Can I sleep train a premature baby or NICU graduate?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-a-premature-or-nicu-baby/

Can I sleep train a premature baby or NICU graduate?
Yes, in most cases, once your pediatrician confirms your baby is ready. Use corrected age (counted from the due date, not the birth date): gentle habit-shaping can begin around 10–12 weeks corrected, and fuller sleep training around 4–6 months corrected, provided weight gain is steady and any medical issues are stable. Night feeds stay until your pediatrician says they can go, which is often later for babies born early.
A note on scope: Dr. Sam is a Doctor of Pharmacy and a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist. Readiness, feeding and any medical question for a baby born early belong to your pediatrician or neonatal follow-up team.
Corrected age, and why it matters
Corrected (adjusted) age is your baby’s age from birth minus the weeks they arrived early (40 minus the gestational age at birth). A baby born 8 weeks early who is 6 months old is about 4 months corrected. The AAP recommends using corrected age during the first 2 years to judge development, so it makes sense to use it for wake windows, nap counts and sleep expectations too.
Corrected ageWhat is realistic
Before the due date to about 10 weeksFeed on your team’s schedule, safe sleep, day–night cues. No training.
10–16 weeksConsistent routine, practice putting down awake, feeds kept as directed
4–6 monthsIndependent sleep onset; night feeds per pediatrician
6 months and beyondFull sleep training; night weaning when cleared
Questions for your pediatrician first
Is weight gain on track on my baby’s own growth curve?
How many night feeds does my baby still need, and may I stop waking them to feed?
Is fortified milk or a special formula schedule a factor overnight?
Are reflux, breathing or oxygen needs, or apnea history stable enough for a sleep plan?
Is there any reason my baby should not be given a few minutes to settle?
What is different for NICU graduates
Feeding comes first, longer. Many preemies need scheduled feeds, including overnight, well past the point a term baby would. Never stretch or drop a feed without clearance.
Home sleep is on the back. Babies are sometimes placed on their stomach or side in the NICU under continuous monitoring. At home, NIH safe sleep guidance says all babies, including those born preterm, sleep on their backs until 1 year: firm and flat, nothing in the crib, no positioners or nests, no inclines.
Medical equipment. A baby discharged on oxygen or a prescribed monitor needs a plan built with the medical team. The AAP and NIH advise against using heart, breathing or motion monitors as a way to reduce SIDS risk; they do not replace safe sleep.
Light and noise. After weeks in a bright, alarm-filled unit, some babies sleep through anything and others startle easily. Dark nights, bright days and continuous white noise help build the day–night rhythm.
Reflux questions are common. Babies with reflux still sleep on their backs. See sleep training a baby with reflux.
Parents carry the NICU with them. Being hyper-alert to every sound is a reasonable response to what you lived through. A plan with defined check-ins lets you respond on purpose rather than on adrenaline.
How the plan itself changes
Schedules run on corrected age. Start with wake windows by age and use the younger band.
Night feeds are written in, at the times and amounts your pediatrician wants.
The approach starts with more parental presence and smaller steps.
Progress is judged alongside weight checks, and the plan pauses for illness or a slowdown in growth.
When to wait
Faltering weight gain, a recent hospital readmission, unstable breathing, an upcoming procedure, or a pediatrician who says not yet. Waiting a month loses nothing.
Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage (foundations first, night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at 10 weeks), using corrected age for those born early, and builds each NICU graduate’s plan around the pediatrician’s feeding instructions. Twins born early have their own notes in sleep training twins.
Frequently asked
Do I use corrected age or actual age for sleep training a preemie?Corrected age, counted from the due date. It is the better guide to sleep maturity, wake windows and nap needs.
When can a premature baby sleep through the night?It varies with growth and feeding needs. Many can once they are past about 6 months corrected and the pediatrician has cleared them to drop night feeds, but some need night feeds longer.
Can my preemie sleep on their stomach like in the NICU?No. Stomach or side positioning in the NICU happens under continuous monitoring. At home, AAP and NIH guidance is the back for every sleep, including for babies born preterm.
Is sleep training harder for NICU babies?Not necessarily. It often starts later and moves in smaller steps, but NICU graduates with stable weight gain generally learn independent sleep well.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Corrected Age for Preemies.Safe to Sleep campaign, NICHD (NIH). Ways to Reduce Baby's Risk.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. # Is there a 2 year old sleep regression?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/2-year-old-sleep-regression/

Is there a 2 year old sleep regression?
Yes. Around age 2, often anywhere from 22 to 30 months, many toddlers who slept well start fighting bedtime, refusing the nap, waking at night or rising early. It is driven by development — independence, language, imagination and new fears — and often by a change such as a new sibling, toilet training or a move to a bed. With steady boundaries it typically passes in 2–6 weeks; a 2-year-old still needs a nap.
What it looks like
Bedtime stretches from 20 minutes to an hour of requests: water, another book, a different blanket.
Nap refusal: playing or shouting through the whole nap period.
Night waking with calling out, or appearing at your bedside if in a bed.
New fear of the dark, shadows or being alone.
Waking for the day at 5 a.m.
Why now
DriverWhat to do about it
Independence and limit-testingOffer two harmless choices inside the routine; keep the order and the ending fixed
Imagination and first fearsTake the fear seriously and briefly; a dim, warm night light; no long searches for monsters
Nap strikeKeep offering the nap daily; see below
Two-year molars (often 23–33 months)Comfort, and pain relief only as your pediatrician directs, for the few days around eruption
Big changes: sibling, toilet training, new room, new daycareOne change at a time where you can; keep sleep rules identical through it
Crib-to-bed moveWait if you can. See when to move to a bed
Schedule driftNap too late or too long, or bedtime no longer matching sleep need
Do not drop the nap
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 11–14 hours of sleep per 24 for ages 1–2 and 10–13 hours for ages 3–5, naps included. Most children nap until somewhere between 3 and 5. A 2-year-old refusing the nap for a week or two is on strike, not finished.
Offer the nap every day at the same time, usually starting around 12:30–1 p.m.
Keep your child in the crib or room for at least an hour of quiet time, asleep or not.
On no-nap days, move bedtime 30–60 minutes earlier.
If the nap is happening but bedtime has become very late, cap the nap at 1.5–2 hours and end it by about 3 p.m.
A schedule that fits most 2-year-olds
Wake between 6 and 7 a.m.
One nap of 1.5–2.5 hours beginning about 5–6 hours after waking.
Bedtime between 7 and 8 p.m., about 4.5–5.5 hours after the nap ends.
Bedtime boundaries that work at this age
Front-load attention. Fifteen minutes of one-to-one play before the routine.
A picture chart of the routine. The chart is the boss, which takes the argument away from you.
Requests go inside the routine: last drink, last toilet trip, two books chosen by your child.
One clear ending phrase, then leave.
Brief, boring responses afterwards. In a bed, a silent walk back every time. See my toddler won’t stay in bed.
Screens off for at least an hour before bed.
Regression or something else?
Ask your pediatrician about regular snoring, mouth breathing or pauses in breathing, restless sleep with sweating, pain, or a sleep change alongside loss of skills. Night terrors (screaming while still asleep, no memory in the morning) are different from nightmares and are worth mentioning too.
If it has gone on longer than six weeks, it has usually stopped being a regression and become the new routine. Actually Sleeping works with toddlers up to age 3, and a plan at this age is mostly about clear, kind limits that both parents hold the same way. Related: the 18 month regression.
Frequently asked
How long does the 2 year sleep regression last?Typically 2–6 weeks when boundaries stay consistent. It lasts longer when new habits, such as lying with the child until asleep, begin during it.
Is my 2 year old ready to stop napping?Probably not. Most children nap until 3–5 years. Keep offering the nap and use quiet time on days it does not happen.
Should I move my 2 year old to a bed during the regression?No, unless there is a safety reason. Changing beds in the middle of a regression usually makes both harder.
Why is my 2 year old suddenly scared at bedtime?Imagination develops quickly around this age and fears come with it. Acknowledge the fear briefly, offer a dim night light, and keep the routine and response the same.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016.

# Is a baby sleep consultant worth it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/is-a-baby-sleep-consultant-worth-it/

Is a baby sleep consultant worth it?
It is worth it when the thing you are missing is not information but a plan fitted to your baby and someone to adjust it night by night. It is usually not worth it if you have never tried one consistent approach for a week or more. Behavioral sleep methods work well in research; consistency is where most families struggle.
What you are actually paying for
The methods themselves are public. Books, courses and free guides describe them well. A consultant charges for three things a book cannot give you:
Fit. A plan built from your baby’s age, feeding, naps, room, temperament and your own limits, instead of an age-band template.
Adjustment. When night 3 looks different from night 2, someone who has seen the pattern before tells you what to change and what to leave alone.
Accountability. Knowing you will report to a person tomorrow makes it easier to follow the plan at 2 a.m.
What the research says about the methods
An American Academy of Sleep Medicine review of 52 treatment studies found that 94% reported behavioral interventions for bedtime problems and night waking were effective, with over 80% of children treated showing clinically significant improvement, maintained for 3 to 6 months. That is evidence that the approaches work. It is not evidence that you need to hire anyone to use them. No trial has tested paid consultants against doing it yourself.
It is often worth it when
You tried a book or course, followed it for at least a week, and sleep is still broken.
Your situation has extra moving parts: reflux under treatment, a premature baby, twins, a toddler who leaves the bed, a baby who shares your room.
You and your partner disagree about what to do at night and need one plan you both trust.
Sleep loss is affecting your health, your work or your mood, and waiting it out no longer feels acceptable.
You know yourself: you will follow a plan with a person behind it and abandon one without.
It is usually not worth it when
You have not yet tried a single approach consistently. Start with a step-by-step guide and give it a fair week.
The trouble started this week with a cold, travel or a new tooth. Give it time to pass.
Your baby has a possible medical issue: loud snoring, pauses in breathing, poor weight gain. See your pediatrician first. Coaching can come after.
You are happy with how things are. Contact naps and night feeds are not problems unless they are problems for you.
A fair way to decide
Write down what you have already tried and for how many nights. If the list is short, try one method properly first. If it is long, the gap is probably fit and follow-through, which is exactly what a consultant sells. Then compare categories honestly: course, app or 1:1 consultant. Each suits a different family.
Questions that tell you whether a specific consultant is worth it
Is there a written guarantee, and what exactly does it promise?
Who writes the plan, and how much live support is included?
Does the intake ask about feeding, growth and medical history?
Will they tell you if they do not think they can help?
The full checklist is in how to choose a sleep consultant.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Dr. Sam writes every plan personally. Families get live support on night one, daily 1:1 check-ins, and naps coached until solid. The outcome is guaranteed in writing: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund. Pricing is custom to your baby and is set on the free consultation.
Frequently asked
Are sleep consultants worth the money?For families who have tried a consistent approach and are still stuck, often yes, because the missing piece is usually fit and follow-through. For families who have not tried anything consistently yet, a free guide followed for a week is the better first step.
How much does a baby sleep consultant cost?It varies widely by format and by how much live support is included. At Actually Sleeping, pricing is custom to your baby and is set on the free consultation. Compare what is included, not only the total.
Can I just do it myself?Many families do. The methods are public and well studied. Doing it yourself works best when you pick one method, write it down, and keep it the same every night for at least a week before judging it.
Is a sleep consultant worth it for a newborn?Only for foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine and realistic expectations. Newborns should not be sleep trained. Some families value that early guidance; many do fine with a good guide.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.

# What does a baby sleep consultant actually do?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/what-does-a-baby-sleep-consultant-do/

What does a baby sleep consultant actually do?
A baby sleep consultant assesses how your baby falls asleep, wakes and naps, writes a plan to change the behavioral parts, and supports you while you carry it out. Good consultants screen for medical red flags and refer you to your pediatrician when they find them. They do not diagnose, prescribe, or make feeding decisions that belong to your pediatrician.
The usual sequence
Intake. A questionnaire or call covering age (and corrected age if your baby was born early), how your baby falls asleep, what happens at each waking, feeding, naps, the sleep space, health history and what you have already tried.
Assessment. The consultant looks for the drivers: a sleep association, a schedule mismatch, an overtired or undertired baby, early morning light, or something that needs a doctor rather than a plan.
The plan. A written document covering the bedtime routine, the schedule, how you respond to wakings, how night feeds are handled (with your pediatrician’s input), and how naps will be approached.
Support while you do it. This is where formats differ most. Some consultants offer one call and a follow-up email. Others reply daily, or are available in real time on the first night.
Adjustment. Babies rarely follow the script exactly. The consultant reads your notes or sleep log and changes timing or responses as needed.
Wrap-up. Guidance for what comes next: nap transitions, illness, travel, a new sibling.
What a consultant should not do
Diagnose. Snoring, breathing pauses, poor weight gain, reflux symptoms and suspected allergies belong with your pediatrician. See sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist.
Recommend medication or supplements for sleep. Questions about medicines go to your pediatrician or pharmacist.
Override your pediatrician on feeding. Whether your baby still needs night feeds is a growth and health question.
Bend safe sleep rules. The AAP advises a firm, flat, non-inclined surface, on the back, without soft bedding, and says weighted swaddles and weighted objects on or near the baby are not safe. A plan should never work around these.
What it is like for you
You still do the nights. A consultant does not usually come to your home and put your baby down; you do it, following the plan, and report what happened. That is deliberate. Your baby is learning to fall asleep with you as the parent in the room, and you are learning what to do the next time sleep goes sideways.
Expect to keep a simple log for the first week or two: when your baby went down, how long it took to fall asleep, each waking and what you did. The log is what lets a consultant adjust the plan instead of guessing.
What a consultant brings that a book does not
Pattern recognition. Someone who has worked with many babies can often tell from a short description whether an early waking is a schedule problem or a light problem, or whether night 4’s setback is normal. The value is less in knowing the method and more in knowing which detail to change.
How formats differ
ElementLighter-touch formatsHigher-support formats
PlanAge-based template, lightly editedWritten from scratch for your baby
First nightYou are on your ownLive support while you do it
Follow-upOne call or a few emailsDaily check-ins
NapsGeneral adviceCoached until they are reliable
How Actually Sleeping handles this: The plan is written personally by Dr. Sam from a detailed intake. A coach supports you live on night one, the team checks in with you 1:1 every day, and naps are coached until solid. The approach is not cry it out and not wait it out.
Frequently asked
Does a sleep consultant come to my house?Most work remotely by video, phone and messaging. Some offer in-home visits. In either case, you are usually the one putting your baby down, because your baby needs to learn to sleep with you, not with a visitor.
Is a sleep consultant the same as a sleep coach?In practice, yes. Neither title is a licensed profession, and people use them interchangeably. Judge the person by their process, support, credentials and what they put in writing, not by the title.
Will a sleep consultant make me stop night feeds?A good one will not decide that for you. Whether your baby still needs to eat at night is a question for your pediatrician, based on age and growth. A plan can teach independent sleep while keeping feeds.
What information should I have ready for a sleep consultant?A few days of notes on bedtime, wakings, feeds and naps, your baby’s birth date and due date, any health history, and a clear list of what you have already tried and for how long.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces & Bed Sharing. 2022.

# How do I choose a baby sleep consultant? Questions to ask before you hire
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-to-choose-a-baby-sleep-consultant/

How do I choose a baby sleep consultant? Questions to ask before you hire
Ask every consultant the same questions and compare the answers in writing: Is there a written guarantee and exactly what does it say? Who writes the plan? What are their credentials? How much live support, for how long? What method, and how much crying? What ages do they work with? How are their reviews verified? Vague answers are an answer.
The questions
1. Is there a written guarantee, and what exactly does it say?
Ask to see the wording. A useful guarantee names a measurable outcome (for example, hours of night sleep), a time frame, what you have to do to qualify, and what happens if it is not met (a refund, or something else). “We guarantee you’ll be happy” or “support until it works” are not outcome guarantees. Many consultants offer none, which is fine as long as they are clear about it. More detail: what a sleep-training guarantee should say.
2. Who writes the plan?
A named person reading your intake, or an age-based template with your baby’s name added? Ask: “If two families with 6-month-olds came to you this week, how different would their plans be?”
3. What are their credentials?
Sleep consulting has no required license. Ask which training they completed, whether they hold any licensed health care credential, and what that credential does and does not cover. See what credentials a sleep consultant should have.
4. How much live support, and for how long?
Is someone available in real time on the first night?
How often do they check in after that: daily, every few days, weekly?
Through what channel, and how fast do they reply?
Does support end on a fixed date, or when sleep is solid? Are naps included?
5. What method do they use, and is crying involved?
Ask them to describe night one in plain words: where you are, what you do when your baby cries, and how long before you go in. Most changes to sleep involve some protest crying, because your baby is learning something new. The honest answer describes how much, and what you do about it. Be wary of “no tears, ever” and of an approach that does not fit your limits. See do sleep consultants use cry it out.
6. What ages do they work with?
Ask what they do with a newborn (foundations, not training), with a 4-month-old, and with a toddler in a big bed. A consultant who works across ages should explain how the plan changes with each.
7. How are their reviews verified?
Testimonials on a website are chosen by the business. Ask whether reviews are from real, identifiable clients (video reviews help), whether any are collected by an independent service that confirms each reviewer was a paying client, and how recent they are.
Four more questions worth asking
What does your intake ask about health? Look for questions on growth, feeding, reflux, prematurity, snoring and breathing.
How do you handle night feeds? The right answer defers to your pediatrician.
Do your plans follow AAP safe sleep guidance? Back to sleep, firm flat surface, nothing soft or weighted in the sleep space.
Have you ever told a family you could not help them? A consultant who screens is a consultant who expects to deliver.
Make the comparison easy
Put each consultant’s answers in a simple table. Differences in support and guarantees tend to matter more than differences in method.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: The guarantee is written into the Terms of Service: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” Full refund if not. Dr. Sam (Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, PharmD, a Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist) writes every plan. There is live support on night one, daily 1:1 check-ins, and naps are coached until solid. It is not cry it out and not wait it out. The practice works with families from newborn to 3 years. Its 129 client video reviews are at actuallysleeping.com/reviews.
Frequently asked
What is the most important question to ask a sleep consultant?Ask how much live support you get and for how long. Most plans fail on nights 2 to 5, when something unexpected happens. A consultant you can reach then matters more than the method named on the website.
Should I ask for references?You can. More useful is a set of reviews you can check: video reviews from identifiable families, or reviews collected by an independent service that confirms each reviewer paid. Ask how recent they are.
Is it a red flag if a consultant has no guarantee?Not by itself. Many good consultants do not guarantee outcomes. It is a red flag if a consultant implies a guarantee in marketing but cannot show you the written wording.
Should both parents be on the consultation call?If you can manage it, yes. Both parents usually handle nights at some point, and a plan works best when both of you have heard the reasoning and agreed to it before night one.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces & Bed Sharing. 2022.
