# Sleep course vs app vs 1:1 sleep consultant: which is right for my family?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-course-vs-app-vs-sleep-consultant/

Sleep course vs app vs 1:1 sleep consultant: which is right for my family?
Pick by how much personalization and live support you need. Books and self-paced courses suit families who follow written instructions well. Apps suit families who want tracking and suggestions. Group programs add peer support. A 1:1 consultant suits families with a complicated situation or a failed attempt behind them. A night nurse is overnight newborn care, not sleep teaching.
The categories side by side
CategoryWhat you getWho adjusts the planLive supportUsually fitsWatch for
Book or free guide (DIY)Explanation of methods and schedulesYouNoneConfident, consistent parents with a straightforward babyMixing methods from several sources
AppSleep logging, schedule or nap suggestions, sometimes chatAn algorithm, or youVaries; often limitedParents who like data and want help with timingSuggestions are only as good as what you log; tracking is not teaching
Self-paced courseVideos and written steps by ageYouUsually none, or an online communityFamilies who want structure and a clear method at their own paceAge-band templates may not fit your baby
Group programCourse material plus group calls or a moderated groupYou, with general inputScheduled, sharedFamilies who want company and some expert accessYour question competes with everyone else’s
1:1 sleep consultantIndividual plan and ongoing supportThe consultant, from your daily notesRanges from one call to daily check-ins and live first-night helpComplex situations, failed attempts, parents who want accountabilitySupport levels and guarantees vary a lot; ask exactly what is included
Night nurse or overnight newborn careA person who cares for your baby overnightNot applicableIn person, overnightNewborn weeks, recovery from birth, multiplesRest for you, but it does not teach your baby to sleep on their own
Cost generally rises as personalization and live support increase.
How to decide
Start with DIY or a course if
Your baby is healthy and growing well.
You have not tried any method consistently yet.
You and your partner agree on how much crying you can accept.
You are good at following written steps for a week without improvising.
Consider an app if
Timing is your main problem: short naps, an early morning, a bedtime that drifts.
You will actually log every sleep and waking for a couple of weeks.
Consider a group program if
You want a method plus the chance to ask questions, and you do not mind waiting for an answer.
Other parents going through the same thing keep you going.
Consider a 1:1 consultant if
You tried a course or book correctly for at least a week and it did not work.
There are complicating factors: reflux under treatment, prematurity, twins, room sharing, a toddler out of the crib, daycare naps.
You know you will give up at 2 a.m. without someone to check in with.
Consider overnight newborn care if
You need sleep yourself in the first weeks and your baby is too young for sleep teaching.
You are recovering from a difficult birth or caring for multiples.
Combining them
Categories are not exclusive. Many families read a book first, then hire a consultant when they get stuck. Some use overnight newborn care early and add a consultant for foundations or for training later. A good consultant will build on what you already know rather than starting over.
The evidence applies to all of them
The behavioral methods behind every category are well studied. An AASM review of 52 studies found 94% reported behavioral interventions effective. A randomized trial of a fully online, self-directed program for children 6 to 36 months found fewer and shorter night wakings and faster sleep onset within three weeks. Format affects how easy it is to stay consistent; the methods are the same.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Actually Sleeping is a 1:1 option at the higher-support end: a plan written by Dr. Sam, live support on night one, daily 1:1 check-ins, and naps coached until solid, with a written refund-backed guarantee. It is a fit for families who want that level of support; for many families a good book or course is enough.
Frequently asked
Is a sleep course as good as a sleep consultant?For a straightforward situation and a consistent family, a course can work well, because the underlying methods are the same. A consultant adds a plan fitted to your baby and someone to adjust it when things do not go as described.
Do baby sleep apps work?They can help with timing and with seeing patterns, because logging shows you what is really happening. Tracking alone does not change how your baby falls asleep. Pair an app with a clear plan.
Can I start with a course and hire a consultant later?Yes, and many families do exactly that. Bring your notes on what you tried and for how many nights. It saves time and shows the consultant where the plan broke down.
What is the cheapest way to sleep train?A free, reputable guide followed consistently. The methods are public and well studied. Pick one, write down exactly what you will do, and keep it the same for at least a week. Spend money when you need personalization or live support, not before.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Mindell JA, et al. Efficacy of an Internet-Based Intervention for Infant and Toddler Sleep Disturbances. Sleep. 2011.

# What are the red flags when hiring a baby sleep consultant?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-red-flags/

What are the red flags when hiring a baby sleep consultant?
Walk away from a consultant who bends AAP safe sleep rules, suggests medication or supplements for sleep, tells you to drop night feeds without your pediatrician, diagnoses medical problems, promises results without written terms, will not describe how much crying is involved, or pressures you to sign before you understand what is included.
Safety red flags (disqualifying)
Anything that conflicts with safe sleep. The AAP advises that babies sleep on their back, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface, without soft toys, pillows, blankets or other bedding. It says weighted swaddles, weighted clothing and weighted objects on or near the baby are not safe, and it advises against commercial devices that claim to reduce the risk of SIDS. A plan that uses any of these, or that props or inclines a baby, is not a plan to follow.
Medication or supplement suggestions for sleep. Melatonin, antihistamines and “natural” sleep products are not a coaching tool. Questions about medicines go to your pediatrician or pharmacist. See is melatonin safe for babies.
Dropping night feeds on the consultant’s say-so. Whether a baby still needs to eat at night depends on age and growth, and that is your pediatrician’s call.
Diagnosing. “It’s silent reflux,” “it’s a tongue tie,” “it’s sleep apnea.” A consultant who hears snoring, breathing pauses or poor weight gain should send you to your pediatrician, not name a condition.
Sleep training a newborn. Newborn work should be foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine. Not leaving a newborn to cry and not stretching feeds.
Honesty red flags
“Guaranteed” in the ads, nothing in writing. If a result is promised, the exact words should be in the agreement you sign.
Medical-sounding titles that are not medical. “Sleep doctor” or “pediatric sleep specialist” from someone who is not a physician or a sleep-medicine clinician. Ask what the credential is and who issued it.
“No tears, ever.” Most babies protest when something about bedtime changes. An honest consultant tells you how much crying to expect and what you will do about it.
Vague about the method. If they cannot describe night one in plain words, you will be guessing when it arrives.
Reviews you cannot check. Only first names, no dates, no way to tell whether the reviewer was a client.
Claims that sound like research but have no source. Ask where a number came from.
Process red flags
No health questions at intake. A good intake asks about growth, feeding, reflux, prematurity and breathing.
The same plan for every baby of the same age. Templates have their place, but then you are buying a course, not a consultant.
Support that disappears after day one. Ask how often they check in, through what channel, and until when.
Pressure. “Only two spots left today” or a discount that expires in an hour. You should be able to read the agreement and sleep on it.
Telling you to stop asking your pediatrician. A consultant works alongside your pediatrician, not instead of them.
Green flags to look for instead
A clear, written description of what is included and for how long.
An intake with real health questions and a willingness to say “check with your pediatrician first.”
A plain description of how crying is handled, matched to your limits.
Willingness to tell you if they do not think they can help.
Reviews from identifiable families, with dates.
For the full list of questions, see how to choose a sleep consultant.
Frequently asked
Is it a red flag if a sleep consultant is not a nurse or doctor?No. Most sleep consultants are not licensed health care providers, and the work is behavioral coaching. It is a red flag if they act like a clinician: diagnosing, suggesting medication, or overriding your pediatrician.
Should a sleep consultant recommend a specific sleep product?Be cautious. Products that incline the baby, weight the baby, or claim to reduce SIDS risk conflict with AAP guidance. A plain crib or bassinet with a fitted sheet is all a plan should need.
What if a consultant says my newborn should sleep through the night?That is a red flag. Newborns need to feed at night. Early work should focus on safe sleep, feeding on cue and a simple routine, with night feeds decided by your pediatrician.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces & Bed Sharing. 2022.

# Do sleep consultants use cry it out?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/do-sleep-consultants-use-cry-it-out/

Do sleep consultants use cry it out?
Some do, many do not, and most use a range of methods. Approaches run from full extinction (cry it out) to graduated checks, staying in the room, and bedtime fading. Research supports several of these, not only cry it out. Ask any consultant to describe night one in plain words, including how much crying to expect and what you will do.
The main approaches
ApproachWhat you doCrying
Extinction (“cry it out”)Bedtime routine, baby down awake, you do not return until morning or a planned feedMost intense, usually shortest
Graduated extinction (timed checks)You check in briefly at planned intervals that lengthenLess intense for many parents; still some crying
Parent in the room (chair or camping out)You stay beside the crib and move further away over daysUsually some protest; lasts longer overall
Bedtime fadingYou temporarily move bedtime later to when your baby is truly sleepy, then bring it earlierOften less; slower
Pick up, put down and other hands-on approachesYou comfort with touch or by lifting until calm, then return baby to the cribVaries with baby; can overstimulate some
More detail on each: cry it out, timed checks, the chair method, bedtime fading, gentle methods compared.
What the research says
An American Academy of Sleep Medicine review of 52 studies found strong support for unmodified extinction and extinction with a parent present, clear support for graduated extinction, and support for positive routines with bedtime fading. The review reported no detrimental effects in the studies it examined. A randomized trial of 43 infants aged 6 to 16 months compared graduated extinction and bedtime fading with a sleep-education control. Both methods improved sleep. Infant cortisol and maternal stress fell more in the intervention groups, and at 12 months there were no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or in parent-child attachment.
So the evidence does not require cry it out. Several approaches with less crying also work. What they have in common is consistency.
Why “no crying at all” is rarely realistic
When you change how your baby falls asleep, your baby notices and protests. That protest is communication, not harm, and it usually fades as the new pattern becomes familiar. A consultant who promises zero tears is either describing a baby who was nearly ready anyway or setting you up to feel you failed. A better promise is a clear plan for how you will respond.
What to ask
“Describe night one for my baby. Where am I, and what do I do when my baby cries?”
“How long would my baby cry before I go in, if at all?”
“Can you adjust the approach if it is too much for us?”
“What is different for a younger baby versus a toddler?”
Matching the method to your family
The best method is the one you will carry out the same way every night. Parents who cannot listen to crying from outside the door often do better staying in the room, even though it takes longer. Parents who find the in-between approaches confusing sometimes prefer a cleaner, faster method. A consultant should ask about this before writing the plan, not after night one.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: The plan is not cry it out and not wait it out. Dr. Sam writes it around your baby and your limits, a coach supports you live on night one, and daily 1:1 check-ins let the plan be adjusted as your baby responds.
Frequently asked
Is cry it out harmful?In the studies reviewed by the AASM, no detrimental effects were reported, and a randomized trial found no differences in emotional or behavioral problems or attachment at 12 months. Many families still prefer other methods, which also work.
Can sleep training work without any crying?Some babies make the change with very little crying, especially with gradual methods. Most protest at least a little because something familiar changed. Plan for some crying and decide in advance how you will respond.
Which sleep training method has the least crying?Approaches with a parent in the room and bedtime fading tend to involve less intense crying but take longer. Less crying per night can mean more nights. Consistency matters more than which method you pick.
Do gentle methods take longer?Usually, yes. Methods where you stay close or change bedtime gradually tend to take more nights than extinction or timed checks. Many families accept that trade for less crying each night.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Gradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.

# When is the right time to hire a baby sleep consultant?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/when-to-hire-a-sleep-consultant/

When is the right time to hire a baby sleep consultant?
There are two good moments. In the newborn weeks, for foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine and realistic expectations, with no crying-based training and no stretching of feeds. And later, when sleep has been a problem for more than two weeks and one consistent attempt has not fixed it. Hiring sooner beats waiting for things to break.
Newborn: foundations, not training
A newborn should not be sleep trained. That does not mean nothing can be done. The newborn weeks are when habits form, and parents can shape them gently:
Safe sleep from night one. Back to sleep, firm flat surface, nothing soft or weighted in the crib or bassinet, room sharing without bed sharing, as the AAP recommends.
Feeding on cue, day and night, with your pediatrician guiding growth.
Day and night cues. Light and activity in the day, dim and quiet at night.
A short, repeatable wind-down that becomes your baby’s signal for sleep.
Some practice in the crib or bassinet when your baby is calm, without any pressure for it to work every time.
Research supports this kind of early guidance. The AASM review found strong support for parent education delivered prenatally or in the first 6 months, in large studies covering over 1,000 parents. See the newborn sleep schedule.
Later: when a problem has settled in
Good signs it is time:
Sleep has been hard for more than two weeks, and it is not explained by illness, travel or a new tooth.
Your baby wakes at about the same times every night and needs the same help each time.
You tried one approach consistently for at least a week and it did not take.
Sleep loss is affecting your health, work, relationship or mood.
A transition is coming: return to work, daycare, a new sibling, a move.
Not yet
Your baby is sick. Recover first; see sleep after illness.
Your pediatrician is looking into weight gain, breathing or reflux. Start once you have the all-clear.
You are about to travel in the next week or two. Start when you have two weeks at home.
You are not sure you want to change anything. If things work for your family, they work.
Is it ever too late?
No. Older babies and toddlers respond well to behavioral plans; they just tend to have more established habits and more opinions. See sleep consultants for toddlers.
Picking the start date
Choose a stretch of about two weeks with no travel, visitors or big schedule changes.
Start on a night when both parents, or a supportive second adult, can be around for the first few nights.
Many families start on a Friday so the hardest nights fall on a weekend.
Do the intake a few days ahead so the plan is ready, not rushed.
Hiring help is not a sign you failed
Parents often wait until they are exhausted because asking for help feels like giving up. It is not. Most families who get stuck have done many things right and are missing one or two details, or need someone to hold the line with them for a week. Getting help earlier usually means fewer hard nights overall.
For age-specific guidance, see the best age to sleep train.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Actually Sleeping works with families from newborn to 3 years. Newborn plans focus on foundations, and no plan forces dropping night feeds; feeding decisions belong to your pediatrician. The written guarantee (“We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.”) applies from 10 weeks: the 14-day clock starts at your baby’s 10-week birthday.
Frequently asked
Can a sleep consultant help with a newborn?Yes, with foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, day and night cues and a simple routine. That is guidance, not sleep training. A consultant should never suggest leaving a newborn to cry or stretching feeds.
Should I wait until the 4 month regression to hire help?You do not have to. Starting foundations earlier can make that period smoother. If sleep has already changed for the worse and stayed that way for more than two weeks, that is a reasonable time to get help.
Is it better to hire a sleep consultant before going back to work?Often, yes. Give yourself about two weeks at home before your start date so new habits settle before mornings get rushed and daycare naps begin. Starting during the first week back adds stress for everyone.
Should I hire a consultant while my baby is teething or sick?Wait until your baby is well. Teething can cause a few unsettled nights; illness is a reason to pause. Start when your baby is healthy and you have two calm weeks ahead.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces & Bed Sharing. 2022.

# Can a sleep consultant help with a toddler, or is it too late?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-for-toddlers/

Can a sleep consultant help with a toddler, or is it too late?
It is not too late. Behavioral sleep methods have been studied in toddlers and young children as well as babies, and they work. Toddler plans look different: more talking, clear limits, a predictable routine, a plan for leaving the bed, and often a visual cue for morning. Expect more negotiation than with a baby, and fast progress once the rules are consistent.
What the research covers
The AASM review of 52 studies covered bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children, not only babies. A randomized trial of a self-directed online program enrolled children 6 to 36 months and found faster sleep onset and fewer, shorter night wakings within three weeks. Toddlers can and do change their sleep.
How toddler sleep problems differ
BabyToddler
Wakes needing a feed, rock or pacifierWakes needing you, a drink, another story, your bed
Protests by cryingProtests by negotiating, stalling, calling out, climbing out
Cannot understand rulesCan understand simple rules and rewards
Schedule is about wake windowsSchedule is often about dropping or shortening the nap
What a good toddler plan includes
A short, fixed routine, often shown as a picture chart, so the order is not up for debate.
Limited choices inside the routine: this pajama or that one, this book or that one.
A plan for curtain calls. One planned extra (a last drink, a last hug), then the same calm response every time.
A plan for leaving the bed or climbing out. See toddler won’t stay in bed.
A morning signal, such as a light that changes color, so “is it morning?” has an answer.
Nap and bedtime timing. Many toddler bedtime battles are a toddler who is not tired yet. See the 2-year-old schedule.
Daytime practice. Talk about the new plan when everyone is calm, not at bedtime.
Common toddler situations a consultant sees
Bed sharing that worked for a while and now does not.
A move from crib to bed that came too early. See when to move to a toddler bed.
Bedtimes that stretch past an hour.
A new sibling, and an older child who suddenly wakes at night.
Separation anxiety at bedtime. See separation anxiety at bedtime.
Night waking that started with an illness and never stopped.
What is harder with a toddler
Habits are older, so the first few nights can be louder. Toddlers test whether the new rule is real. They also have more ways to delay. The trade-off is that toddlers understand explanations, respond to praise and simple rewards, and can see their own progress on a chart. Many families find toddlers change faster than they feared once both parents respond the same way.
Getting everyone on the same plan
Toddlers are quick to notice which adult gives in. Before night one, agree on the exact words and actions for each situation: calling out, getting up, asking for one more thing. Write them down and share them with anyone who does bedtime, including grandparents and sitters.
When to check with your pediatrician first
Loud snoring most nights, pauses in breathing, mouth breathing, very restless sleep, or daytime sleepiness that seems unusual. These can point to a medical cause. See sleep consultant vs pediatric sleep specialist.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Actually Sleeping works with families from newborn to 3 years, so toddlers are in scope. Dr. Sam writes the plan around your child’s age, room and bed setup, with live support on the first night and daily 1:1 check-ins.
Frequently asked
Is 2 too old for sleep training?No. Two-year-olds can learn new sleep habits, and many respond well to clear routines, simple rules and rewards. The approach changes from a baby’s, with more explanation and more planning for stalling and leaving the bed.
Can a sleep consultant help my toddler stay in their bed?Yes. A plan usually covers what you say and do each time your toddler gets up, a morning signal, and timing changes. Consistency from every adult at bedtime is what makes it work.
Should I move my toddler to a big bed to fix sleep?Usually not. A move rarely fixes a sleep problem and can add one, because a toddler in a bed can get up. Sort out sleep in the crib first if your child is still in one.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Mindell JA, et al. Efficacy of an Internet-Based Intervention for Infant and Toddler Sleep Disturbances. Sleep. 2011.

# What should a sleep-training guarantee actually say?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-guarantee-what-it-should-say/

What should a sleep-training guarantee actually say?
A real guarantee is written in the agreement, not only in marketing. It names a measurable result (such as hours of night sleep), a time frame, when that time frame starts, what you must do to qualify, and what you get if the result is not met. If any of those five parts is missing, you have a slogan, not a guarantee.
The five parts of a guarantee worth having
A measurable outcome. Something you can count: hours of continuous night sleep, number of wakings, nights in a row. “Better sleep” and “a happier family” cannot be measured.
A time frame. Within how many days or nights.
A start point. When the clock starts. The first night of the plan? A certain age? This matters most for young babies.
Your side of it. What counts as following the plan, and how that is shown. Daily notes or check-ins are a fair way to show it; vague terms that can always be read against you are not.
The remedy. What happens if the outcome is not met. A full refund, a partial refund, extra sessions, or continued support. Know which one before you pay.
Common wording and what it really means
WordingWhat it really means
“Satisfaction guaranteed”No defined outcome. Ask what happens if you are not satisfied.
“We’ll support you until it works”More support, not money back. Can be valuable, but it is not a refund.
“Results guaranteed” with no detailAsk for the written terms. If there are none, there is no guarantee.
“Most babies sleep through in a week”A claim, not a guarantee. Ask where the figure comes from.
Specific hours, specific days, refund namedA real outcome guarantee. Now read the conditions.
Fair conditions versus unfair ones
Every outcome guarantee has conditions, and that is reasonable. A consultant cannot be responsible for a plan that was not followed. Fair conditions:
Following the written plan consistently.
Reporting each day what happened, so the plan can be adjusted.
A minimum age, because young babies still need to feed at night.
Conditions that make a guarantee hollow:
Terms that can never be checked, such as “perfect compliance” with no way to show it.
Exclusions so broad that any normal event (a cold, a tooth) cancels it.
A remedy you only learn about after you ask for it.
Questions to ask
“Can I read the exact guarantee wording before I sign?”
“What does ‘through the night’ mean, in hours?”
“When does the clock start for my baby?”
“How is following the plan measured?”
“If it is not met, what do I receive?”
Get it before you pay
Read the full wording before you pay, not after. Save a copy. If something is unclear, ask for it to be clarified in writing.
No guarantee is not a deal-breaker
Many consultants do not guarantee outcomes, and many of them are excellent. What matters is that they are clear about it. The real problem is a guarantee that appears in advertising but not in writing.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: The guarantee is written into the Terms of Service, word for word: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund. The 14-day clock starts at the baby’s 10-week birthday, so younger babies can begin with foundations first. Daily 1:1 check-ins are how the team sees whether the plan is being followed and working.
Frequently asked
Do sleep consultants offer money-back guarantees?Some do, many do not. Ask to read the exact wording before you sign. A money-back guarantee should say what result is promised, by when, what you must do, and that a refund is the remedy.
What does ‘sleeping through the night’ mean in a guarantee?It should be a number of hours, stated in writing. Without a number, you and the consultant may mean very different things. Ask before you start, not after a disappointing week.
Is it fair for a guarantee to require following the plan?Yes. No one can promise results from a plan that was not followed. The fair version defines how following the plan is shown, for example through daily check-ins, so it can be checked.
Why would a guarantee have a minimum age?Young babies need to feed at night, so expecting a long night stretch early is not reasonable. A minimum age, or a clock that starts at a set age, keeps the promise realistic.

# Is online sleep coaching as effective as in-person?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/online-vs-in-person-sleep-coaching/

Is online sleep coaching as effective as in-person?
There is no trial comparing remote and in-person sleep coaching head to head that we are aware of. A randomized trial of a fully online, self-directed program did improve sleep in children 6 to 36 months within three weeks. Because you are the one doing the nights either way, the quality of the plan and the support matters more than whether the coach is in the room.
What the evidence shows
A randomized trial of 264 mothers and children aged 6 to 36 months tested an online program that gave personalized recommendations from an algorithm, with no live coach. Compared with a control group, children in the program fell asleep faster and had fewer and shorter night wakings. Mothers’ sleep, mood and confidence improved. Changes appeared within the first week, with more by the second.
That does not prove remote coaching beats in-person coaching. It does show that behavioral sleep help can work without anyone in your home.
Why remote often works
You do the nights anyway. In both formats, your baby needs to learn to fall asleep with you, not with a visitor. A coach in the house still hands the job back to you.
Support in real time. Messaging and video mean you can get an answer at 9 p.m. on night two, which is when most plans wobble.
Your baby behaves normally. A stranger in the room can change how a baby or toddler acts at bedtime.
Daily adjustment. A remote coach reading your notes every day can change the plan as often as an in-person one.
Access. You choose by quality and fit, not by who lives nearby.
Where in-person can help
Parents who want someone physically present on the first night for reassurance.
Room setups that are hard to judge from photos or video.
Families who prefer to talk face to face and do not like messaging.
What to check in any remote service
Response time. How fast do they reply in the evening and overnight on the first nights?
Live first night. Is someone actually available while you do it?
Daily review. Who reads your log, and how often?
Room check. Do they ask for a photo or video of the sleep space to check it against AAP safe sleep guidance: firm, flat, non-inclined, nothing soft or weighted?
A named person. Do you know who writes your plan and who answers your messages?
Making remote coaching work for you
Keep your phone nearby but on silent during the first nights, so you can message without waking the house.
Write short notes as you go: times, what happened, what you did. Your coach can only adjust what they can see.
Send a quick video of the room and of bedtime if your coach asks. It replaces much of what an in-person visit would show.
Ask questions as they come up rather than saving them for a weekly call.
Self-paced online versus coached online
“Online” covers very different things. A self-paced course or app gives you material and leaves the adjusting to you. Coached remote support gives you a person who reads what happened and changes the plan. The trial above shows a well-designed self-directed program can help; families with more complicated situations often want the person. See course vs app vs consultant.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Actually Sleeping is fully remote, based in Coconut Grove, Florida. The plan is written by Dr. Sam, a coach supports you live on night one, and the team checks in with you 1:1 every day. More than 700 families have been coached this way since the practice was founded in 2025.
Frequently asked
Can a sleep consultant help without seeing my baby?Yes, if they gather enough detail. Photos or video of the room, a few days of sleep notes and a thorough intake give a remote consultant what they need. You do the nights in either format.
Is virtual sleep training safe?The format does not change safety. What matters is that the plan follows AAP safe sleep guidance and that the consultant checks your sleep space, defers to your pediatrician on feeding and health, and never suggests medication.
Does an in-person sleep consultant stay overnight?Some offer overnight visits. Even then, you usually do the settling yourself with the coach advising, because your baby needs to learn to sleep with you. Overnight care where someone else does the nights is a different service.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Efficacy of an Internet-Based Intervention for Infant and Toddler Sleep Disturbances. Sleep. 2011.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces & Bed Sharing. 2022.

# What credentials should a baby sleep consultant have?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-credentials/

What credentials should a baby sleep consultant have?
Sleep consulting has no required license. Certifications come from private training programs that set their own standards, so the letters after a name vary in meaning. Ask what training they completed, whether they hold a licensed health care credential, what that credential covers, and how they screen for medical issues. Judge the answers alongside their process, support and written commitments.
What the title does and does not mean
Anyone can call themselves a sleep consultant or sleep coach. There is no single standard credential. A 2018 survey of 142 practicing sleep coaches in 17 countries found education ranging from high school diplomas to doctoral degrees. Only 20% were or had been licensed health care providers, and 38% carried malpractice insurance. Most respondents named a formal sleep coach training program as the most important qualification. The authors suggested their findings could inform discussions about training and credentialing standards.
None of this means consultants are unqualified. It means you have to ask.
Types of background you will see
BackgroundWhat it can addWhat it does not make them
Private sleep consultant certificationStructured training in behavioral methods and schedulesA licensed health care provider
Licensed nurseClinical training, infant care, recognizing when to referA sleep-medicine specialist
Licensed pharmacistMedication and supplement knowledge; see belowA physician or a sleep-medicine specialist
Psychologist in behavioral sleep medicineClinical expertise in behavioral treatment of sleep problemsA physician
Physician in sleep medicineDiagnosis and treatment of sleep disordersUsually not a day-to-day coach
Experience as a parent or caregiver onlyEmpathy and practical tipsTrained in screening or methods
What a pharmacist’s training does and does not add
A Doctor of Pharmacy is a professional doctorate centered on medications: how they work, how they interact, and how they are used safely. For a family, that background is useful in specific ways:
Clear answers on why melatonin, antihistamines and “natural” sleep products are not a fix for a baby’s sleep, and when to take a medication question to the pediatrician.
Understanding how a parent’s own medications or caffeine relate to breastfeeding, and where to look it up.
Context on reflux medicines and other treatments a baby may already be on, without changing them.
What it does not add: a pharmacist is not a physician, does not diagnose sleep disorders, and is not your baby’s doctor. Behavioral sleep coaching is a different skill, built through training and experience with many families. A pharmacist who coaches sleep should say this plainly.
Questions to ask
“What sleep training did you complete, and who ran it?”
“Do you hold a license, and in which field?”
“What questions do you ask to rule out medical causes?”
“When do you refer a family back to the pediatrician?”
“How many families have you worked with?”
Credentials are one input
A strong credential with thin support can do less for your family than a well-trained coach who answers you every day. Weigh credentials together with who writes the plan, how much live support you get, and what the consultant commits to in writing. See how to choose a sleep consultant.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Dr. Sam is Dr. Samantha Abrahamson, PharmD, a Doctor of Pharmacy and Pennsylvania-licensed pharmacist. She is not a physician and does not give medical advice; your pediatrician remains the authority on your baby’s health. She writes every family’s plan personally, and the practice has coached more than 700 families.
Frequently asked
Are sleep consultants certified?Many hold certifications from private training programs, which vary in content, length and standards. There is no single required credential. Ask which program they completed, what it covered, and whether it included screening for medical issues.
Is a sleep consultant a medical professional?Usually not. In one survey of practicing sleep coaches, only 20% were or had been licensed health care providers. Even those who are should not diagnose or treat as part of coaching.
Does it matter if my sleep consultant is a nurse or pharmacist?It can help with screening and with medication questions, and a license brings professional accountability. It does not make them a sleep-medicine specialist, and it does not replace your pediatrician for anything medical.
Who should I see instead of a sleep consultant?Your pediatrician, if you notice snoring, breathing pauses, poor weight gain or unusual daytime sleepiness. They may refer you to a sleep-medicine specialist. Coaching can follow once medical causes are ruled out.
ReferencesIngram DG, Mindell JA, Puzino K, Walters RM. A Survey of Practicing Sleep Coaches. Behavioral Sleep Medicine. 2018.

# How long does it take to see results with a sleep consultant?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-how-long-for-results/

How long does it take to see results with a sleep consultant?
Many families see the first changes within the first week, with more by the second, if the plan is followed consistently. Naps usually take longer than nights. In a randomized trial of an online program for children 6 to 36 months, improvements appeared within the first week. Timelines stretch with illness, inconsistency, travel or an older, well-established habit.
What the research shows
In a randomized trial of 264 families with children aged 6 to 36 months, a self-directed online program reduced the time to fall asleep and the number and length of night wakings. Improvements appeared within the first week, with additional benefit by the second. An AASM review of 52 studies found that improvements from behavioral interventions were maintained for 3 to 6 months.
A typical shape
Before night one: intake, plan, and any changes to the room or schedule.
The first few nights: often the hardest. Protest is normal while your baby learns a new way to fall asleep.
End of the first week: many families see shorter settling and fewer wakings.
Second week: nights usually consolidate. A short bump, sometimes called an extinction burst, is common and does not mean the plan failed.
Naps: usually lag behind nights. Daytime sleep pressure is lower, so naps take longer to become reliable.
What speeds results up
Every adult responding the same way, every time.
A plan fitted to your baby’s actual schedule and sleep drivers.
Daily review of what happened and quick adjustments.
A healthy baby and two calm weeks at home.
What slows them down
Changing methods mid-way. Each switch resets the learning.
Giving in on a hard night after holding steady on easier ones. Your baby learns to protest longer.
Illness, travel, daylight saving time or starting daycare in the middle.
A schedule that leaves your baby overtired or not tired enough at bedtime. See wake windows by age.
Night feeds that are still needed. That is fine; it changes what “through the night” looks like for now.
When to worry the plan is not working
If you have been consistent for 7 to 10 nights and nothing has improved, something in the plan needs to change: timing, the response, or a missed medical issue. A consultant should spot this from your log. See sleep training not working and how long sleep training takes.
Results by age
Newborns: foundations, not results on a clock. The goal is safe sleep, good feeding and a routine your baby starts to recognize.
Older babies: the trials cited here enrolled children 6 to 16 months and 6 to 36 months, and both found that sleep improved.
Toddlers: often a louder first few nights, because habits are older and toddlers test limits, then steady progress once every adult responds the same way.
How to measure progress
Keep a simple log: time down, time asleep, each waking and how long it lasted, and nap lengths. Compare week to week, not night to night. One bad night inside a better week is normal.
Ask before you hire
“What do you expect in week one and week two for a baby like mine?”
“How long are naps supported?”
“What happens if we are not seeing progress by day 10?”
How Actually Sleeping handles this: The written guarantee sets the timeline: “We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan.” If that does not happen, the family receives a full refund. For younger babies, the 14-day clock starts at the 10-week birthday. Naps are coached until solid, with no fixed end date.
Frequently asked
How many nights does sleep training take?It varies by baby, age and method. In one randomized trial, improvements appeared within the first week and grew by the second. Plan for two calm weeks and judge progress after about a week of consistency.
Why are naps taking longer than nights?Sleep pressure is lower during the day, so it is harder for a baby to fall asleep and stay asleep for a nap. Naps commonly lag behind nights and need their own patience.
Is it normal for sleep to get worse before it gets better?A short setback a few nights in is common. It often means your baby is testing whether the new pattern is real. Stay consistent; if it lasts more than a few nights, check in with your coach.
ReferencesMindell JA, et al. Efficacy of an Internet-Based Intervention for Infant and Toddler Sleep Disturbances. Sleep. 2011.Mindell JA, et al. Behavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006.Gradisar M, et al. Behavioral Interventions for Infant Sleep Problems: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2016.

# Sleep consultant vs night nurse vs postpartum doula: what’s the difference?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-consultant-vs-night-nurse-vs-postpartum-doula/

Sleep consultant vs night nurse vs postpartum doula: what’s the difference?
A night nurse cares for your baby overnight so you can sleep. A postpartum doula supports you and your household in the weeks after birth. A sleep consultant writes a plan and coaches you to change how your baby sleeps, while you do the nights. The first two give you rest now; the third aims to make you need less help later.
Side by side
Night nurse or overnight newborn carePostpartum doulaSleep consultant
Main focusYour baby, overnightYou and your householdYour baby’s sleep habits
Who does the nightsThey doVaries; some offer overnight shiftsYou do
Typical timingNewborn weeks and monthsLate pregnancy and the weeks after birthNewborn foundations through toddler years
In personYesUsuallyOften remote
GoalRest for you nowRecovery, confidence, practical helpIndependent sleep that lasts
What it does not doTeach your baby to sleep without help, unless that is agreedSleep training, as a ruleCare for your baby overnight
Night nurse or overnight newborn care
Someone comes to your home in the evening and cares for your baby until morning: bringing the baby to you for breastfeeds or giving bottles, changing, settling and putting the baby back down. Some are licensed nurses; many are experienced newborn care providers without a nursing license. The title is used loosely, so ask what training and licenses they hold.
Best for: the newborn weeks, recovery from a difficult birth, twins or triplets, or a parent who needs protected sleep for health reasons.
Postpartum doula
A postpartum doula supports the parent in the weeks after birth. That can include feeding support and referrals, newborn care teaching, emotional support, light household help, and time for you to rest or shower. Some offer overnight shifts.
Best for: first-time parents who want hands-on teaching, families without nearby relatives, and anyone who wants support focused on their own recovery.
Sleep consultant
A consultant assesses how your baby sleeps, writes a plan, and supports you while you carry it out. With a newborn the work is foundations: safe sleep, feeding on cue, a simple routine. Later it can include teaching your baby to fall asleep independently. See what a sleep consultant does.
Best for: families who want sleep to improve in a way that lasts after the help ends.
Using more than one
These roles fit together. A common sequence is overnight newborn care or a doula in the first weeks, then a sleep consultant once you want the nights to change for good. If you have overnight care while working with a consultant, share the plan so everyone responds to your baby the same way.
Questions to ask any of them
What training and licenses do you hold?
What exactly will you do, and what will I do?
How will you handle feeding, and how do you work with my pediatrician?
Safety applies to all of them
Whoever puts your baby down should follow AAP safe sleep guidance: alone, on the back, on a firm, flat, non-inclined surface, without soft toys, pillows, blankets or bedding, and never weighted swaddles or products. Ask any overnight helper to confirm this before the first night.
How Actually Sleeping handles this: Actually Sleeping is a sleep consultant: remote, working with families from newborn to 3 years, with newborn plans focused on foundations and night feeds left to your pediatrician. If you have a night nurse or doula, the plan can be shared so everyone follows it.
Frequently asked
Is a night nurse a real nurse?Sometimes. Some overnight newborn care providers are licensed nurses; many are not. The title is used loosely. Ask what training and licenses they hold, and what they do if your baby seems unwell.
Can a night nurse sleep train my baby?Some offer it, but it is not the core of the role. If you want sleep training, agree on one written plan with whoever does the nights, so your baby gets the same response from every adult.
Do I need a doula or a sleep consultant?In the first weeks after birth, a doula supports your recovery and confidence. If what you want is for your baby’s sleep to change and stay changed, a sleep consultant is the closer fit. Many families use both at different times.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces & Bed Sharing. 2022.

# Does Benadryl (diphenhydramine) help a baby or toddler sleep, and is it safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/benadryl-diphenhydramine-for-baby-sleep/

Does Benadryl (diphenhydramine) help a baby or toddler sleep, and is it safe?
No. Diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy. In a randomized trial of babies 6 to 15 months old who woke at night, it worked no better than a placebo. It can cause excitement instead of drowsiness in children, and too much can cause seizures or heart problems. Use it only for a reason your child’s pediatrician agrees with.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
Diphenhydramine is an older antihistamine. In adults it causes drowsiness, which is why it appears in many “PM” and nighttime products. Children are not small adults. The same medicine that makes a parent sleepy can make a toddler wired, and the trial evidence in babies shows it does not fix night waking.
What the evidence and the regulators say
The label position. The National Library of Medicine’s drug page states that diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy. It also says not to use it in children 2 to 5 years old unless a doctor directs it, and lists excitement, especially in children, as a side effect.
The trial. The TIRED study randomized babies 6 to 15 months old who woke two or more times a night to diphenhydramine or placebo. Its safety board stopped the trial early because the medicine was no more effective than placebo. Only 1 of 22 babies on the medicine improved, compared with 3 of 22 on placebo.
Overdose risk. The FDA warns that taking more than the recommended amount can lead to serious heart problems, seizures, coma or death. It asks families to store medicines out of children’s reach and sight, and to check labels, because many combination products also contain diphenhydramine.
Travel. CDC travel guidance for clinicians says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1, and that antihistamines and decongestants have not been shown to help ear pain on flights.
Why it so often backfires
When an antihistamine does sedate, it changes how a child falls asleep for one night. It does not change how the child falls asleep the next night, or what happens between sleep cycles. If your child wakes at 1 and 4 a.m. because they fall asleep being fed or rocked at bedtime, a sedating medicine leaves that pattern untouched. Paradoxical excitement adds a wired, overtired child to the same problem.
Hidden diphenhydramine
Read the active ingredients on every allergy, cold, “nighttime” and itch product in the house. Giving two products that both contain diphenhydramine is one of the ways children get too much. Keep all of them locked up and out of sight.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is there a medical reason my child is not sleeping, such as allergies, eczema itch, ear pain or snoring?”
“If my child needs an allergy medicine, which one fits their age, and is it one that affects sleep?”
“Is my child’s sleep within the normal range for their age, or is this something to evaluate?”
What actually helps sleep instead
A consistent bedtime and a short, predictable routine in the same order every night. The AAP calls good sleep habits the best medicine and puts routines first.
A dark, quiet room and the same sleep space for naps and night.
How your child falls asleep. A child who falls asleep on their own at bedtime is far more likely to resettle on their own at 2 a.m. This is the piece medicines never touch.
A safe sleep space for babies: on the back, on a firm, flat surface, with no soft bedding.
If the waking is a pattern and not a medical problem, that is coaching territory. Actually Sleeping builds a written plan for that pattern, with daily support while you carry it out.
Frequently asked
Can I give Benadryl to my baby to sleep on a plane?Not to make them sleep. Its drug label says diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy, and CDC travel guidance says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1. Feeding or sucking during descent helps ear pressure. Ask your pediatrician before any travel medicine.
My toddler got hyper after Benadryl. Is that normal?It is a known reaction. The National Library of Medicine lists excitement, especially in children, as a side effect of diphenhydramine. If your child had an unusual reaction, tell your pediatrician, and call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 if you are worried about the amount given.
Is a children’s nighttime cold medicine the same thing?Many contain diphenhydramine or another antihistamine alongside other ingredients. Read the active ingredients. The FDA does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children under 2, and labels say not to use them under 4.
What should I do if my child swallowed Benadryl by accident?Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away, or 911 if your child is hard to wake, having a seizure or struggling to breathe. The FDA warns that too much diphenhydramine can cause serious heart problems and seizures.
ReferencesMedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine). Diphenhydramine.Merenstein D, et al. The Trial of Infant Response to Diphenhydramine (TIRED study). Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2006;160:707-12. Summary in Am Fam Physician. 2006;74(9):1619-1620.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA warns about serious problems with high doses of the allergy medicine diphenhydramine (Benadryl). 2020.CDC Yellow Book. Traveling Safely with Infants and Children.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Should You Give Kids Medicine for Coughs and Colds?HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Melatonin for Kids: What Parents Should Know.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces and Bed Sharing. 2022.

# Is magnesium safe for toddler sleep, and does it work?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/magnesium-for-toddler-sleep/

Is magnesium safe for toddler sleep, and does it work?
There is very little research on magnesium for sleep, and almost none in toddlers. NIH notes conflicting results even in adults. Magnesium from food is safe, but supplements above the upper limit can cause diarrhea, nausea and cramping, and extremely high amounts can affect the heart. Ask your child’s pediatrician before giving any magnesium supplement, spray or powder.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
Magnesium is an essential mineral, and toddlers need it. That does not make a supplement a sleep aid. The research that exists is small, mostly in adults, and inconsistent. For a healthy toddler eating a varied diet, I would not reach for magnesium to fix bedtime battles or night waking.
What the evidence says
Very little research. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH) states that there is very little research on magnesium for insomnia, and that a 2022 review found conflicting results and called for larger, longer studies.
Food is the main source. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements lists legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains, leafy greens such as spinach, fortified cereals, and milk and yogurt as sources. It states that magnesium naturally present in food and drinks is not harmful.
Supplements have upper limits. NIH sets upper limits for magnesium from supplements and medicines for children, and says not to go above them unless a health care provider recommends it.
Too much causes problems. Excess magnesium from supplements or medicines can cause diarrhea, nausea and abdominal cramping. Extremely high intakes can cause an irregular heartbeat.
Interactions. Magnesium can interfere with some antibiotics if taken too close together in time. If your child takes any regular medicine, ask your pharmacist about spacing.
Sprays, lotions, bath flakes and gummies
The NIH evidence summaries cover magnesium taken by mouth. I found no good studies showing that magnesium sprays, lotions or bath products improve a child’s sleep. Gummies add another problem: they look like candy. Any supplement in the house should be stored up high and out of sight, because NIH notes that supplement labels do not always match what is in the bottle and that many supplements have not been tested in children.
Why magnesium often seems to work
Parents usually start a supplement on a bad week. Sleep regressions, illnesses and schedule changes often settle on their own within days or weeks. A new bedtime ritual, such as a warm bath with a lotion, can also help simply because it is calm and predictable. The routine may be doing the work, not the mineral.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Does my child’s diet give enough magnesium, or is there a reason to test or supplement?”
“Could restless sleep be linked to iron, snoring or something else worth checking?”
“Does a supplement interact with any medicine my child takes?”
What actually helps sleep instead
Same bedtime, same order, every night. Toddlers relax when they know what comes next.
A calm last hour. Dim lights and no screens; the AAP notes that blue light from devices can suppress natural melatonin.
Clear, kind limits on stalling and extra requests, held the same way by every adult.
Falling asleep independently. A toddler who drifts off without a parent present is better able to settle between sleep cycles.
See also toddler won’t stay in bed and the 2 year old sleep regression.
Frequently asked
Can I put magnesium lotion on my toddler at bedtime?Check with your pediatrician first. The NIH evidence summaries on magnesium and sleep concern magnesium taken by mouth, and there is very little research even there. A calm massage can be a pleasant part of a routine with or without the magnesium.
What are the side effects of too much magnesium in children?NIH lists diarrhea, nausea and abdominal cramping from too much supplemental magnesium, and irregular heartbeat with extremely high intakes. If a child swallows a supplement by accident, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
Which foods give a toddler magnesium?NIH lists legumes, nuts and seeds (in toddler-safe forms), whole grains, leafy greens such as spinach, fortified cereals, and milk and yogurt. NIH also notes that magnesium naturally present in food is not harmful, so food is the place to start before any supplement.
Is magnesium better than melatonin for kids?Neither is a first-line sleep fix for a toddler. Both are sold as supplements with looser rules than medicines, and the AAP recommends consistent routines first. Ask your pediatrician before using either.
ReferencesNational Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Sleep Disorders and Complementary Health Approaches: Usefulness and Safety.NIH Office of Dietary Supplements. Magnesium: Fact Sheet for Consumers.National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). 10 Things To Know About Dietary Supplements for Children and Teens.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Melatonin for Kids: What Parents Should Know.

# Does gripe water help a baby sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/gripe-water-and-baby-sleep/

Does gripe water help a baby sleep?
There is no good evidence that it does. Gripe water is usually sold as a dietary supplement, not a tested medicine, so ingredients and quality vary. A study of 335 mothers found babies given gripe water were no less likely to have colic. Fussy evening crying usually peaks around 6 weeks and eases by 3 to 4 months. Ask your pediatrician before using it.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
Gripe water is a traditional remedy for gas, colic and fussiness. Ingredients vary from product to product, so “gripe water” does not describe one thing. What the products share is a lack of evidence that they help a baby sleep or cry less.
What the evidence and the regulators say
Study evidence. A cross-sectional study of 335 mothers of babies 1 to 6 months old found that about 64% had given gripe water. Colic was actually more common in the babies who received it, as was constipation. The authors concluded that gripe water does not prevent excessive crying from colic. A study like this shows an association, not cause and effect, but it gives no support for a benefit.
Regulation. Many gripe water products are labeled as dietary supplements. NIH notes that the federal rules for supplements are less strict than those for medicines, that many supplements have not been tested in children, and that “natural” does not necessarily mean safe.
Quality problems have happened. In 2007 the FDA warned parents about a gripe water product after lab testing found Cryptosporidium, a parasite, and the product was linked to illness in a 6-week-old baby.
Why gripe water seems to work
Colic follows a predictable curve. The AAP describes fussing that typically peaks around 6 weeks and drops off by 3 to 4 months. Anything started at the peak will appear to work as the curve comes down. That is not the same as better sleep.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is this crying normal colic, or could there be a medical cause?” The AAP advises checking with your pediatrician before trying remedies.
“Is my baby feeding and gaining well?”
“If I am breastfeeding, is it worth trying to remove a food from my diet? If formula feeding, should we consider a different formula?”
“Is anything my baby takes, including supplements, safe at this age?”
What actually helps a fussy baby
The AAP’s colic tips are practical and drug-free: walking with your baby in a carrier, rocking, white noise, a pacifier, a tummy-down hold across your knees with a back rub while your baby is awake, and avoiding overfeeding. Take turns with another adult; even an hour or two away helps you stay steady. If your baby falls asleep while held, place them in the crib on their back. If you feel overwhelmed and no one can take over, it is okay to lay your baby on their back in the crib and step out for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.
What helps sleep once the colic phase passes
Day and night cues: bright, social days and dim, quiet nights.
A short bedtime routine in the same order each evening.
Some chances to fall asleep in the crib, drowsy but awake, once your baby is a few months old. This builds the skill that later lets a baby link sleep cycles.
Safe sleep every time: on the back, on a firm, flat surface, with no soft bedding.
Sleep foundations can start from the newborn weeks without restricting feeds. Actually Sleeping works with families from newborn to 3 years, and feeding decisions always stay with the pediatrician.
Frequently asked
Is gripe water safe for newborns?Ask your pediatrician before giving it. Products are commonly sold as dietary supplements with looser rules than medicines, ingredients vary, and in 2007 the FDA warned about a contaminated gripe water product linked to a 6-week-old baby’s illness.
Does gripe water help with gas at night?There is no good evidence that it does. A study of 335 mothers found colic and constipation were more common, not less, in babies given gripe water. Burping, avoiding overfeeding and a tummy-down hold while awake are reasonable first steps.
When does colic stop?The AAP says fussing typically peaks around 6 weeks and drops off by 3 to 4 months, although colicky crying can last until about 6 months. Ask your pediatrician to rule out a medical cause if crying is intense.
Can I give gripe water every night before bed?Not without your pediatrician’s advice. Routine nightly use has no shown benefit for sleep. A predictable routine, a dark room and safe sleep on the back do more for night sleep than any remedy.
ReferencesJain K, Gunasekaran D, Venkatesh C, Soundararajan P. Gripe Water Administration in Infants 1-6 Months of Age: A Cross-sectional Study. J Clin Diagn Res. 2015;9(11):SC06-SC08.National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). 10 Things To Know About Dietary Supplements for Children and Teens.U.S. Food and Drug Administration (archived). Warning about a gripe water product contaminated with Cryptosporidium. September 21, 2007.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Colic Relief Tips for Parents.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces and Bed Sharing. 2022.

# Are natural or homeopathic baby sleep drops and teething tablets safe?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/homeopathic-and-natural-baby-sleep-remedies/

Are natural or homeopathic baby sleep drops and teething tablets safe?
Not reliably. The FDA has approved no homeopathic product and has not reviewed them for safety or effectiveness. FDA testing of homeopathic teething tablets found belladonna levels that sometimes far exceeded the label, a risk the agency called unnecessary for children under 2. Herbal “sleep” products have weak evidence. Check with your child’s pediatrician before using any of them.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
“Natural” and “homeopathic” are marketing and regulatory categories. They do not mean tested, gentle or safe for babies. Some of these products contain plant extracts that are poisonous in larger amounts, and manufacturing control has been a documented problem.
What the FDA says about homeopathic products
No approvals. The FDA states that there are no FDA-approved products labeled as homeopathic, and that homeopathic products have not been reviewed by the FDA for safety and effectiveness.
Risky ingredients. The FDA warns that homeopathic makers use sources that include known poisons or toxins, and that poor manufacturing controls can produce products that exceed their labeled strength. Some are marketed for infants and children.
Teething tablets. FDA lab analysis of homeopathic teething tablets found belladonna alkaloids in amounts that varied from tablet to tablet and, in some, far exceeded the label. The FDA said this poses an unnecessary risk to infants and children under 2. The FDA also lists homeopathic teething tablets among teething products associated with serious risks.
Cough and cold. The FDA advises against giving homeopathic cough and cold medicine to children younger than 4 and says it is not aware of any proven benefits of these products.
Herbal and supplement “sleep drops”
Chamomile: NIH says there is no conclusive evidence from clinical trials on whether it helps sleep. People allergic to ragweed or related plants can react to it.
Valerian: clinical trials have had inconsistent results, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s 2017 guideline recommended against valerian for chronic insomnia in adults.
Labels you cannot fully trust: the AAP notes that some sleep supplements have been found to contain other substances, such as CBD or serotonin. Read every ingredient. See is melatonin safe for babies.
Supplements in general: NIH notes that many have not been tested in children, may contain contaminants, and sometimes do not match their labels.
Safer ways to ease teething
The FDA suggests gently rubbing your baby’s gums with a clean finger or offering a firm rubber teether (not liquid-filled, and not frozen), with supervision. It warns against benzocaine products for teething and against teething jewelry such as amber necklaces, which have been linked to strangulation and choking. For pain medicine, see does teething medicine help a baby sleep, and ask your pediatrician.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is this product safe at my baby’s age, and is there any reason to use it?”
“Could my baby’s waking have a medical cause we should look at?”
“Which pain reliever, if any, is appropriate for my baby’s age and weight?”
What actually helps sleep instead
Predictability: the same bedtime window and the same short routine each night.
Environment: dark room, steady white noise if you use it, and a safe, empty crib.
How your baby falls asleep: babies who practice falling asleep in the crib are better at resettling between sleep cycles. No drop or tablet teaches that skill.
Short-lived events stay short: comfort a teething or unwell baby fully, then return to the usual routine once they are well.
Frequently asked
Are homeopathic teething tablets FDA approved?No. The FDA states that no homeopathic products are FDA-approved and that they have not been reviewed for safety and effectiveness. FDA testing of teething tablets found belladonna levels that sometimes far exceeded the label.
Is chamomile tea okay for a toddler’s sleep?Ask your pediatrician first. NIH says there is no conclusive clinical-trial evidence that chamomile helps sleep, and people allergic to ragweed or related plants can react to it. Never sweeten anything with honey for a baby under 12 months.
Are natural sleep drops safer than medicine?Not necessarily. NIH notes that “natural” does not necessarily mean safe, that many supplements have not been tested in children, and that some contain contaminants or do not match their labels.
What should I use for teething at night instead?The FDA suggests rubbing the gums with a clean finger or a firm rubber teether, not frozen. Ask your pediatrician whether a pain reliever is appropriate for your baby’s age and weight, and use the label directions.

# Can low iron (ferritin) cause restless sleep in a toddler?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/iron-deficiency-and-restless-toddler-sleep/

Can low iron (ferritin) cause restless sleep in a toddler?
It can play a part. Restless legs that disturb sleep are listed by the AAP as a sign of more significant iron-deficiency anemia, and sleep guidelines ask clinicians to check ferritin in children with restless legs. Iron deficiency in infancy has also been linked to altered sleep patterns later. Never start iron on your own; ask your child’s pediatrician about testing.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
Iron matters for the brain, and low iron has real links to sleep. But most toddlers who toss and turn are not iron deficient, and iron supplements are dangerous in an accidental overdose. The right step is a conversation with the pediatrician and, if they think it fits, a blood test. Not a supplement from the store.
What the evidence says
Signs of iron deficiency. The AAP lists pale skin, irritability, fatigue or needing more naps, and cravings for non-food items such as ice or dirt. In more severe anemia it lists restless leg syndrome that interferes with healthy sleep.
Long-term sleep effects. A study of 4-year-olds followed from infancy found that children who had iron-deficiency anemia as babies had differences in how their sleep stages were organized across the night on overnight sleep studies, compared with children who had not.
Restless legs in children. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s 2025 guideline says clinicians should check iron studies, including ferritin, in patients with clinically significant restless legs syndrome, and it suggests iron treatment for children with restless legs when ferritin is below a set level. Which test, which product and how long are clinical decisions.
Restless sleep disorder. Sleep experts have defined a separate “restless sleep disorder” with criteria that include a sleep study, but they note the current evidence applies to ages 6 to 18. In toddlers, restless sleep is a symptom to evaluate, not a diagnosis to assume.
Who is at higher risk
Too much cow’s milk. The AAP advises no cow’s milk before 12 months, and after age one no more than 24 ounces a day, because milk is low in iron and fills children up.
Breastfed babies after 4 months without iron-rich foods yet. The AAP recommends iron supplementation for partially or fully breastfed babies starting at 4 months until iron-containing foods are eaten; ask your pediatrician how this applies to your baby.
Babies born early or small, whom the AAP flags for earlier iron support.
The AAP calls for iron screening around the first birthday, with timing that depends partly on how your baby is fed.
Why not just try an iron supplement
Federal rules require this warning on iron products: “Accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.” Iron given without a test can also mask the real cause of a sleep problem. If your child ever swallows iron pills or chewables, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately.
What to ask the pediatrician
“My toddler is restless, kicks or seems uncomfortable at night. Should we check iron and ferritin?”
“How much milk should my child drink each day?”
“Could snoring, mouth breathing or pauses in breathing be part of this?”
What actually helps sleep instead
Iron-rich foods by day, as your pediatrician suggests, and milk kept within the AAP limit.
A steady schedule with naps that fit your child’s age, so bedtime does not arrive overtired.
The same calm routine every night, and a child who falls asleep on their own.
Watch, then decide: a week of notes on bedtime, wakings and movements makes the pediatrician visit far more useful.
Frequently asked
What are signs of low iron in a toddler?The AAP lists pale skin, irritability, fatigue or needing more naps, and craving non-food items such as ice or dirt. In more severe anemia it lists restless legs that disturb sleep. Your pediatrician can check with a blood test.
Should I give my toddler an iron supplement for restless sleep?Not without testing and your pediatrician’s direction. Federal labeling warns that accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6, and most restless sleep has other causes.
Can drinking too much milk affect my toddler’s sleep?Indirectly. The AAP advises no more than 24 ounces of milk a day after age one, because milk is low in iron and can crowd out iron-rich foods. Low iron is linked to restless legs that disturb sleep.
Does iron deficiency as a baby affect sleep later?One long-term study found 4-year-olds who had iron-deficiency anemia in infancy had differences in how their sleep stages were organized. This is one reason the AAP recommends iron screening around the first birthday.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Iron Deficiency and Anemia in Babies, Children and Teens.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Where We Stand: Vitamin D and Iron Supplements for Babies.Peirano PD, Algarín CR, Garrido MI, Lozoff B. Iron Deficiency Anemia in Infancy Is Associated with Altered Temporal Organization of Sleep States in Childhood. Pediatr Res. 2007;62(6):715-719.American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
