# Is it safe to give a baby or toddler melatonin for a flight or jet lag?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/melatonin-for-flights-and-jet-lag-toddler/

Is it safe to give a baby or toddler melatonin for a flight or jet lag?
Not without your pediatrician’s direction. The AAP says melatonin should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician. It is sold as a supplement, product strength varies widely, and child poisonings rose sharply over the past decade. Light, meals and naps on local time shift a young child’s body clock without a supplement.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
A one-off dose for travel can sound harmless. The problems are the same as with nightly use: you cannot be sure how much is in the product, there is little research in babies and toddlers, and travel bags are where curious toddlers find gummies. For a young child, I would plan the trip around light and schedule instead.
What the evidence and the regulators say
Pediatrician first. The AAP says melatonin should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises parents to talk with a health care professional before giving melatonin or any supplement to children.
Unregulated strength. Melatonin is sold as a dietary supplement. The AASM cites a study in which melatonin content ranged from less than half to more than four times the amount on the label, with chewables varying most. CDC travel guidance also notes melatonin is not regulated by the FDA.
Poisonings. A CDC report found pediatric melatonin ingestions rose about 530% from 2012 to 2021. Children 5 and younger made up most reports, and two children under 2 died.
Jet lag research is in adults. NIH notes melatonin may help jet lag, but that evidence comes from adults, and long-term safety is not established.
No help for ears. CDC guidance says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1 and have not been shown to help ear pain on flights; swallowing does. Let babies nurse or suck a bottle or pacifier on descent.
How the body clock actually shifts
CDC travel guidance gives an average adaptation of about 1.5 hours a day after flying west and 1 hour a day after flying east. Bright morning light helps the clock move earlier; evening light pushes it later. CDC also notes jet lag disturbs children’s sleep just as it does adults’. So the tools are the same for a toddler: light, meals and sleep timing.
A travel plan that does not need a supplement
On the plane: any safe sleep counts. Feeding, holding and the motion all help.
On arrival: get outside in daylight in the local morning, and eat on local time.
Naps: keep them, but cap long ones so the night stays long.
Evenings: dim the room an hour before local bedtime and run your usual routine.
Night wakings: keep them dark, quiet and boring.
Short trips: for a small time difference or a few days, staying near home time can be easier.
More detail is in keeping your baby sleeping while traveling.
Packing safety
If an adult in the family takes melatonin, pack it in a locked or zipped compartment and never leave it on a hotel nightstand. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 if a child swallows any.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is there any reason my child should not fly right now, such as an ear infection?”
“Is melatonin appropriate for my child at all? If so, which product and timing?”
“Which medicines should I pack for illness on the trip?”
What actually helps sleep instead
A child who falls asleep on their own at home brings that skill on vacation. The same routine, sleep sack and white noise travel well. When you get home, go straight back to the usual schedule.
Frequently asked
Can I give my 1 year old melatonin for a long flight?Only if your pediatrician recommends it. The AAP says melatonin should only be used after a discussion with your pediatrician, and product strength varies widely. Feeding, holding and daylight on arrival are the usual tools.
How long does jet lag last in a toddler?CDC travel guidance gives an average adjustment of about 1 to 1.5 hours a day, faster going west than east. Morning daylight and local mealtimes help the clock shift. The CDC notes jet lag disturbs children’s sleep just as it does adults’.
Does melatonin help with jet lag?NIH notes it may help jet lag, but that evidence comes from adults. In young children the AAP and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine advise talking with a health care professional before giving it.
What should I do if my toddler eats melatonin gummies?Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Call 911 if your child collapses, has a seizure, has trouble breathing or cannot be woken. CDC reported a 530% rise in child melatonin ingestions from 2012 to 2021.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Melatonin for Kids: What Parents Should Know.American Academy of Sleep Medicine. Health Advisory: Melatonin Use in Children and Adolescents.Lelak K, et al. Pediatric Melatonin Ingestions, United States, 2012-2021. MMWR. 2022;71(22).National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Sleep Disorders and Complementary Health Approaches: Usefulness and Safety.CDC Yellow Book. Jet Lag Disorder.CDC Yellow Book. Traveling Safely with Infants and Children.

# Can I give cough and cold medicine at bedtime to a baby or toddler?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/cough-and-cold-medicine-at-bedtime-toddler/

Can I give cough and cold medicine at bedtime to a baby or toddler?
For young children, generally no. The FDA does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children under 2, product labels say not to use them under 4, and the AAP says to use them at 4 to 6 only if your child’s doctor recommends it. Saline, suction, a cool-mist humidifier and, after age 1, honey are the usual night-time helpers.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
A coughing, stuffy child at 10 p.m. is hard on everyone, and the medicine aisle looks like the answer. For babies and young toddlers it is not. These products do not shorten a cold, and combination products make it easy to double up on an ingredient.
What the regulators say
FDA: does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for children younger than 2. Manufacturers label them “do not use in children under 4 years of age.” The FDA also advises not to give homeopathic cough and cold medicine to children younger than 4.
FDA: cough or cold medicine “will not change the natural course of a cold or make it go away faster.”
AAP: over-the-counter cough and cold medicine is not recommended under 4; from 4 to 6, use only if your child’s doctor recommends it.
AAP: many children with a cough or stuffy nose are happy, play normally and sleep well. Treat symptoms when they cause discomfort or trouble sleeping.
Night-time comfort that is recommended
Saline: plain saline drops or spray to loosen mucus, followed by gentle suction for babies. Squeeze the bulb before placing it in the nostril. Suctioning before feeds and sleep helps.
Cool-mist humidifier near the sleep space but out of reach, cleaned as directed. The FDA advises against warm-mist humidifiers.
Fluids through the day, which thin mucus.
Honey for children 1 year and older. The AAP says research shows honey is better than store-bought cough syrups at reducing how often and how badly children cough at night. Never give honey to a baby under 12 months; CDC warns it can cause botulism.
Mentholated chest rub only for children 2 and older, per the AAP, and stored out of reach.
Safe sleep stays the same when your baby is sick
The AAP says babies should always sleep flat on their backs on a firm surface, and that propping a baby on towels or pillows or inclining the mattress is not safe, even with congestion. Swings, car seats and carriers are not safe for sleep.
When to call
The FDA lists a fever of 100.4°F or higher in a baby 2 months or younger, or 102°F or higher at any age, as reasons to call.
The AAP says call 911 for a baby struggling for each breath or with bluish lips, and call the doctor for breathing much faster than normal or coughing that stops your baby from sleeping, eating or playing.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is this a cold, or could it be an ear infection, croup or asthma?”
“Which fever or pain reliever, if any, is right for my child’s age and weight?”
“Is honey okay for my child, and how much?”
What helps sleep during and after a cold
Comfort freely while your child is sick, inside your normal bedtime routine. Once your child is well, go back to the usual way of falling asleep. Night feeds and extra cuddles that crept in during illness tend to stay unless you return to the routine. See getting sleep back on track after illness.
Frequently asked
What can I give my 1 year old for a cough at night?The AAP suggests honey for children 1 and older, saline and suction for congestion, a cool-mist humidifier and fluids. Over-the-counter cough and cold medicines are not recommended for this age. Ask your pediatrician how much honey to use.
Can I use vapor rub on my baby?The AAP lists mentholated rubs for children 2 years and older only. For younger babies, use saline drops, gentle suction and a cool-mist humidifier, and ask your pediatrician about anything else.
Should I raise the crib mattress for a stuffy baby?No. The AAP says propping a baby on towels or pillows or inclining the mattress is not safe, even with congestion. Keep your baby flat on the back on a firm surface and use saline and suction before sleep.
Do cough medicines help children sleep?The FDA says they do not change the course of a cold and does not recommend them under 2; labels say not to use them under 4. The AAP notes honey works better than store-bought syrups for night coughing in children over 1.
ReferencesU.S. Food and Drug Administration. Should You Give Kids Medicine for Coughs and Colds?HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Coughs and Colds: Medicines or Home Remedies?CDC. Infant and Toddler Nutrition: Foods and Drinks to Avoid or Limit.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). My baby has a stuffy nose. How can I help them sleep safely?

# Do vitamin D drops or probiotics affect a baby’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/vitamin-d-probiotics-and-baby-sleep/

Do vitamin D drops or probiotics affect a baby’s sleep?
Not in any proven way. The AAP recommends vitamin D for most babies for bone health, not sleep, and a randomized trial found a higher vitamin D dose gave no sleep benefit over the standard dose. Probiotic trials for colic have mixed results, and the FDA has approved no probiotic as a drug for infants. Ask your pediatrician before changing either.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
Vitamin D drops are a routine part of infant care for many babies, and you should keep giving them as your pediatrician advised. They are not a sleep treatment, and giving more will not improve sleep. Probiotics are a different story: optional, variable products with mixed evidence for colic and no proven effect on sleep.
Vitamin D: what the evidence says
Why babies get it. The AAP recommends that all infants receive a vitamin D supplement, except babies drinking enough vitamin D-fortified formula. Breastfed babies specifically need it. Your pediatrician will tell you which product and how much.
Sleep. In the VIDI randomized trial, infants given a higher daily vitamin D dose had no sleep benefit up to age 2 compared with the standard dose. The researchers saw an association between higher vitamin D blood levels and better sleep, but an association does not show that vitamin D causes better sleep.
More is not better. The AAP notes that fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the body and at very high levels could make a child sick. Use the measuring device that comes with the product and never double up.
Probiotics: what the evidence says
Colic trials are mixed. Trials of one probiotic strain found benefits in breastfed babies with colic, while a later trial that included formula-fed babies found no benefit. Less crying, where it happened, is not the same as longer sleep.
Regulation. The FDA states it has not approved any probiotic product for use as a drug or biological product in infants of any age. Probiotics are commonly sold as foods or dietary supplements.
Preterm babies. In 2023 the FDA warned that probiotic products given to hospitalized preterm infants had contributed to serious infections, including one infant death. If your baby was born early, do not start a probiotic without your pediatrician.
Why parents notice a change
Babies change fast. A new supplement often starts in the same weeks as a growth spurt, a shift in naps or the natural easing of colic around 3 to 4 months. It is easy to credit the drops with a change the calendar made.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Does my baby need vitamin D drops, given how they are fed?”
“Is a probiotic reasonable for my baby’s crying, and which one, if any?”
“My baby was born early. Is any supplement unsafe for them?”
What actually helps sleep instead
Light by day, dark by night. Morning light and a dark room at night support the body clock as it develops in the first months.
A short routine in the same order before bed.
Practice falling asleep in the crib, on the back, in an empty, flat sleep space.
A schedule that fits your baby’s age, so bedtime does not come overtired.
For age-by-age timing, see wake windows by age.
Frequently asked
Does vitamin D make babies sleep better?There is no proof that it does. A randomized trial found a higher vitamin D dose gave no sleep benefit over the standard dose up to age 2. Give vitamin D for bone health as your pediatrician advises.
Can vitamin D drops keep my baby awake?There is no good evidence of that at recommended amounts. Give the drops at whatever time of day is easiest to remember. Use only the product and amount your pediatrician recommends, and never double up.
Do probiotics help a colicky baby sleep?Evidence is mixed. Trials of one strain found less crying in some breastfed babies, but not in a trial that included formula-fed babies, and none showed a clear sleep benefit. The FDA has approved no probiotic as a drug for infants.
Are probiotics safe for premature babies?Talk to your pediatrician first. In 2023 the FDA warned that probiotic products given to hospitalized preterm infants contributed to serious infections, including a death. The FDA also states it has not approved any probiotic as a drug for infants of any age.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Where We Stand: Vitamin D and Iron Supplements for Babies.Tampere University DOMLab. New results on early-life vitamin D and sleep (VIDI randomized trial; Sleep Med. 2026, doi:10.1016/j.sleep.2026.108913).HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Dietary Supplements for Toddlers.Sung V, Cabana MD, D'Amico F, et al. Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 for managing infant colic: protocol for an individual participant data meta-analysis. BMJ Open. 2014;4:e006475.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA Raises Concerns About Probiotic Products Sold for Use in Hospitalized Preterm Infants. October 26, 2023.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). # Do allergy medicines affect a toddler’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/allergy-medicine-and-toddler-sleep/

Do allergy medicines affect a toddler’s sleep?
They can, in both directions. Older antihistamines can cause drowsiness or, in some children, excitement, and should never be used just to make a child sleep. Newer ones can cause mild sleepiness. Decongestants can make it harder to fall asleep. Treated nasal allergies, on the other hand, can improve sleep. Choose with your child’s pediatrician.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
Untreated nasal allergies disturb sleep, and the right treatment can help. The wrong product, or the right one used for the wrong reason, can make nights worse. The goal is to treat the allergy, not to sedate the child.
How each type of medicine relates to sleep
Older (first-generation) antihistamines, such as diphenhydramine, can cause drowsiness, the AAP notes. They can also cause excitement in children, and the drug label says diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy. CDC guidance says antihistamines are contraindicated under age 1. More in Benadryl and baby sleep.
Newer antihistamines are described by the AAP as non-sedating, though they may cause mild sleepiness, especially after the first dose. Ask your child’s doctor whether one suits your child.
Cetirizine and levocetirizine. In 2025 the FDA added a warning about rare but severe itching after stopping long-term use, usually after months or years of daily use. If your child takes one daily, ask the pediatrician how long to continue and how to stop.
Oral decongestants can make children act hyper, feel anxious or have a racing heart, the AAP warns, and some can make it harder to fall asleep. Ask before using them.
Steroid nasal sprays are called the most effective treatment for nasal allergy by the AAP, which says they can help a child breathe more easily and may improve sleep.
Montelukast carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events. Listed effects include bad or vivid dreams, sleepwalking and trouble sleeping. The FDA says it should be reserved for allergies that other medicines have not controlled, and to stop it and contact a health care professional right away if mood or behavior changes.
How allergies themselves affect sleep
The AAP notes that a blocked nose makes it hard to sleep, and that poor sleep leads to daytime drowsiness and low energy. Saline rinses and sprays are a drug-free daily option the AAP mentions. Tracking whether night symptoms follow a season, a pet or dust exposure gives your pediatrician useful information.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Are these allergies, a run of colds or something else, such as enlarged adenoids?”
“Which treatment fits my child’s age, and is it sedating or stimulating?”
“How long should my child take a daily antihistamine, and how do we stop?”
“My child snores or breathes through the mouth at night. Should that be checked?”
The AAP advises using over-the-counter allergy products only with your child’s doctor’s advice. Bring a list of everything your child takes, including supplements.
What actually helps sleep instead
Treat the nose, not the bedtime: the right allergy plan removes a reason to wake.
Keep the bedroom simple: wash bedding regularly and keep pets out if they are a trigger.
Same routine and same bedtime every night, with dim light in the last hour.
Independent sleep: once your child breathes comfortably, the way they fall asleep decides how well they resettle overnight.
Frequently asked
Can I give my toddler an allergy medicine to help them sleep?No. Treat allergies when your pediatrician says they need treatment, not to cause sleep. The drug label says diphenhydramine should not be used to make a child sleepy, and some children become excited instead.
Does cetirizine make toddlers sleepy?Newer antihistamines are generally non-sedating but can cause mild sleepiness, especially after the first dose, the AAP says. In 2025 the FDA also warned of rare severe itching after stopping long-term use.
Can montelukast cause nightmares in children?The FDA boxed warning lists bad or vivid dreams, sleepwalking and trouble sleeping among possible effects. Stop the medicine and contact your child’s health care professional right away if mood or behavior changes.
Do nasal allergies cause poor sleep?Yes. The AAP lists difficulty sleeping because it is hard to breathe through the nose, and drowsiness and low energy from poor sleep. It notes steroid nasal sprays may improve sleep. Ask your pediatrician which treatment fits.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Allergy Medicine for Children.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Allergic Rhinitis: All About Nasal Allergies in Children.MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine). Diphenhydramine.CDC Yellow Book. Traveling Safely with Infants and Children.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA requires warning about rare but severe itching after stopping long-term use of oral allergy medicines cetirizine or levocetirizine. May 16, 2025.U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA requires Boxed Warning about serious mental health side effects for asthma and allergy drug montelukast (Singulair). March 4, 2020.

# Are essential oils, lavender products or sleep sprays safe for babies?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/essential-oils-lavender-and-baby-sleep/

Are essential oils, lavender products or sleep sprays safe for babies?
Use caution. There is no good evidence they improve a baby’s sleep, and NIH says aromatherapy research needs larger, better studies. Undiluted oils can irritate skin, several oils are poisonous if swallowed, and repeated skin use of lavender and tea tree oils has been linked to breast growth in young boys. Keep oils out of the crib and out of reach, and ask your pediatrician first.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
A calming scent can be a pleasant part of an adult’s evening. For a baby, the potential harms are concrete and the sleep benefit is unproven.
What the evidence and the regulators say
Weak evidence for sleep. NIH reports that a 2021 review suggested aromatherapy may improve sleep quality, but the researchers said larger and more rigorous studies are needed. These studies were not in babies.
Skin. The AAP notes that some people develop skin irritation when pure, undiluted oils are applied directly to the skin.
Hormone-like effects. A report in the New England Journal of Medicine described three young boys who developed breast growth after repeated use of products containing lavender or tea tree oil. It resolved after the products were stopped, and lab tests showed the oils had weak estrogen-like and anti-androgen effects. The authors concluded the oils probably caused it; NIH notes it is unclear whether the oil was responsible. Either way, it is a reason for caution with daily use on young children.
Poisoning. The CPSC requires child-resistant packaging for wintergreen oil because it contains methyl salicylate, and warns of serious injury or death if young children swallow it. It also requires child-resistant packaging for thin, oily products such as some baby, bath and massage oils, because children under 5 who swallow and inhale them can develop chemical pneumonia.
Chest rubs. The AAP lists mentholated chest rubs for children 2 years and older only.
Diffusers and pillow sprays
I found no good evidence that diffusing oils or spraying bedding improves a baby’s sleep. Sprays put product on the sleep surface, and diffusers put a hot or wet device with a bottle of concentrated oil within reach as babies start to move. Keep the AAP’s safe sleep rule simple: the crib holds only the baby, on the back, on a firm, flat surface, with no soft bedding or other objects.
If you use oils at home
Store every bottle locked and out of sight. Child-resistant is not child-proof.
Never apply undiluted oil to a baby’s skin, and do not put oils near the face or hands.
Read “sleep” and “calming” product labels for melatonin or other active ingredients.
Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away if a child swallows any oil.
What to ask the pediatrician
“Is any scented product safe on my baby’s skin, given eczema or sensitive skin?”
“My child has asthma or wheezes. Should we avoid scents and diffusers at home?”
“What is safe for congestion at my baby’s age?”
What actually helps sleep instead
Cues your baby can learn: the same bath, feed, song and sleep sack in the same order. Predictability is what calms.
A dark, cool, quiet room, with steady white noise if it helps.
Falling asleep in the crib so that waking between sleep cycles does not require a parent.
If you want a calm scent in the routine, a freshly washed sleep sack does the job. Families who want help building the routine itself can work with Actually Sleeping, where the plan is written by Dr. Sam.
Frequently asked
Is it safe to diffuse lavender in my baby’s room?There is no good evidence it improves a baby’s sleep, and diffusers bring concentrated oil within reach. If you use one, keep it and the oil out of reach and outside the crib area, and ask your pediatrician, especially if your child has asthma or wheezes.
Can lavender baby wash cause problems?A NEJM report linked repeated use of lavender and tea tree products to breast growth in three young boys, which resolved after stopping. NIH notes the cause is not certain. Unscented products avoid the question.
Which essential oils are most dangerous for children?The CPSC requires child-resistant packaging for wintergreen oil, which contains methyl salicylate, and warns of serious injury or death if young children swallow it. Treat every oil as a poison and call 1-800-222-1222 if swallowed.
Are baby sleep sprays safe?Their benefit is unproven, and sprays put product on the sleep surface. Read labels for melatonin or other active ingredients, keep the crib empty and flat, and ask your pediatrician before using them.
ReferencesNational Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NIH). Sleep Disorders and Complementary Health Approaches: Usefulness and Safety.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Aromatherapy for Children.Henley DV, Lipson N, Korach KS, Bloch CA. Prepubertal Gynecomastia Linked to Lavender and Tea Tree Oils. N Engl J Med. 2007;356:479-85.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. Warning on a wintergreen essential oil sold without child-resistant packaging. 2026.U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission. CPSC Requires Child-Resistant Packaging for Common Household Products Containing Hydrocarbons, Including Some Baby Oils.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Coughs and Colds: Medicines or Home Remedies?HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Safe Sleep: Back is Best, Avoid Soft Bedding, Inclined Surfaces and Bed Sharing. 2022.

# Can asthma or ADHD medicines affect a young child’s sleep?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/asthma-and-adhd-medicines-and-toddler-sleep/

Can asthma or ADHD medicines affect a young child’s sleep?
Yes, some can. Montelukast carries an FDA boxed warning that includes vivid dreams, sleepwalking and trouble sleeping. Oral steroids can change behavior and appetite. Stimulants for ADHD commonly cause trouble falling or staying asleep, though AAP ADHD guidance starts at age 4 with parent training first. Never stop a prescribed medicine on your own; talk to your child’s pediatrician.
A note on scope from Dr. Sam, Doctor of Pharmacy: as a pharmacist, I can explain how a medicine, supplement or remedy relates to sleep. This page is general information for parents. Check with your child’s pediatrician before giving your child any medicine, supplement or remedy, and follow the product label.
The short answer from a pharmacist
For young children, asthma comes up far more often than ADHD. Both conditions and their medicines can change sleep. The fix is almost never to stop the medicine at home. It is to tell the prescriber exactly what you are seeing, so they can adjust the plan.
Asthma: the condition affects sleep too
The AAP uses nighttime flare-ups as one way to grade asthma: rare night symptoms fit milder asthma, while flare-ups more than once a week fit moderate asthma, and severe asthma can disrupt sleep often. The AAP stresses that overall control matters most. A child who coughs or wheezes at night may need a better controller plan, not a sleep fix.
Asthma medicines and sleep
Montelukast. The FDA requires a boxed warning about serious neuropsychiatric events. Listed effects include bad or vivid dreams, sleepwalking, trouble sleeping, agitation and anxiety. It is approved for asthma from age 1. The FDA says to stop it and contact a health care professional right away if mood or behavior changes.
Oral steroids for flare-ups. The AAP lists behavior change and increased appetite among short-term side effects, which go away after the course ends.
Inhaled steroids. The AAP says side effects are few, such as a mouth yeast infection or hoarseness. A spacer and rinsing the mouth lower the risk.
Albuterol. The National Library of Medicine lists shaking and nervousness among common side effects. If your child seems wound up after a bedtime treatment, mention it, but do not skip a rescue medicine your child needs to breathe.
ADHD medicines in young children
Age. The AAP’s ADHD guideline covers children aged 4 to 18. Toddlers are outside it.
First-line care for preschoolers is parent training in behavior management, not medicine, per the AAP.
Stimulants and sleep. The National Library of Medicine lists difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep among common side effects of methylphenidate, and advises asking your doctor or pharmacist how late in the day a missed dose can be taken.
If behavior is a concern in a young child, ask your pediatrician to look at sleep as part of the picture.
What to ask the pediatrician
“My child’s sleep changed after starting this medicine. Is that a known effect, and what are our options?”
“Is my child’s asthma well controlled if they wake with coughing?”
“Could snoring or breathing pauses be part of the problem?”
“Is there a better time of day to give this medicine?” Your pharmacist can help with timing questions too.
What actually helps sleep instead
Control the condition first: follow the asthma action plan and keep triggers out of the bedroom.
A fixed bedtime and wake time, even on weekends.
A predictable, screen-free wind-down in the same order each night.
Calm, consistent responses to night wakings, so sleep is not rewarded with play.
Children with medical conditions still learn to fall asleep independently. Actually Sleeping plans around the pediatrician’s treatment, never instead of it.
Frequently asked
Can montelukast cause sleep problems in toddlers?It can. The FDA boxed warning lists bad or vivid dreams, sleepwalking and trouble sleeping among possible effects. Stop it and contact your child’s health care professional right away if mood or behavior changes.
Do steroids for asthma keep children awake?The AAP lists behavior change and increased appetite among short-term side effects of oral steroids, and says they go away when the course ends. Tell your pediatrician if sleep is badly affected, but finish the course unless told otherwise.
Can my 3 year old be given ADHD medicine?The AAP ADHD guideline covers ages 4 to 18, and for preschoolers it recommends parent training in behavior management as first-line treatment. Any medicine question for a young child belongs with your pediatrician.
Does night coughing mean my child’s asthma is not controlled?It can. The AAP uses nighttime flare-ups as one measure of asthma severity and stresses overall control. Tell your pediatrician how often your child coughs or wakes at night, and bring your child’s asthma action plan to the visit.
ReferencesHealthyChildren.org (AAP). Mild, Moderate, Severe Asthma: What Do Grades Mean?U.S. Food and Drug Administration. FDA requires Boxed Warning about serious mental health side effects for asthma and allergy drug montelukast (Singulair). March 4, 2020.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). What are Corticosteroids?MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine). Albuterol Oral Inhalation.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). AAP Updates Guidelines on Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder.MedlinePlus (National Library of Medicine). Methylphenidate.

# Newborn sleep in the first 4 weeks: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/newborn-sleep-0-to-4-weeks/

Newborn sleep in the first 4 weeks: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the pediatrician
In the first 4 weeks, sleep comes in short pieces spread across day and night. HealthyChildren says newborns sleep about 16 to 17 hours a day, often only 1 or 2 hours at a time, and healthy babies vary widely. There is no official sleep target at this age. Feed on cue, keep every sleep safe, and call the pediatrician for fever, poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.
What is normal in the first month
A newborn has no working body clock yet. The AAP notes that babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months, so sleep lands evenly across 24 hours and night is not yet different from day.
Newborn sleep is about half active (REM) sleep, according to the AAP. Grunting, twitching, eye movements and short cries during sleep are common and do not always mean your baby is awake. The AAP also describes periodic breathing: pauses of 5 to 10 seconds followed by a burst of faster breathing. It is generally considered normal and is outgrown by about the middle of the first year.
MeasureWhat the sources say
Official hours targetNone. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) makes no recommendation under 4 months because normal sleep varies so widely and evidence on health outcomes is insufficient.
Total sleepAbout 16 to 17 hours a day (HealthyChildren). A review of observational studies found an average of 14.6 hours at 0 to 2 months, with a normal spread of about 9 to 20 hours.
Length of a stretchOften only 1 or 2 hours at a time (HealthyChildren).
PatternNone yet. Day sleep and night sleep look the same.
What parents find hardest
Day–night mix-up. The AAP suggests keeping daytime normal and bright, with ordinary household noise, and keeping nights dark and quiet, with contact limited to feeding, burping, changing and gentle soothing.
Sleeping only on you. Very common now. Contact naps are fine while you are awake and alert. When you get drowsy, move your baby to their own flat, empty sleep space.
Evening fussiness. The AAP says about one in five babies develop colic, usually between the second and fourth weeks, and the fussy period tends to fall between 6 p.m. and midnight.
Your own exhaustion. This is where the riskiest sleep happens. The AAP warns that sleeping with a baby on a couch or armchair raises the risk of a sleep-related death up to 67 times. If you think you might doze while feeding, do not sit on the sofa.
Safe sleep from the first night
On the back for every sleep, naps included. The AAP says the side position is just as dangerous as the stomach.
A firm, flat surface with a fitted sheet and nothing else. Crib bumpers and inclined sleepers (more than 10 degrees) have been banned products under federal law since November 12, 2022.
Share a room, not a bed. The AAP says sharing a sleep surface raises risk 5 to 10 times when a baby is under 4 months.
If your baby falls asleep in a car seat, swing or carrier, move them to a flat sleep surface on their back as soon as you can.
If you swaddle, always place your baby on the back, keep the hips loose, avoid overheating, and never use weighted swaddles. No hat indoors once you are home.
Night feeds
Newborns eat around the clock. How often to feed, whether to wake a sleepy baby to eat, and when a longer stretch is fine are decisions for your pediatrician, based on your baby’s weight gain. Nothing on this page is a reason to cut a feed.
When to call the pediatrician
A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby 3 months or younger. The AAP says to call immediately, even without other symptoms.
Your baby is hard to wake for feeds, feeds poorly, or seems floppy or unusually sleepy.
Breathing that stops for more than 20 seconds: the AAP says call 911.
Crying that seems like pain or illness, or you feel low and unable to cope. The AAP asks parents to tell their doctor about both.
What you can start now
Foundations can start in the first weeks: light days, dark nights, a short wind-down you repeat before the longest sleep, and safe sleep every time. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage. Night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at your baby’s 10-week birthday: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. You can hear from other parents on our reviews page. For more on this stage, see the newborn sleep rhythm and how infant sleep cycles develop.
Frequently asked
How many hours should a newborn sleep?There is no official target. The AASM makes no recommendation under 4 months because normal sleep varies so widely. HealthyChildren says newborns sleep about 16 to 17 hours a day, and a review of studies found healthy babies at 0 to 2 months anywhere from about 9 to 20 hours.
Is it normal for my newborn to grunt and twitch while asleep?Yes. About half of newborn sleep is active sleep, when grunts, twitches and brief cries are common. Short breathing pauses of 5 to 10 seconds followed by faster breathing are also described as normal by the AAP. Pauses longer than 20 seconds need a 911 call.
Can my newborn sleep in the swing or car seat?Not for routine sleep. The AAP says sitting devices such as car seats, swings and strollers are not recommended for routine sleep, especially under 4 months. If your baby dozes off in one, move them to a firm, flat surface on their back as soon as possible.
ReferencesParuthi S, et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med. 2016;12(6):785–786.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Getting Your Baby to Sleep.Galland BC, Taylor BJ, Elder DE, Herbison P. Normal sleep patterns in infants and children: a systematic review of observational studies. Sleep Med Rev. 2012;16(3):213–222.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). # Sleep at 1 month: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-1-month/

Sleep at 1 month: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 1 month, sleep is still scattered and short, and evening crying often builds. The AAP says fussing usually peaks at about 3 hours a day by 6 weeks, then eases. There is no official sleep target before 4 months. This is also the start of the highest-risk window for SIDS, so safe sleep for every sleep matters most now.
What is changing in weeks 4 to 8
Your baby is waking up to the world. By 2 months, the CDC lists milestones such as calming down when spoken to or picked up, looking at your face, and smiling when you talk or smile. Those first social smiles make evenings more fun and also more stimulating, which is part of why the late-day stretch gets harder.
The body clock is still forming. Night and day begin to separate a little, but long, predictable night sleep is not expected yet. Tummy time also matters this month: the AAP suggests building up to 15 to 30 minutes a day, in short sessions, by 7 weeks. Awake, supervised tummy time is the counterweight to back sleeping.
Crying and sleep at 1 to 2 monthsWhat the AAP and studies report
Peak of fussingUsually about 3 hours a day by 6 weeks
Usual time of dayBetween 6 p.m. and midnight
When it easesDown to 1 or 2 hours a day by 3 to 4 months; colicky crying can last until 6 months
Total sleep, 0 to 2 monthsAverage 14.6 hours; normal spread about 9 to 20 hours (review of observational studies)
Official hours targetNone under 4 months (AASM)
What parents find hardest
The evening witching hours. Cluster feeding and crying from late afternoon are typical. A dim room, low noise and a calm adult help more than changing tactics every few minutes.
Catnaps that last one cycle. Short daytime sleeps are expected at this age. They are not a sign you are doing something wrong.
Waking when put down. Many babies startle on the transfer. Laying your baby down feet first and keeping a hand on the chest for a moment is a common trick worth trying; it is a rule of thumb, not a study finding.
Sleep debt in parents. Trade shifts if you can. Protecting one adult’s 4 to 5 hour block is a practical rule of thumb many families use.
Safe sleep matters most right now
The NICHD Safe to Sleep campaign reports that most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months of age, and that 72% occur in months 1 to 4. Everything below applies to every nap and every night.
Back to sleep, on a firm, flat surface, with nothing in the sleep space. The AAP says the side is just as risky as the stomach.
Room-share without bed-sharing. Never sleep with your baby on a sofa or armchair.
Pacifiers reduce SIDS risk even if they fall out after your baby is asleep. If you breastfeed, the AAP suggests waiting until breastfeeding is established.
If you swaddle, stop as soon as your baby shows any sign of trying to roll. The AAP notes some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months.
Night feeds
Feeding on cue at night is still normal at this age. How often to feed, and whether a longer stretch is fine, is your pediatrician’s decision based on growth. Do not stretch or drop feeds on your own.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Any rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher: the AAP says call immediately for babies 3 months or younger.
Crying that changes in sound, comes with vomiting, fever or poor feeding, or feels like pain. The AAP advises checking with your pediatrician first to rule out a medical cause.
Noisy, laboured breathing in sleep, or pauses longer than 20 seconds (call 911).
You feel depressed or close to the edge. Tell your doctor; it is common and treatable.
Foundations now, plan later
Foundations can start now: a predictable wind-down, a dark room for the longest sleep, and safe sleep every time. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage, with night feeds left in place. The 14-day guarantee clock starts at your baby’s 10-week birthday: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Parents describe their experience on our reviews page. See also the newborn rhythm guide and pacifiers and sleep.
Frequently asked
Why is my 1 month old so fussy in the evening?Evening fussiness is common. The AAP says it tends to happen between 6 p.m. and midnight and that fussing usually peaks at about 3 hours a day by 6 weeks before easing by 3 to 4 months. Check with your pediatrician first to rule out a medical cause.
Should my 1 month old be sleeping through the night?No. There is no official sleep target before 4 months, and the AAP says regular sleep cycles do not appear until about 4 months. Short stretches and night feeds are normal now. Your pediatrician decides how often your baby should feed.
Is SIDS risk highest at 1 month?The risk window is now. The NICHD Safe to Sleep campaign reports most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, with 72% in months 1 to 4. Back sleeping, an empty flat surface and room-sharing without bed-sharing all lower risk.
ReferencesCDC. Milestones by 2 Months.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). A Parent's Guide to Safe Sleep.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Colic Relief Tips for Parents.Galland BC, Taylor BJ, Elder DE, Herbison P. # Sleep at 2 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-2-months/

Sleep at 2 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
At 2 months, many babies begin to show one slightly longer stretch, but sleep is still irregular and night feeds are normal. There is no AASM sleep target until 4 months. The big safety change is rolling: the AAP says some babies start working on it as early as 2 months, and swaddling must stop at the first sign.
What is changing at 2 months
By 2 months, the CDC lists milestones such as holding the head up during tummy time, moving both arms and legs, making sounds other than crying, and smiling back at you. More control and more awareness mean your baby is now easier to engage and easier to overstimulate.
Studies show a longest stretch that varies enormously. A review of observational studies found the longest sleep period in babies 0 to 5 months averaged 5.7 hours, with a normal spread from about 2 to nearly 10 hours. Some 2 month olds give you a 5 hour block. Many do not yet. Both are normal.
At 0 to 5 monthsAverage in studiesNormal spread
Longest single sleep stretch5.7 hoursAbout 1.8 to 9.6 hours
Daytime sleeps per day3.1About 1 to 5
Night wakings, 0 to 2 months1.70 to about 3
Those figures come from parent reports pooled across many studies, so treat them as a picture of normal variety, not targets. Daytime sleeps are a common pattern, not a rule.
What parents find hardest
The swaddle question. Many babies still settle best swaddled just as they start to wriggle onto their side. Watch closely for rolling attempts.
Relying on motion. Swings and car rides work, but the AAP says sitting devices are not recommended for routine sleep, especially under 4 months.
Late, unpredictable bedtimes. Bedtime often drifts late because the body clock is still forming. An earlier bedtime usually becomes possible over the next couple of months.
Short naps. One sleep cycle and awake is common. Some babies resettle if you give them a minute.
Safe sleep at 2 months
Stop swaddling as soon as your baby shows any sign of trying to roll. The AAP says rolling usually happens around 3 to 4 months, but some babies start working on it as early as 2 months. A swaddled baby who rolls to the stomach cannot push up.
No weighted swaddles, weighted sleep sacks or weighted objects. The AAP says they are not safe.
Back to sleep for every sleep, on a firm, flat surface. Keep room-sharing without bed-sharing.
Most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, according to the NICHD. You are in the middle of that window.
Night feeds
Night feeds are expected. Whether your baby can go longer between feeds is your pediatrician’s call at the 2-month visit, based on growth. Use that visit to ask directly.
When to talk to the pediatrician
A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher: call immediately at this age.
Your baby does not yet smile back, react to loud sounds, or lift the head during tummy time. These are on the CDC’s 2-month list; raise any concern early.
Crying that is getting worse instead of better, or comes with poor feeding or vomiting.
Frequent snoring or breathing that sounds like a struggle during sleep.
Getting ready for the next stage
Foundations can start now: a short wind-down, a dark room, and one calm put-down a day when your baby is drowsy rather than fully asleep. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage. Night feeds stay in place, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at the 10-week birthday, which is just around the corner: We guarantee that your baby will sleep 8–12 hours through the night within 14 days of consistent, correct implementation of your sleep plan. Families share their results on our reviews page. Related: the 2-month schedule guide, dropping the swaddle, and the best age to sleep train.
Frequently asked
When should I stop swaddling my 2 month old?As soon as your baby shows any sign of trying to roll over. The AAP says some babies start working on rolling as early as 2 months. Until then, swaddle only for back sleeping, keep the hips loose, and never use a weighted swaddle.
How long should a 2 month old sleep at night?There is no official target before 4 months. In a review of studies, the longest stretch for babies 0 to 5 months averaged 5.7 hours, ranging from under 2 to nearly 10 hours. A shorter stretch at 2 months is common and not a problem in itself.
Can I start sleep training at 2 months?Not formal sleep training, and nothing that cuts feeds. Foundations are appropriate: a repeatable wind-down, a dark room, and some drowsy put-downs. Talk to your pediatrician about feeding before changing anything at night.

# Sleep at 3 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-3-months/

Sleep at 3 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 3 months, crying usually starts to ease and nights may get a little more organized, but there is still no AASM sleep target until 4 months. The main changes are physical: rolling usually arrives around 3 to 4 months, so the swaddle has to go at the first sign, and the bassinet will soon be outgrown.
What is changing at 3 months
Colic is on its way out for most families. The AAP says colicky fussing declines to 1 or 2 hours a day by 3 to 4 months and generally stops by then, though it can last until 6 months.
Your baby is getting stronger. By 4 months, the CDC lists pushing up onto elbows or forearms during tummy time, holding the head steady, and bringing hands to mouth. Hands to mouth is a real self-settling tool, and many babies begin sucking fingers in the crib now.
The body clock is maturing. The AAP says regular sleep cycles appear at about 4 months, so the next few weeks are a period of change rather than a settled state.
Change at 3 monthsWhat to doSource
Rolling attempts (usually around 3 to 4 months)Stop swaddling at the first sign; use arms-free sleepwearAAP
Pushing up on hands and kneesStop using the bassinet; CPSC says bassinets are not meant for use beyond about 5 months or once a baby can do thisCPSC
Pushing up on hands and knees, or 5 monthsRemove hanging crib toys and mobiles, whichever comes firstAAP
Total sleep in studies, from 3 monthsAverage 13.6 hours; normal spread about 9 to 18 hoursGalland 2012
What parents find hardest
Leaving the swaddle. Expect a few rougher nights while your baby learns to sleep with free arms. Many families try one arm out first; that is a common approach rather than a studied one.
Naps that stay short. One cycle and awake is still common. Daytime sleeps averaged about 3 a day in studies of babies 0 to 5 months, with a lot of variation.
Expecting the newborn tricks to keep working. Bouncing and rocking may stop working as your baby becomes more alert. A darker room and fewer moving parts often help.
Safe sleep at 3 months
Back to sleep for every sleep. Rolling is about to make positioning harder; the rule does not change until your baby can roll both ways.
No weighted products, no inclined surfaces over 10 degrees, no bumpers.
Keep room-sharing, ideally for at least the first 6 months, per the AAP. Bed-sharing risk is highest under 4 months.
Most SIDS deaths happen between 1 and 4 months, according to the NICHD. Do not relax the basics yet.
Night feeds
Some babies naturally space out night feeds now; others do not. Either way, how many night feeds your baby needs is your pediatrician’s call, not a calendar’s.
When to talk to the pediatrician
A rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in a baby 3 months or younger: call immediately.
Crying that is increasing rather than settling, or continues past what you were told to expect.
Frequent snoring, struggling to breathe, or breathing pauses longer than 20 seconds (call 911).
Not yet bringing hands to mouth or lifting the head and chest on the tummy as 4 months approaches.
Next steps
This is a good age to build the habit of a short, identical wind-down and to practise putting your baby down drowsy. Actually Sleeping works with families from the newborn stage, and the 14-day guarantee clock starts at the 10-week birthday, which your baby has now passed. You can read what other families say on our reviews page. Related: how to drop the swaddle, the 3-month schedule, and how sleep cycles develop.
Frequently asked
Is it normal for my 3 month old to still cry in the evenings?Yes, though it should be easing. The AAP says colicky fussing usually falls to 1 or 2 hours a day by 3 to 4 months and can last until 6 months. If it is getting worse, or comes with poor feeding or fever, call your pediatrician.
When should my 3 month old move out of the bassinet?The CPSC says bassinets and cradles are not intended for use beyond about 5 months, or once a baby can push up on hands and knees, whichever comes first. Check your product’s own limits, which may be lower, and move to a crib in your room.
How much should a 3 month old sleep?The AASM sets no target before 4 months. In a review of studies, babies from 3 months averaged 13.6 hours in 24 hours, with a normal spread from about 9 to 18 hours. Look at how your baby feeds, grows and behaves, not just the hours.

# Sleep at 4 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-4-months/

Sleep at 4 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
From 4 months, the AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours of sleep per 24 hours, including naps, and the AAP supports that range. Sleep cycles become more adult-like around now, so many babies start waking more between cycles. Rolling is common, teething may begin, and the AAP suggests putting babies 4 months and older to bed drowsy.
What is changing at 4 months
The AAP says babies do not have regular sleep cycles until about 4 months. Once they do, there are more brief wake-ups between cycles. A baby who was rocked fully asleep may now need the same help several times a night. That is the change people call the 4-month regression; it is a developmental step that tends to stick.
By 4 months, the CDC lists pushing up onto elbows during tummy time, holding the head steady, bringing hands to mouth, chuckling, and moving or making sounds to keep your attention. Teething can also start: the AAP says it typically begins by about 4 to 7 months.
Measure at 4 monthsFigureSource
Recommended total sleep12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including napsAASM, supported by AAP
Average total in studies, from 3 months13.6 hoursGalland 2012
Daytime sleeps, 0 to 5 monthsAbout 3 on average, often 3 to 4Galland 2012
Night wakings, 3 to 6 months0.8 on average, 0 to 3 is within normalGalland 2012
The nap count is a common pattern, not a rule. Some 4 month olds take three long naps, others four or five short ones.
What parents find hardest
Frequent waking after months of better nights. Often a sleep-association problem appearing, not hunger. Ask the pediatrician before assuming either way.
Rolling in the crib. Babies roll onto their tummy and get annoyed, or practise rolling instead of sleeping.
Short naps. Naps of a single sleep cycle are very common at this age.
Distracted daytime feeds that shift calories into the night.
Safe sleep at 4 months
Still place your baby on the back for every sleep. The AAP says that once your baby rolls both ways, back to tummy and tummy to back, you do not need to keep turning them over, as long as the sleep space is empty.
No swaddle once rolling attempts begin. Arms-free sleep sacks only, and never weighted.
Keep room-sharing without bed-sharing, ideally for at least the first 6 months.
If you still use a bassinet, plan the move: the CPSC says they are not meant for use beyond about 5 months or once a baby can push up on hands and knees.
Night feeds
Some 4 month olds still need one or more night feeds and some do not. That decision belongs to your pediatrician, based on weight gain. The plan you choose should work around those feeds, not cut them.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Fever above 101°F (38.3°C). The AAP says teething does not cause a fever that high, so it needs a look.
Frequent snoring, laboured breathing, or daytime sleepiness that seems excessive.
Sudden frequent waking with fever, ear pulling, vomiting or poor feeding.
Not yet holding the head steady or pushing up on the forearms.
Where to go from here
This is the age when learning to fall asleep without being fed or rocked starts to pay off, and the AAP’s own advice for babies 4 months and older is to put them to bed drowsy and not rush in at every sound. Actually Sleeping writes plans for this stage that keep any pediatrician-approved night feeds in place. Real parent stories are on our reviews page. Related: the 4-month sleep change, the 4-month schedule, and the feed-to-sleep association.
Frequently asked
How many hours should a 4 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for babies 4 to 12 months, and the AAP supports that range. Healthy babies vary, so look at mood, feeding and growth along with the total.
Is the 4-month regression real?Something real does change. The AAP says regular sleep cycles appear around 4 months, which means more brief wakings between cycles. Babies who need feeding or rocking to fall asleep often need the same help each time they surface.
My 4 month old rolls onto their tummy in the crib. What do I do?Keep placing your baby on the back. The AAP says once your baby rolls comfortably both ways you do not need to keep turning them, provided there are no blankets, pillows, toys or bumpers in the crib. Make sure the swaddle is gone.
Is my 4 month old teething?Possibly. The AAP says teething typically starts by about 4 to 7 months. It can cause a slight rise in temperature, but not above 101°F (38.3°C). A higher fever is not from teething; call your pediatrician.

# Sleep at 5 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to the pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-5-months/

Sleep at 5 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to the pediatrician
At 5 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. This is mostly an equipment month: the CPSC says bassinets are not meant for use beyond about 5 months, the AAP says to remove mobiles by 5 months, and the crib mattress should be lowered before your baby can sit. Short naps and early waking are the common complaints.
What is changing at 5 months
Your baby is getting close to the CDC’s 6-month milestones: rolling from tummy to back, pushing up with straight arms, and leaning on the hands while sitting. More strength means more movement in the crib and more ways to get stuck awake.
Teething can be part of the picture. The AAP says teething typically starts by about 4 to 7 months and that timing varies a lot. Interest in the world also jumps, so feeds get distracted and short.
Equipment check at 5 monthsGuidanceSource
Bassinet or cradleNot intended for use beyond about 5 months, or once your baby can push up on hands and kneesCPSC
Mobile or hanging crib toysRemove at 5 months or when your baby gets up on hands and knees, whichever comes firstAAP
Crib mattressLower it before your baby can sit up aloneMedlinePlus, AAP
SwaddleGone once your baby shows signs of trying to rollAAP
Crib itselfSlats no more than 2 3/8 inches apart; crib made after June 2011AAP
What parents find hardest
Short naps. One sleep cycle and awake is common at this age. A darker room helps more often than parents expect.
Very early waking. Light, a too-late or too-early bedtime, and long daytime gaps can all drive early waking. Adjust one thing at a time.
The first night in the crib. A new space can bring a few unsettled nights. Keep the routine identical so only one thing changes.
Distracted daytime feeds. A quiet room for some feeds keeps calories in the day.
Safe sleep at 5 months
Back to sleep for every sleep until the first birthday, even if your baby then rolls.
Room-share in a crib or play yard next to your bed, ideally until at least 6 months. No sleeping together on a couch or armchair.
The crib stays empty: no bumpers, pillows, blankets or soft toys. Crib bumpers are banned products under federal law.
No weighted sleep sacks or weighted blankets.
Night feeds
Some 5 month olds still feed once or twice at night, some more. Whether that should change is your pediatrician’s decision. Starting solids is also their call; the AAP advises not before about 6 months.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Fever above 101°F (38.3°C): the AAP says this is not teething.
Snoring on most nights, gasping, or breathing pauses during sleep.
A sudden change in sleep alongside feeding refusal, vomiting or fewer wet diapers.
Not rolling or pushing up with straight arms as 6 months approaches.
Where to go from here
If nights have become a series of short wake-ups that need feeding or rocking, the cause is usually how your baby falls asleep, not a lack of sleep pressure. Actually Sleeping writes plans for this age around any feeds your pediatrician wants kept. Families talk about what changed for them on our reviews page. Related: short 30-minute naps, the 5-month schedule, and when a baby will not sleep in the crib.
Frequently asked
Should my 5 month old be out of the bassinet?Usually yes, or very soon. The CPSC says a bassinet or cradle is not intended for use beyond about 5 months, or once a baby can push up on hands and knees. Your product may have a lower limit; check the label. A crib in your room keeps room-sharing going.
How much sleep does a 5 month old need?The AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for babies 4 to 12 months, and the AAP supports that range. Healthy babies sit at different points in it.
When do I lower the crib mattress?Before your baby can sit up alone, according to MedlinePlus and the AAP. Then move it to the lowest setting before your baby can stand. Many families lower it as soon as rolling and pushing up start, to stay ahead of the milestone.

# Sleep at 6 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-6-months/

Sleep at 6 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 6 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. The AAP says it is normal for a 6 month old to wake briefly at night and go back to sleep within a few minutes. In studies, babies 6 to 11 months averaged about 2 daytime naps. Solids usually start around now, and room-sharing is recommended for at least the first 6 months.
What is changing at 6 months
By 6 months, the CDC lists rolling from tummy to back, leaning on the hands to support sitting, knowing familiar people, and laughing. Sitting and rolling give your baby new things to practise at 2 a.m.
Several things also wind down around now. The AAP says periodic breathing of infancy is generally outgrown by about 6 months, and colicky crying, which can last until 6 months, is usually over. Separation anxiety can begin in the second half of the first year, and the AAP notes that nightmares can start as young as 6 months.
At about 6 monthsFigureSource
Recommended total sleep12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including napsAASM
Average total in studies, from 6 months12.9 hours (spread about 9 to 17)Galland 2012
Daytime naps, 6 to 11 months2.2 on average (about 1 to 3.5)Galland 2012
Longest stretch, 6 to 24 months8.3 hours on average (about 3 to 14)Galland 2012
Room-sharingAt least the first 6 monthsAAP
Many 6 month olds take 3 naps and are heading toward 2. That is a common pattern, not a rule.
What parents find hardest
Waking every 2 hours. Brief waking is normal; needing a full rescue every time usually points to how your baby falls asleep at bedtime.
Sitting up in the crib and not knowing how to lie back down. Daytime practice helps.
The room-sharing decision. The AAP minimum is about to pass. Some families move the crib now, others later. Both are reasonable if the sleep space is safe.
New foods causing a few unsettled nights or changes in digestion.
Safe sleep at 6 months
Back to sleep until the first birthday. If your baby rolls both ways, you can leave them in the position they choose, with nothing else in the crib.
The NICHD reports more than 90% of SIDS deaths happen before 6 months, but it and the AAP both say safe sleep practices continue to age 1.
Lower the mattress before your baby can sit unassisted, and to the lowest setting before standing.
No bottle in bed. The AAP says putting a baby down with milk, formula or juice risks tooth decay; feed first, then put down.
Night feeds
Some healthy 6 month olds still take a night feed. Whether to keep it, reduce it or drop it is your pediatrician’s decision. If the pediatrician says feeds are no longer needed, change them gradually.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Frequent snoring, gasping, or loud or heavy breathing in sleep. The AAP lists snoring and sleep apnea among common childhood sleep problems.
Fever above 101°F (38.3°C), or waking with ear pulling and fever.
Not rolling, or not reaching for toys, by 6 months.
Any question about starting solids, which the AAP advises not before about 6 months.
Where to go from here
If your baby wakes often and needs you to get back to sleep, the most effective change is usually at bedtime. Actually Sleeping builds that change into a written plan with live support. Families describe it in their own words on our reviews page. Related: a 6 month old waking every 2 hours, the 6-month schedule, and night weaning, if your pediatrician agrees.
Frequently asked
Is it normal for a 6 month old to wake at night?Yes. The AAP says it is normal for a 6 month old to wake during the night and go back to sleep after a few minutes. Studies of babies 3 to 6 months recorded 0 to 3 wakings as within the normal range. Frequent wakings that each need a parent are worth addressing.
Should my 6 month old move to their own room?The AAP recommends room-sharing for at least the first 6 months. After that it is a family decision. Wherever your baby sleeps, keep them on the back on a firm, flat, empty surface until the first birthday.
How many naps should a 6 month old take?There is no rule. In a review of studies, babies 6 to 11 months averaged 2.2 daytime naps, with a normal spread from about 1 to 3.5. Many 6 month olds take 3 naps and move to 2 over the next couple of months.

# Sleep at 7 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-7-months/

Sleep at 7 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 7 months, the AASM range is still 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Night waking often creeps back: in studies, babies 7 to 11 months woke slightly more on average than babies 3 to 6 months. Sitting, early crawling and separation anxiety are common reasons. Many babies move from 3 naps to 2 around now, as a common pattern rather than a rule.
What is changing at 7 months
Your baby is working toward the CDC’s 9-month milestones: getting into a sitting position alone, sitting without support, and moving things from hand to hand. New motor skills tend to get practised in the crib.
The emotional side is shifting too. The AAP says separation anxiety can begin in the second half of the first year and can disrupt sleep for several months, with babies waking and crying anxiously for a parent.
A first tooth may also arrive. The AAP says teething typically starts by about 4 to 7 months and can cause a slight temperature rise, but not above 101°F (38.3°C). A higher fever is not teething.
Age band in studiesAverage night wakingsNormal spread
0 to 2 months1.70 to about 3.4
3 to 6 months0.80 to about 3.0
7 to 11 months1.10 to about 3.1
1 to 2 years0.70 to about 2.5
Source: a systematic review of observational studies (Galland 2012). The small rise at 7 to 11 months matches what many parents notice: a baby who had been sleeping longer starts waking again.
What parents find hardest
New night wakings. Often tied to new skills or separation anxiety. Keep your response calm and consistent so a two-week phase does not become a habit.
Sitting or rolling and getting stuck. Give plenty of floor time in the day to practise getting down.
Fighting the third nap. In studies, babies 6 to 11 months averaged about 2 naps a day. Many drop the late catnap around now; bedtime often needs to move earlier while that happens.
Early waking. Light leaks and a bedtime that is too late are frequent causes.
Safe sleep at 7 months
Back to sleep until the first birthday; if your baby rolls both ways, let them settle where they land, in an empty crib.
The mattress should already be lowered for sitting. Move it to the lowest setting before your baby can pull to stand.
Keep the crib away from windows, blind cords and anything climbable.
No pillows, blankets or soft toys yet. The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations run to age 1.
Night feeds
A 7 month old waking more is not automatically hungry, and is not automatically not hungry. Ask your pediatrician whether night feeds are still needed before you change anything.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Waking that comes with fever, ear pulling, vomiting, rash, or a cough that worsens lying down.
Snoring most nights or breathing that looks like hard work.
A fever above 101°F (38.3°C) blamed on teething: the AAP says teething does not cause that.
Your baby is not yet rolling or bearing weight on the hands while sitting.
Where to go from here
A clear, repeatable response to night waking helps more than any single trick. Actually Sleeping helps families set that response up in a written plan, and parents describe the process on our reviews page. Related: the 7-month schedule, nap transitions, and early morning waking.
Frequently asked
Why did my 7 month old start waking at night again?Common causes are new motor skills, separation anxiety, illness and a change in naps. Studies found slightly more night waking on average at 7 to 11 months than at 3 to 6 months. If there is fever or pain, see the pediatrician; otherwise, keep your response consistent.
Should my 7 month old be on 2 naps?Many are, but it is a common pattern rather than a rule. Babies 6 to 11 months averaged 2.2 daytime naps in a review of studies. If the third nap makes bedtime late or is refused most days, it may be time to drop it.
How much should a 7 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for babies 4 to 12 months, and the AAP supports this. Studies found an average of about 12.9 hours for babies from 6 months.

# Sleep at 8 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the doctor
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-8-months/

Sleep at 8 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to call the doctor
At 8 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Clinginess and bedtime protest are very common because stranger and separation anxiety are emerging; the AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months. SIDS becomes less common after 8 months, but safe sleep rules still apply until the first birthday.
What is changing at 8 months
Your baby now knows exactly who you are, and minds when you leave. The AAP describes stranger anxiety as one of the first emotional milestones and says separation anxiety starts around the same time, usually peaking between 10 and 18 months. By 9 months, the CDC lists being shy, clingy or fearful around strangers and reacting when you leave by looking, reaching or crying.
Physically, many babies are pulling toward sitting, crawling and the first attempts to stand. The AAP and MedlinePlus say the crib mattress should be at its lowest setting before your baby can stand.
Safe sleep after 8 monthsWhat changesWhat does not
SIDS riskNICHD: SIDS is less common after 8 monthsSafe sleep practices continue until the first birthday
PositionIf your baby rolls both ways, you need not reposition themAlways place on the back to start
MattressLowest setting before your baby can standFirm, flat, tight-fitting
Crib contentsNothing new yetNo pillows, blankets, bumpers or soft toys before age 1
Nightmares are possible too. The AAP says they can start as young as 6 months and tend to come in the second half of the night. A baby who wakes frightened and settles quickly once you arrive is behaving normally. Studies of babies 7 to 11 months recorded about one night waking on average, with up to about three still within the normal range.
What parents find hardest
Crying the moment you leave the room. The AAP notes children accept separation more easily when it is part of a predictable routine. A short, identical goodbye each night helps.
Waking and calling for a parent. The AAP says a child with separation anxiety may need reassurance several times, night after night. Keep visits brief and boring.
Practising crawling or standing in the crib. Floor time in the day takes the novelty out of it.
The 3-to-2 nap transition. Studies of babies 6 to 11 months found an average of about 2 naps a day; most 8 month olds are on two, as a common pattern.
Night feeds
Separation anxiety can look like hunger. A baby who wants you may also want to feed. Ask your pediatrician whether your baby still needs a night feed; if yes, keep it, and keep it calm and separate from falling asleep.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Waking with fever, ear pain, vomiting, or a cough that is worse lying down.
Regular snoring, mouth breathing or pauses in breathing at night.
Your baby does not seem to know familiar people, or does not respond to their name by 9 months.
Anxiety so intense that daytime life is very hard, or that does not ease at all over months.
Where to go from here
Separation anxiety is a reason to be warm and predictable at bedtime, not a reason to abandon a plan. Actually Sleeping often works with families at exactly this age, and other parents share their experience on our reviews page. Related: separation anxiety at bedtime, the 8 to 10 month sleep regression, and the 8-month schedule.
Frequently asked
Why does my 8 month old cry as soon as I leave the room at bedtime?This is usually separation anxiety, a normal stage. The AAP says it often begins in the second half of the first year and usually peaks between 10 and 18 months. A short, predictable goodbye and calm, brief returns work better than sneaking out.
Is SIDS still a risk at 8 months?Less so, but not zero. The NICHD says SIDS is less common after 8 months and that safe sleep practices should continue until the first birthday. Keep your baby on the back to start, on a firm, flat, empty surface.
When do I lower the crib mattress all the way?Before your baby can stand. MedlinePlus and the AAP say to have the mattress at its lowest position before your child learns to stand. At 8 months, many babies are close, so it is safer to do it now.

# Sleep at 9 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-9-months/

Sleep at 9 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 9 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and studies found an average of about 12.6 hours for babies from 9 months. Most babies take 2 naps as a common pattern. Bedtime protest is typical because babies now understand that you still exist when you leave, and the CDC lists clinginess with strangers as a 9-month milestone.
What is changing at 9 months
The CDC’s 9-month milestones explain a lot of what happens at bedtime. Each one has a sleep side.
CDC 9-month milestoneHow it can show up at night
Looks for objects when dropped out of sightYour baby knows you are just outside the door and calls for you
Reacts when you leave (looks, reaches for you, or cries)Protest at the moment you put them down
Is shy, clingy, or fearful around strangersHarder settling with a new sitter or at daycare
Gets to a sitting position by herself; sits without supportSitting up in the crib instead of lying down
Lifts arms up to be picked upA very clear request at 2 a.m.
None of these is a problem. They are signs of healthy development that happen to collide with sleep.
What is normal
In a review of observational studies, babies from 9 months averaged 12.6 hours of sleep per 24 hours, with a normal spread from about 9.4 to 15.8 hours. Babies 6 to 11 months averaged 2.2 naps a day. Two naps is a common pattern now, not a rule; some babies still take a short third nap on long days.
What parents find hardest
Bedtime protest. Keep the routine short and identical. A predictable routine is what the AAP says helps children accept separation.
Standing in the crib and not knowing how to get down. Practise bending and sitting in the day.
Daycare naps. New faces and noise can mean short naps at daycare and an overtired evening. An earlier bedtime on daycare days is a reasonable rule of thumb.
Early waking. Check light, noise and the length of the afternoon awake stretch.
Safe sleep at 9 months
Mattress at the lowest setting now; many 9 month olds can pull up.
Crib away from windows and cords. No pillows, blankets, bumpers or toys in the crib before age 1.
Back to sleep to start; if your baby rolls both ways, leave them in the position they choose.
No bottle in bed. The AAP links falling asleep with a bottle to tooth decay.
Night feeds
Whether a 9 month old needs a night feed is your pediatrician’s decision. If your pediatrician says feeds are no longer needed, reduce them gradually rather than stopping suddenly.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping or noisy breathing in sleep.
Night waking with fever, ear pain, vomiting or diarrhoea.
Your baby is not yet sitting without support, not babbling, or does not look when you call their name. These are on the CDC’s 9-month list.
Very loud, inconsolable screaming episodes early in the night. Usually harmless, but worth describing to the doctor if they recur.
Where to go from here
If bedtime has turned into an hour of protest, the fix is usually a shorter routine and one consistent response. Actually Sleeping can write that plan with you; parents talk about it on our reviews page. Related: the 9-month schedule, separation anxiety at bedtime, and daycare naps.
Frequently asked
How much should a 9 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for babies 4 to 12 months. In a review of studies, babies from 9 months averaged 12.6 hours, with a normal spread from about 9.4 to 15.8 hours.
Why does my 9 month old stand up in the crib and cry?Pulling up is new and exciting, and many babies cannot yet get down. Practise sitting down from standing during the day. Make sure the mattress is at the lowest setting, and use the same short response each time.
Is clinginess at 9 months normal?Yes. The CDC lists being shy, clingy or fearful around strangers, and reacting when you leave, as 9-month milestones. The AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months.

Normal sleep patterns in infants and children: a systematic review of observational studies. Sleep Med Rev. 2012;16(3):213–222.HealthyChildren.org (AAP).
