# Sleep at 10 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-10-months/

Sleep at 10 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 10 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Pulling up and cruising are the big sleep disruptors, and the AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months. Most babies still take 2 naps as a common pattern. The mattress must be at its lowest setting before your baby can stand.
What is changing at 10 months
By 12 months, the CDC lists pulling up to stand and walking while holding on to furniture. Many 10 month olds are already doing both, and the crib rail is the perfect thing to pull on. The AAP describes the window from 10 to 18 months as the usual peak of separation anxiety.
Language is coming too. By 12 months, the CDC lists understanding “no” and calling a parent “mama” or “dada”. Babies who can call you, will.
Standing in the cribWhat helps
Stands, then cries because they cannot get downPractise squatting and sitting from standing during the day, many times
Stands as soon as you lay them downLay them down once; avoid repeated lay-downs that turn into a game
Mattress heightLowest position before your baby learns to stand (AAP, MedlinePlus)
Climbing riskRail height checks start now; keep furniture and toys away from the crib edge
The tips in the first two rows are common practical advice, not study findings.
What is normal
In a review of studies, babies 7 to 11 months averaged 1.1 night wakings, with anything from 0 to about 3 within the normal range, and babies 6 to 11 months averaged about 2 naps a day. A temporary dip during a big motor leap is common. Total sleep holds steady: babies from 9 months averaged 12.6 hours per 24 hours in the same review.
What parents find hardest
Bedtime standing protests that stretch settling to an hour.
Short second naps or nap refusal. This is usually a phase. Most babies are not ready for one nap at 10 months.
Early waking as daylight and noise wake a lighter sleeper.
Illness. Colds and ear infections often start around daycare age and can reset sleep habits.
Safe sleep at 10 months
Lowest mattress position, crib away from windows and blind cords.
Still nothing in the crib: the AAP’s recommendations apply until the first birthday.
Place on the back to start. If your baby rolls or sits, there is no need to reposition.
Furniture near the crib should be anchored so it cannot tip.
Night feeds
If your pediatrician wants a night feed kept, keep it. If they say it is no longer needed, a gradual change is easier on everyone. Ask before you decide either way.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping, or restless sleep with heavy breathing.
Sudden waking with crying that suggests pain, especially with fever.
Your baby is not yet pulling up, or not babbling, as the first birthday approaches.
Recurring screaming episodes early in the night where your baby does not seem awake.
Where to go from here
Standing protests usually fade in one to two weeks with a consistent response, which is a practical observation rather than a study result. If yours have not, Actually Sleeping can help you set up a plan. Parents talk about how that went on our reviews page. Related: the 10-month schedule, the 8 to 10 month regression, and early waking.
Frequently asked
My 10 month old stands in the crib and will not lie down. What do I do?Practise getting down from standing during the day, lower the mattress fully, and use one calm response at night. Repeatedly laying your baby down can become a game. Most babies stop once getting down becomes easy.
Should my 10 month old drop to one nap?Usually not yet. A review of napping studies found the big drop in two-nap days happens at 12 to 18 months. Babies 6 to 11 months averaged about 2 naps a day. A few days of nap refusal is usually a phase.
Is separation anxiety worse at 10 months?It can be. The AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months and that it can disrupt sleep for several months. A predictable bedtime routine helps children accept the separation.

# Sleep at 11 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-11-months/

Sleep at 11 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to talk to your pediatrician
At 11 months, the AASM range is 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Most babies still take 2 naps: a large review found the big shift to one nap happens between 12 and 18 months. Nap refusal at this age is usually a phase. Keep the crib empty and your baby on the back to start until the first birthday.
What is changing at 11 months
Your baby is close to the CDC’s 1-year milestones: pulling up to stand, walking while holding furniture, waving bye-bye, understanding “no”, and playing games like pat-a-cake. That is a lot of new ability and a lot of new reasons to stay awake.
Separation anxiety is often near its peak; the AAP places the usual peak between 10 and 18 months.
Sleep need does not fall off a cliff at the birthday. A review of studies found babies from 9 months averaged 12.6 hours per 24 hours and babies from 12 months averaged 12.9 hours, so expect much the same total sleep for the next few months.
Two naps or oneMore likely a phaseMore likely real readiness
AgeUnder 12 months12 to 18 months, when most babies shift (review of studies)
PatternRefuses a nap for a few days, then takes it againRefuses the second nap most days for two weeks or more
MoodCranky by late afternoonCopes well until bedtime on one nap
NightsNight waking or early waking increasesNights stay steady
The age row comes from a systematic review of napping studies. The other rows are a rule of thumb many families find useful, not a study finding.
What parents find hardest
Nap strikes. Keep offering the second nap. Babies who drop to one nap too early often start waking at night or before 6 a.m.
Bedtime battles. More awareness, more protest. Shorter routines usually beat longer ones.
Illness. Each cold can bring a week of rough nights. Comfort your baby fully while sick, then return to the usual routine once they are well.
Dreading the first birthday change in daycare rooms, which often move to one nap at a set age.
Safe sleep at 11 months
The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations cover babies up to 1 year. Keep the crib empty and start every sleep on the back until then.
No bottle in bed: the AAP says milk, formula or juice in bed can cause tooth decay.
Mattress at the lowest setting. Check the rail height against your baby as they grow.
Keep the crib away from windows and blind cords, and anchor nearby furniture.
Night feeds
Ask your pediatrician at the 12-month check about night feeds and the move to whole milk; both are their call. Changes to night feeds should follow that advice, not a birthday.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness that seems excessive.
Night waking with fever, ear pulling, or crying that suggests pain.
Your baby is not yet pulling to stand, babbling, or using gestures like waving as 12 months approaches.
Night terrors or screaming episodes that keep happening.
Where to go from here
If short naps and early waking are feeding each other, a clear daily rhythm usually fixes both. Actually Sleeping can help set that up; families describe what changed on our reviews page. Related: nap transitions, the 10 to 11 month schedule, and getting sleep back after illness.
Frequently asked
Is my 11 month old ready for one nap?Probably not yet. A systematic review of napping studies found the big shift away from two naps a day happens between 12 and 18 months. A few days of nap refusal at 11 months is usually a phase. Keep offering two naps.
Can my 11 month old have a blanket in the crib?The AAP’s safe sleep recommendations apply until the first birthday and call for a crib with no blankets, pillows, bumpers or soft toys. Use a wearable blanket or sleep sack instead. Ask your pediatrician about changes after age 1.
How much sleep does an 11 month old need?The AASM recommends 12 to 16 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for babies 4 to 12 months. A review of studies found babies from 9 months averaged about 12.6 hours, with healthy babies on both sides of that.

# Sleep at 12 months: what’s normal at the first birthday and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-12-months/

Sleep at 12 months: what’s normal at the first birthday and when to get help
At the first birthday, the AASM range shifts from 12 to 16 hours for babies to 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours for 1 to 2 year olds, including naps. Most 1 year olds still take 2 naps; the move to one usually happens between 12 and 18 months. The AAP’s infant safe sleep recommendations cover the first year.
What changes at the first birthday
By 1 year, the CDC lists pulling up to stand, walking while holding furniture, waving bye-bye, calling a parent “mama” or “dada”, and looking for things you hide. First steps may be close. Separation anxiety is often strong; the AAP says it usually peaks between 10 and 18 months.
At the first birthdayBeforeAfter
AASM recommended sleep12 to 16 hours (4 to 12 months)11 to 14 hours (1 to 2 years)
Average total in studies12.6 hours (from 9 months)12.9 hours (from 12 months)
Daytime naps in studies2.2 on average (6 to 11 months)1.2 on average (1 to 2 years)
AAP infant safe sleep recommendationsApplyWritten for babies up to 1 year
Sources: AASM consensus statement; Galland 2012 review; AAP. The nap figures are averages across many children and show a gradual shift, not a switch on the birthday.
What is normal
Two naps is still the most common pattern at 12 months. A systematic review found a dramatic drop in two-nap days between 12 and 18 months, and fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping altogether before age 2. Among babies under 12 months who napped, naps averaged about 3.1 hours a day in total; for 1 to 2 year olds the average was 2.3 hours.
What parents find hardest
The 12-month nap wobble. Many babies refuse one nap for a week or two. Keep offering both; most settle back.
Walking practice. Standing and cruising in the crib continue.
Daycare moving to one nap before your child is ready. An earlier bedtime helps bridge the gap.
Milk changes. If your pediatrician moves your child from formula or changes feeds, expect some adjustment.
Safe sleep after the first birthday
The crib remains the safest place to sleep. Keep the mattress at its lowest setting.
The AAP advises not putting a child to bed with a bottle of milk, formula or juice, because of tooth decay. Feed first, brush teeth, then bed.
Move to a bed when your child is 35 inches (89 cm) tall or the rail is below about three-quarters of their height, per the AAP and MedlinePlus. Most 1 year olds are nowhere near.
Ask your pediatrician before adding a pillow or blanket.
Night feeds
Whether a 1 year old still needs anything at night is a question for the 12-month visit. Your pediatrician decides; a sleep plan works around that decision.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping, or pauses in breathing. The AAP lists sleep apnea signs as frequent snoring, problems breathing at night, daytime sleepiness, attention difficulty and behavior problems.
Waking with pain or fever.
Your child is not yet pulling to stand, using gestures, or saying any special name for a parent.
Where to go from here
If the year has ended with nights still broken, this is a very workable age to change it. Actually Sleeping coaches families through toddlerhood; you can see what parents say on our reviews page. Related: the 12-month regression, the 12-month schedule, and nap transitions.
Frequently asked
How much should a 1 year old sleep?The AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for children 1 to 2 years old, and the AAP supports it. Babies under 12 months fall in the 12 to 16 hour range, so the two ranges overlap at the first birthday.
Should my 1 year old be on one nap?Most are still on two. A review of napping studies found the big drop in two-nap days happens between 12 and 18 months. Move to one nap when your child consistently refuses the second for a couple of weeks and copes well without it.
Can my 1 year old have a pillow or blanket now?The AAP’s infant safe sleep recommendations are written for babies up to 1 year. There is no rush to add anything after that. A sleep sack keeps a toddler warm without loose bedding. Ask your pediatrician before you add a pillow.

# Sleep at 15 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-15-months/

Sleep at 15 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 15 months, the AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours of sleep per 24 hours, including naps. This is prime time for the 2-to-1 nap transition: a large review found two-nap days drop sharply between 12 and 18 months. First steps, new words and strong attachment to a comfort object are all typical, and all can show up at bedtime.
What is changing at 15 months
By 15 months, the CDC lists taking a few steps alone, trying to say one or two words besides “mama” or “dada”, pointing to ask for help, showing affection with hugs and kisses, and hugging a stuffed toy. Toddlers now have opinions, and bedtime is a natural place to express them. Separation anxiety is often still strong; the AAP says it usually peaks between 10 and 18 months.
Nap transition, 2 to 1What the research shows
When it usually happensA dramatic drop in two-nap days between 12 and 18 months (Staton 2020)
Naps per day, 1 to 2 years1.2 on average, spread about 0.4 to 2.1 (Galland 2012)
Total nap time, 1 to 2 yearsAbout 2.3 hours on average among children who nap (Staton 2020)
Stopping naps altogetherFewer than 2.5% stop before age 2 (Staton 2020)
As a rule of thumb rather than a research finding, most families find the one-nap switch goes more smoothly with a nap that starts around midday and an earlier bedtime for the first few weeks.
What parents find hardest
The in-between stage. Two naps make bedtime too late; one nap leaves your child melting down by 5 p.m. Many families alternate for a week or two.
Daycare on one nap, home on two. Mismatched schedules are common. Follow daycare’s pattern on weekends if your child copes.
Bedtime stalling. More words, more requests. The AAP lists stalling and resisting going to bed among the most common sleep problems in children.
Walking in the crib. New walkers often practise at night for a week or two.
Safe sleep at 15 months
The crib is still the safest bed. The AAP and MedlinePlus give 35 inches (89 cm) tall as the point to move out of a crib, or when the rail is below about three-quarters of your child’s height.
Keep the crib away from windows and the mattress at its lowest setting.
If your child gets attached to a comfort toy, ask your pediatrician about having it in the crib. A sleep sack remains a safe way to keep warm.
No bottle in bed; the AAP links it to tooth decay.
Night feeds
If your toddler still wakes for milk, ask your pediatrician whether that is needed for nutrition. They decide; you can then change the habit gently if they agree it is no longer needed.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring on most nights, breathing pauses, or noisy breathing with an open mouth.
Night waking that comes with fever, ear pain or crying that suggests pain.
Your child is not yet taking any steps, not trying any words, or not pointing to ask for things.
Where to go from here
A planned nap transition with a matching bedtime is the most common fix at this age. Actually Sleeping can build one for your child; parents share their stories on our reviews page. Related: nap transitions, daycare naps, and the 12 to 14 month schedule.
Frequently asked
When should my 15 month old switch to one nap?When your child consistently refuses or struggles with the second nap and copes well on one. A systematic review found the big drop in two-nap days happens between 12 and 18 months, so 15 months is a very common time.
How much sleep does a 15 month old need?The AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for children 1 to 2 years old, and the AAP supports this range. Studies found 1 to 2 year olds averaged about 12.6 hours.
Why does my 15 month old fight bedtime now?New words, new walking and stronger opinions all arrive at once. The AAP lists stalling and resisting going to bed among the most common childhood sleep problems. A short, predictable routine with clear limits usually helps within a couple of weeks.

# Sleep at 18 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-18-months/

Sleep at 18 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 18 months, the AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and most toddlers are on one nap. Climbing, separation worries and screen habits are the common sleep disruptors. The AAP says to avoid screens before 18 months, cap entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day from 18 months to age 5, and switch screens off an hour before bed.
What is changing at 18 months
By 18 months, the CDC lists walking without holding on, climbing on and off a couch or chair without help, trying to say three or more words, and moving away from you while checking you are still close. Climbing is the one that matters most at night.
The AAP says separation anxiety usually peaks between 10 and 18 months and fades during the last half of the second year. Many toddlers are right at the top of that curve now.
Screens and sleep from 18 monthsAAP guidance
Before 18 monthsAvoid TV and mobile apps
18 months to age 5Cap entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day
Before bedTurn off all screens at least 60 minutes before bedtime
BedroomKeep TVs, computers, tablets and phones out, especially at night
The AAP notes that screen viewing contributes to problems with sleep and attention. A calm hour without screens before bed is one of the simplest changes with real backing.
What is normal
In a review of studies, children 1 to 2 years averaged 12.6 hours of sleep per 24 hours, with a normal spread of about 10 to 15 hours, about 1 nap a day, and 0.7 night wakings on average. Total nap time among nappers averaged 2.3 hours. One nap is the common pattern now, not a rule. A few toddlers still need a second short nap on some days, and that is fine.
What parents find hardest
Bedtime refusal. “No” is a new and powerful word. Offer small choices (which pyjamas, which book) inside a fixed routine.
Climbing attempts. A sleep sack makes leg-over-the-rail harder, a practical tip rather than a studied one.
Night waking for a parent. Often separation-related. Short, calm, identical responses work best.
Early waking after the move to one nap. An earlier bedtime for a few weeks usually helps.
Safe sleep at 18 months
Move out of the crib when your child is 35 inches (89 cm) tall or the rail is below about three-quarters of their height (AAP, MedlinePlus), or once they can climb out (AAP).
If they climb out before you have a bed ready, the AAP suggests putting the crib mattress on the floor.
Anchor dressers and other furniture so they cannot tip; keep chairs away from windows.
Night feeds
If your toddler still wakes for milk, your pediatrician can tell you whether it is needed. The AAP advises against a bottle of milk or juice in bed because of tooth decay.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness and irritability that could point to sleep apnea.
Your child is not walking, has fewer than three words, or does not point to show you things.
Night terrors that keep happening.
Where to go from here
Most 18-month sleep trouble is a mix of new independence and old habits. Actually Sleeping helps families sort out which is which; parents describe that on our reviews page. Related: the 18-month regression, the 18-month schedule, and separation anxiety at bedtime.
Frequently asked
How much should an 18 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for children 1 to 2 years, and the AAP supports this. Studies found children this age averaged about 12.6 hours, with healthy children on both sides of that.
Does screen time affect my toddler’s sleep?The AAP says screen viewing contributes to sleep problems. It advises turning off all screens at least an hour before bed, keeping devices out of the bedroom, and capping entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day from 18 months to age 5.
My 18 month old is trying to climb out of the crib. What now?Lower the mattress fully and use a sleep sack. The AAP says the transition can happen once your toddler can climb out; if they do before you have a bed, put the crib mattress on the floor. Anchor furniture and clear the room.

# Sleep at 21 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-21-months/

Sleep at 21 months: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 21 months, the AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps. Most toddlers take one nap, and dropping it entirely is rare: a large review found fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2. Nap refusal, bedtime stalling and early waking are the usual complaints, and they are usually phases rather than signs your child has outgrown sleep.
What is changing at 21 months
Your toddler is heading toward the CDC’s 2-year milestones: running, kicking a ball, walking up a few stairs, saying two words together like “more milk”, and noticing when someone else is upset. Imagination and understanding are growing fast, which can bring new worries at bedtime.
The AAP says separation anxiety usually fades during the last half of the second year and around the second birthday, so many families see it easing now.
Nap strike or real readinessWhat the research says
Children who stop napping before age 2Fewer than 2.5% (Staton 2020)
Average naps per day, 1 to 2 years1.2 (Galland 2012)
Average nap time, 1 to 2 yearsAbout 2.3 hours among children who nap (Staton 2020)
Children who have stopped napping by age 3About one in three (Staton 2020)
So a 21 month old refusing the nap is almost always in a phase. Keep offering it at the same time in a dark room. Quiet time in the crib still counts as rest.
What is normal at night
Studies of children 1 to 2 years recorded an average of 0.7 night wakings, with up to about 2.5 within the normal range, and a longest stretch averaging 8.3 hours across 6 to 24 months. An occasional night waking at 21 months is ordinary. Several every night is worth addressing.
What parents find hardest
Nap refusal that lasts a week or two. Keep the nap; adjust its timing slightly later if your child is not tired.
Bedtime stalling. One more book, one more drink. Decide the limits before bedtime starts and state them once.
Early waking. Check light, check nap length, and avoid starting the day very early with milk and TV.
A new sibling or move. Big changes often show up at bedtime first. Keep the routine identical.
Safe sleep at 21 months
Keep the crib while it is safe. Move out at 35 inches (89 cm) tall, when the rail is below about three-quarters of your child’s height, or once your toddler can climb out (AAP, MedlinePlus).
Install operable window guards above the first floor and keep climbable furniture away from windows (AAP).
Anchor dressers and bookshelves.
Night feeds
Most toddlers this age do not need milk at night, but your pediatrician decides that for your child. If they agree it can go, change it gradually.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, mouth breathing, or pauses in breathing.
Daytime sleepiness, trouble paying attention or behavior problems that might be linked to poor sleep. The AAP lists these among sleep apnea signs.
Few words, not combining any words as 2 approaches, or loss of skills your child had.
Night terrors that keep happening.
Where to go from here
Holding steady through a nap strike is often all it takes. When it is not, Actually Sleeping can help you work out what is driving it; parents share results on our reviews page. Related: early morning waking, the 18-month to 2-year schedule, and false starts at bedtime.
Frequently asked
My 21 month old refuses the nap. Is the nap over?Very unlikely. A systematic review found fewer than 2.5% of children stop napping before age 2. Keep offering the nap at a steady time in a dark room for at least two weeks; most toddlers go back to napping.
How much should a 21 month old sleep?The AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for children 1 to 2 years old. The AAP supports this range. Total sleep matters more than the exact split between nap and night.
Why does my toddler wake so early?Common causes are morning light, a bedtime that is too early or too late, and a nap that is too long or too early. Reward a later start: keep the room dark and boring until your chosen wake-up time.

J Clin Sleep Med. 2016;12(6):785–786.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Healthy Sleep Habits: How Many Hours Does Your Child Need?CDC. Milestones by 2 Years.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Separation Anxiety & Sleeping Trouble in Young Children.HealthyChildren.org (AAP). Emotional and Social Development: 8 to 12 Months.Staton S, et al. # Sleep at 2 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-24-months/

Sleep at 2 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 2 years, the AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and nearly all 2 year olds still nap once a day. Bedtime stalling, the crib-to-bed question and early night terrors are common. The AAP says separation anxiety usually fades around the second birthday, and the time to leave the crib is at 35 inches tall or when your child can climb out.
What is changing at 2 years
By 2 years, the CDC lists running, kicking a ball, walking up a few stairs, saying at least two words together, and noticing when others are hurt or upset. Toddlers now understand more than they can say, which makes bedtime both more negotiable and more emotional.
Separation anxiety usually fades around the second birthday, according to the AAP. Night terrors, which the AAP says happen most often in toddlers and preschoolers, may start to appear.
Signs it is time to leave the cribGuidanceSource
HeightMove to a bed when your child is 35 inches (89 cm) tallAAP, MedlinePlus
Rail heightMove when the side rail is below about three-quarters of their height (roughly nipple level)AAP
ClimbingTransition once your toddler can climb outAAP
While waiting for a bedPut the crib mattress on the floorAAP
Room safetyAnchor furniture, gate the bedroom door and the top of the stairsAAP
If none of these apply, there is no medical reason to rush. Many families keep the crib until closer to 3, which is a common choice rather than a rule.
What is normal
In a review of studies, 2 to 3 year olds averaged 12.0 hours of sleep per 24 hours, with a normal spread of about 9.7 to 14.2 hours. Among those who napped, naps averaged about 1.9 hours at 2 to 3 years. Almost all children still nap at 2; by 3, about one in three have stopped.
What parents find hardest
Stalling. The AAP lists stalling and resisting going to bed among the most common sleep problems in children.
A new sibling or a new bed at the same time. Changing one thing at a time is a sensible rule of thumb.
Night terrors. Screaming early in the night without really waking. The AAP says to stay calm and keep your child safe; most are much shorter than the 45-minute maximum it describes.
Climbing out of the crib once and then doing it every night.
Screens creeping into the evening. The AAP advises turning off all screens at least 60 minutes before bed and capping entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day from 18 months to age 5.
Night feeds
Most 2 year olds do not need to eat overnight, but your pediatrician decides that for your child. The AAP advises against a bottle of milk or juice in bed because of tooth decay.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping, pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness and behavior changes that could signal sleep apnea.
Night terrors that keep happening, or any night event that looks like a seizure.
Fewer than two-word phrases, not running, or loss of skills your child had.
Where to go from here
A firm, short routine with one consistent response is still the backbone at 2. Actually Sleeping works with families until age 3, and you can hear from them on our reviews page. Related: the 2-year regression, the 2-year schedule, and when to move to a toddler bed.
Frequently asked
How much should a 2 year old sleep?The AASM recommends 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for children 1 to 2 years old, and the AAP supports it. In a review of studies, 2 to 3 year olds averaged about 12 hours.
When should my 2 year old move out of the crib?When your child reaches 35 inches (89 cm), when the rail is below about three-quarters of their height, or when they can climb out, per the AAP and MedlinePlus. If none applies, there is no need to rush.
Are night terrors normal at 2?They are common in toddlers and preschoolers, according to the AAP. They happen early in the night, the child does not fully wake, and most are short. Stay calm and keep your child safe. If they keep happening, talk with your pediatrician.

# Sleep at 2½ years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-30-months/

Sleep at 2½ years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
At 2½, the AASM range is still 11 to 14 hours per 24 hours, including naps, and most children still nap; about a third have stopped by age 3. Imagination is taking off, so fears, nightmares and night terrors become more common. Big-bed escapes are frequent, and the CDC lists turning doorknobs as a 30-month skill, so room safety matters.
What is changing at 2½
By 30 months, the CDC lists saying about 50 words, using things to pretend, following simple routines when told, and using the hands to twist things, like turning doorknobs or unscrewing lids. Pretend play means a richer inner world, and with it new fears of the dark, monsters and dreams.
The AAP says nightmares can begin as early as 6 months and peak between 3 and 12 years. Night terrors are most common in toddlers and preschoolers. It helps to know the difference.
NightmareNight terror
WhenSecond half of the night, when dreaming is most intenseEarly in the night, often before parents go to bed
Your childWakes, is scared, wants comfort, may remember itScreams or thrashes but is not really awake
How longCalms once comfortedCan last up to 45 minutes; most are much shorter
What to doGo quickly, comfort, then encourage sleepStay calm, keep your child safe, do not try to wake them
All rows come from the AAP’s HealthyChildren guidance.
What is normal
In a review of studies, 2 to 3 year olds averaged 12.0 hours per 24 hours. Among those who napped, naps averaged about 1.9 hours. About one in three children has stopped napping by age 3, so a 2½ year old who still naps is typical, and one who naps on some days is too. The AASM range for 1 to 2 year olds, 11 to 14 hours, still applies; its 3 to 5 year range of 10 to 13 hours starts at the third birthday.
What parents find hardest
Leaving the bed. Once in a big bed, many toddlers test it every night. A calm, boring, identical return works better than discussion.
Fears at bedtime. Take them seriously, keep the answer short, and avoid scary content before bed.
Naps that make bedtime late. Shortening the nap is often better than dropping it.
Toilet training adding night trips and new reasons to call out.
Safe sleep at 2½
A doorknob-turner can leave the room. The AAP suggests a safety gate across the bedroom door and one at the top of the stairs.
Anchor dressers and shelves; latch or tape drawers so they cannot be used as steps (AAP).
Keep beds away from windows and use window guards above the first floor (AAP).
Night feeds
Night milk is rarely needed now, but your pediatrician decides. Brush teeth after the last milk; the AAP warns against milk in bed because of tooth decay.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Snoring most nights, gasping or breathing pauses, or daytime sleepiness and behavior changes.
Night terrors that keep happening.
Fears that are severe, daily, and get in the way of daytime life.
Few words, no pretend play, or loss of skills.
Where to go from here
Most bedtime battles at 2½ come down to clear, repeated limits delivered calmly. Actually Sleeping helps families set those up; their experiences are on our reviews page. Related: when a toddler will not stay in bed, moving to a toddler bed, and bedtime fading.
Frequently asked
Is my 2½ year old having nightmares or night terrors?Nightmares happen later in the night; your child wakes scared and wants comfort. Night terrors happen early in the night; your child screams but is not really awake. The AAP says to comfort after nightmares and stay calm and keep your child safe during terrors.
Should my 2½ year old still nap?Most still do. A systematic review found about one in three children have stopped napping by age 3, and among nappers aged 2 to 3, naps averaged about 1.9 hours. A shorter nap is often better than none.
My toddler opens the bedroom door at night. Is that a safety issue?It can be. The CDC lists turning doorknobs as a 30-month skill. The AAP suggests a safety gate across the bedroom door and at the top of stairs, anchored furniture, and window guards above the first floor.

# Sleep at 3 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-at-36-months/

Sleep at 3 years: what’s normal, what’s hard, and when to get help
From age 3, the AASM recommends 10 to 13 hours of sleep per 24 hours, including naps. About a third of children have stopped napping by their third birthday, and most of the rest stop over the next two years. Bedtime negotiation, fears and early waking are common. Regular snoring is worth raising with your pediatrician because sleep apnea affects an estimated 2% of children.
What is changing at 3
By 3 years, the CDC lists holding a conversation with at least two back-and-forth exchanges, asking who, what, where and why questions, joining other children to play, and calming down within 10 minutes after you leave, such as at a childcare drop-off. Your child can now argue about bedtime fluently.
The AASM range drops at the third birthday: 10 to 13 hours for 3 to 5 year olds, compared with 11 to 14 hours for 1 to 2 year olds. In a review of studies, children aged 2 to 3 averaged 12.0 hours per 24 hours. Night terrors remain common at this age, according to the AAP, and usually happen early in the night.
Napping at 3 and afterWhat the research shows (Staton 2020)
Stopped napping by age 3About 33%
Stopped by age 3 to 4About 57%
Stopped by age 4 to 5About 80%
Average nap, ages 3 to 4, among nappersAbout 1.7 hours
If your 3 year old still naps and falls asleep at a reasonable bedtime, there is no reason to stop. If the nap pushes bedtime late night after night, shortening it or swapping it for quiet time are both reasonable.
What parents find hardest
Negotiating. Requests, questions and “one more” at bedtime. Write the routine down or draw it, and follow it the same way every night.
Coming out of the room. A calm, silent return each time is the usual approach.
Fears and nightmares. The AAP says nightmares peak between 3 and 12 years and happen in the second half of the night. Go quickly, comfort, and encourage sleep.
Dropping the nap. The in-between months, when some days need a nap and some do not, are often the hardest. An earlier bedtime on no-nap days helps.
Sleep and safety at 3
Keep the bedroom safe for a child who wanders: anchored furniture, a gate at the top of the stairs, window guards above the first floor (AAP).
Turn screens off at least an hour before bed and keep devices out of the bedroom (AAP).
Cap entertainment screen time at 1 hour a day through age 5 (AAP).
Night waking and milk
Most 3 year olds do not need to eat at night, but if your child still wakes for milk, check with your pediatrician before changing it. Brush teeth after the last milk of the day.
When to talk to the pediatrician
Frequent snoring, problems breathing at night, daytime sleepiness, trouble paying attention or behavior problems. The AAP lists these as signs of sleep apnea and estimates it affects about 2% of children.
Night terrors that keep happening.
Sleep that is very short, very restless, or suddenly worse alongside other changes.
Your child is hard to understand most of the time or is not joining in play with other children.
Where to go from here
At 3, sleep plans work through clear rules your child can understand and predict. Actually Sleeping works with families up to age 3; parents describe the experience on our reviews page. Related: a toddler who will not stay in bed, false starts at bedtime, and early waking.
Frequently asked
How much sleep does a 3 year old need?The AASM recommends 10 to 13 hours per 24 hours, including naps, for children 3 to 5 years old, and the AAP supports this range. Your child may sit anywhere in that range and be well rested.
Should my 3 year old still nap?Many do. A systematic review found about a third of children have stopped napping by age 3 and about 57% by age 3 to 4. If the nap does not push bedtime late, keep it. If it does, shorten it or swap it for quiet time.
Is snoring in a 3 year old a problem?Occasional snoring with a cold is common. Frequent snoring, breathing problems at night, daytime sleepiness, trouble paying attention or behavior problems are signs of sleep apnea, which the AAP estimates affects about 2% of children. Tell your pediatrician.

# How fast does sleep training work? What 129 families reported
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/how-fast-does-sleep-training-work-129-family-reviews/

How fast does sleep training work? What 129 families reported
In 129 client video reviews of Actually Sleeping, 115 parents said how many nights it took to see the change they describe. 45 of those 115 (39%) named the first night, 76 (66%) said within three nights, and 102 (89%) within a week. The median was 2 nights.
The numbers
Parent-reported time to the result they describeFamiliesShare of the 115 who gave a numberOn the first night4539%Within 3 nights7666%Within 7 nights10289%Within 14 nights10894%
14 of the 129 reviews did not state a number of nights and are left out of the percentages. A few families described a longer stretch, up to 45 nights; they are included.
By the child’s age at the start
AgeFamilies with a numberMedian nightsWithin 3 nightsWithin 7 nightsUnder 4 months15211 (73%)12 (80%)4–6 months24218 (75%)22 (92%)7–9 months262.517 (65%)24 (92%)10–12 months263.513 (50%)22 (85%)Over 12 months24117 (71%)22 (92%)
How to read this (and how not to)
It is not a study. These are families who hired one coaching service and then chose to record a video review. Families with slower or mixed results are less likely to record one, so the real spread is wider than this table.
Results are self-reported. “Night 1” means the parent said they saw the change on the first night. Parents described different changes: falling asleep without help, fewer wakings, or a full night.
There is no comparison group. The numbers say nothing about how these babies would have slept without coaching, or with a different approach.
Every family had 1:1 support. A custom plan, live help on the first night and daily check-ins. Timelines for families working alone may differ.
What published research says
An American Academy of Sleep Medicine task force reviewed 52 treatment studies of behavioral approaches to bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. 94% of the studies reported that the approaches worked, and more than 80% of treated children showed clinically significant improvement that was maintained for three to six months. That review is about behavioral approaches in general, not about any one company.
Where the data comes from
Each number is counted from the public video reviews at actuallysleeping.com/reviews, summarized on our reviews page. No names or identifying details are used here. Counted on November 9, 2026.
Frequently asked
How long does sleep training usually take?In 115 parent video reviews of Actually Sleeping that gave a number, the median was 2 nights and 89% reported the change within a week. These are self-selected reviews of a coached program, not a clinical study, so treat them as one service’s reported outcomes.
Does sleep training work on the first night?Sometimes. 45 of 115 parents (39%) in these reviews said they saw the change on night one. Many others needed several nights, and a few needed weeks. A hard second or third night is common and is not a sign that it has failed.
Is this data independent?No. It is published by Actually Sleeping and counted from its own clients’ public video reviews. Independently collected, purchase-verified reviews are on Feefo.
Does age change how fast it works?In this set the differences between age groups are small and the groups are too small to draw firm conclusions. The table shows each group’s count so you can judge that for yourself.
ReferencesBehavioral treatment of bedtime problems and night wakings in infants and young children. Sleep. 2006 (AASM review)Actually Sleeping client video reviews
